| 3 | GUID read via `vtbl[2]` matches the expected identifier | the vtable moved, or wrong object |
| 4 | effective `TieredCompilation` is off | an environment variable overrode the app; **the whole design depends on this** |
| 5 | the loaded `DarzasDominion.dll` fingerprint matches | wrong apphost, or a game patch |
| 6 | every target's IL hash found in the compilation stream within N seconds | a target was inlined, renamed-by-rebuild, or removed |
| 7 | each target's field offsets resolved to plausible values | layout changed |
| 8 | the bridge handshake succeeded (or was explicitly disabled) | relay not running; **not fatal** |

Check 6 is the subtle one. A method that the JIT never reports was either never called or was
inlined into its caller. The response is to fall back to a documented alternative target
([CLIENT-FINDINGS.md](CLIENT-FINDINGS.md) §9.3 already gives a fallback for each), and to **log
which target was missed** — because "the hook installed but three of four detours never fired" is
otherwise indistinguishable from "the dodge is bad".

---

## 10. What this design deliberately does not do

- **No IL rewriting.** The methods are flattened state machines from a decompiler; rewriting their
  IL to inject a call is a large, risky job for no gain over a native detour.
- **No hooking of `System.Private.CoreLib`.** It is ReadyToRun and tiering is off, so those methods
  are never JITted and a `compileMethod` hook cannot see them. Nothing in the design needs them.
- **No manual mapping / reflective loading.** It buys nothing here and costs the PE loader, TLS
  callbacks, exception-directory registration and a module list that disagrees with the runtime's.
- **No driver.** Everything runs in user mode at the user's own privilege level.
- **No modification of the game's files** in the recommended path (§3.2). If §3.1's proxy DLL is
  chosen, that is the one place this changes, and it should be an explicit decision.

```

`docs/hook/HOOK-BUILD-MATRIX.md`:

```md
# Hook build matrix — the verified build, and how to re-verify it

## What this file is

This is the human-readable half of [`hook/known-build.json`](../../hook/known-build.json). The JSON is the
authority: [`hook/tools/Fingerprint.ps1`](../../hook/tools/Fingerprint.ps1) reads it, compares the installed game
against every value it records, and exits non-zero on a mismatch, so nothing here overrides it. What
this document adds is the part a machine cannot carry — what each pinned value means, what breaks
when it changes, which of the numbers the gate actually compares and which are only recorded, which
of the counter-intuitive findings in this build were *measured* and must not be "cleaned up", and the
exact command sequence that re-establishes all of it after a game patch. It is Phase 0 deliverable 4
of [IMPLEMENTATION-PLAN.md](IMPLEMENTATION-PLAN.md), and the reason that phase exists is the
reason it deserves care: a hook with a wrong target fingerprint does not print a wrong log line, it
patches the wrong function in a live process.

## The verified build

Recorded **2026-10-07** from `E:\SteamLibrary\steamapps\common\Darza's Dominion`. Every value below is
quoted from `hook/known-build.json`; the last column names the check `Fingerprint.ps1` runs, or says that
the value is recorded rather than compared.

| pinned value | recorded as | what it is | if it changes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `game.version` | `5.8.2` | the client release every citation, RVA and field offset in this directory is relative to | record only — nothing compares it. A change does not fail the gate; it means every document here has to be re-read |
| `game.steamAppId` | `1895130` | the Steam product the recorded install came from | record only — a change means this is not the product the research was done against |
| `assembly.file` | `DarzasDominion.dll` | the assembly the four targets live in; the gate joins it to the game path | every path in the tooling stops resolving |
| `assembly.size` | `50216960` | the root apphost's assembly, in bytes. Two apphosts ship with **different** builds | fails `assembly size`; the size is also how the gate recognises the other apphost's file |
| `assembly.sha256` | `B34181534DAE0114970446985E40755F9559F15711DF9461167BABA1FD88CEF8` | content hash of that file | fails `assembly SHA-256`. This is the check that catches an edit which preserves length: the first version of the gate compared size only, and a one-byte flip passed every check |
| `assembly.sizeOpenGlVariant` | `50831360` | the `OpenGL\DarzasDominion.exe` apphost's own build of the same assembly | the gate reports `which apphost: OpenGL variant -- NOT the analysed build` and compares against the OpenGL pair instead |
| `assembly.sha256OpenGlVariant` | `8158393955A9D07E67B0BA04EDC326201C31025DBB327F02DA54B913ACCA984C` | content hash of the OpenGL build | as above. Only the root apphost's build has been analysed |
| `assembly.managedNativeHeaderRva` | `0` | COR20 `ManagedNativeHeader` RVA; 0 means the image has no ReadyToRun/native header | fails `assembly not ReadyToRun`. If the assembly ever ships ReadyToRun, a `compileMethod` hook stops seeing its methods and the hook design needs rework (HOOK-ARCHITECTURE §1 fact 1, §10) |
| `assembly.mustBeIlOnly` | `true` | the COR20 flags requirement, read as `ILONLY` set | fails `assembly ILONLY set`; without it the loader may run code the JIT hook never sees |
| `assembly.comImageFlags` | `0x00000001` | the recorded flag word itself (`COMIMAGE_FLAGS_ILONLY`) | record of the same fact as the row above; a different value has to be explained before anything is patched |
| `assembly.mvid` | `CBF722C0-56DB-027D-6115-AA7A24CE5307` | the module's identity, read by `il_index.py` from the `Module` table | **not** compared by the gate — it is one of the known gaps and must be re-checked in-process at attach (HOOK-ARCHITECTURE §9 check 5). A change means a different module image is loaded |
| `runtime.tfm` | `net9.0` | target framework in `DarzasDominion.runtimeconfig.json` | fails `target framework` |
| `runtime.version` | `9.0.20` | the .NET 9 servicing line | record only — the gate compares `coreclrBuild`, not this field |
| `runtime.coreclrBuild` | `9.0.2026.41315` | file version of `coreclr.dll` and `clrjit.dll` (the gate normalises `9,0,2026,41315 @Commit: …` to four numeric parts) | fails `coreclr.dll version` / `clrjit.dll version`; a runtime update can move the JIT interface, so §4.1's validation sequence has to be re-run before anything is installed |
| `runtime.tieredCompilation` | `false` | `System.Runtime.TieredCompilation` in the app's own `runtimeconfig.json` | fails `TieredCompilation off`. This is the single assumption the hook rests on: with tiering off each method is compiled once and a detour is permanent. If a patch flips it, either force `DOTNET_TieredCompilation=0` in the launcher environment or the approach is invalid (HOOK-ARCHITECTURE §1 fact 2, §9 check 4) |
| `jit.vtableCodeSlotCount` | `4` | how many leading slots of `g_CILJit`'s vtable point into the image | fails `JIT vtable code slots`; the count is how the gate proves it has the right object before writing anything |
| `jit.compileMethodSlot` | `0` | the slot the detour patches | reported as information. It has been slot 0 on every .NET version |
| `jit.getVersionIdentifierSlot` | `2` | the slot the hook reads a JIT/EE GUID from, to validate the object | **not** compared by the gate — the hook does it at install time. Slot 2 is right on .NET 5+; the widely copied implementations hardcode slot 4, which was correct only up to .NET Core 3.1 (HOOK-ARCHITECTURE §4.1, §9 check 3) |

The gate is read-only: it opens the game's files for reading and writes nothing except its report. It
exits **0** when every check passes, **1** on any mismatch (naming the component and the
expected/actual pair), and **2** when it cannot run at all. Two of the values above are deliberately
not script-checked — the MVID and the GUID slot — because both are properties of the *running*
process rather than of a file on disk.

## The six targets

Quoted from the `targetMethods` block. `ilHashVersion` is `1` for all six.

| role | declaring type | method | arity | metadata token | RVA | IL size | IL hash | citation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| frame tick | `DarzasDominion.Graphics.DarzaWindow` | `Update` | 1 | `0x06001FC5` | `0xD54A8` | 1286 | `CF8779CF0191990E9D6365940CC6A59EEBC990BB20E6428648BF99E69241629D` | `Graphics/DarzaWindow.cs:1727` |
| spawn | `DarzasDominion.Darza.Game.Objects.Projectile` | `ProcessProjectileData` | 16 | `0x06005214` | `0x3E4D9C` | 2014 | `8A7928BDA06EDE4F76FFE66E4C80978864E37654603D1CE3ADC83D79719DA55A` | `Objects/Projectile.cs:810` |
| collision | `DarzasDominion.Darza.Game.Objects.Projectile` | `HitCharacter` | 0 | `0x0600521F` | `0x3E64FC` | 989 | `D6F353B8CF67A24344899064EBC13D292095508E6C1C13F36A65081F0ED108B2` | `Objects/Projectile.cs:1514` |
| escape | `DarzasDominion.Darza.Game.World` | `RequestEscape` | 0 | `0x06002964` | `0x162E4C` | 335 | `6E3B9F4CD77B5E8AE6B060B85233B20B00E88F054DFFC4AB380C04458C030A2D` | `Game/World.cs:12984` |
| movement integrator | `DarzasDominion.Darza.Game.World` | `hehe\ueb2c\ue5a5\uee82\ue9c5\uef68` | 2 | `0x06002961` | `0x1621B8` | 2574 | `1E41504101BED2A28539A69A46C2384E4FB24956F04EBDD199A1ED4C72737028` | `Game/World.cs:12666` |
| aim target selection | `DarzasDominion.Darza.Game.AimbotSystem` | `FindTarget` | 2 | `0x06002837` | `0x14C9EC` | 1580 | `B8E646CD86A27DB5DA2B830B40AA85C0E5BD1BF4AB5B936CB2360BE8869C9124` | `Game/AimbotSystem.cs:179` |

The line in the IL dump that each target was found at is recorded as `ilDumpLine`: 500932 (frame
tick), 1978316 (spawn), 1981122 (collision), 780182 (escape), 778772 (movement integrator), 726472
(aim target selection).

### The movement target's name, and why it is written that way

**The name in that row is not the name the decompiler prints, and the two cannot be searched for each
other.** ilspycmd renders this method as `World.hehe_EB2C_E5A5_EE82_E9C5_EF68(float, float)`. The
metadata string heap holds a *different* string of nine private-use code points (`U+EB2C`, `U+E5A5`,
`U+EE82`, `U+E9C5`, `U+EF68` and the `hehe` prefix). A whole-file search of the 89 MB IL dump for
`EB2C_E5A5_EE82_E9C5_EF68` returns **zero hits** — so the natural move reports "this method is not in
this build" and is wrong.

Three consequences, all of them in the tooling:

- [`hook/tools/il_targets.py`](../../hook/tools/il_targets.py) lists candidates on a type **without** relying on
  the name: declaring type, parameter count, return and parameter types from the signature blob, IL
  size, and the IL dump's RVA line. It never writes the record — `il_index.py` stays the one
  authority — so target selection gained a tool without gaining a second source of truth.
- every build log prints obfuscated names escaped (`il_index.ascii_name`), because printing the raw
  string killed the tool with `UnicodeEncodeError: 'charmap' codec can't encode characters in
  position 58-62`. The console code page has no glyphs for private-use code points; nothing was wrong
  with the resolution.
- `il_index.py --check` now compares **`hook/known-build.json` against the generated table** and exits
  non-zero on a mismatch. `apply_to_record` used to name the four Phase 0 keys literally, so adding
  this target printed "5 targets" and wrote four — and the build script reads that record to build
  the hook's compiled table. A silent truncation with every line of output correct.

The row's `arity` is `2` and the signature is confirmed as `void (float, float)` from the metadata
itself, which is what distinguishes it from the three other arity-2 methods on `World` that also take
two `float`s; the IL dump's own body confirms the rest (code size 2574 = `0xa0e`, and locals
`Character`, `bool`, `float32`, `Angle`, `Vector3` matching `World.cs:12666`).

The five hashes are **distinct**, and `il_index.py` refuses a table in which two targets share one —
identical hashes would mean the matching is broken.

**The IL hash is the identity. The metadata token, the RVA and the dump line are diagnostics.** Three
reasons, all of them recorded in HOOK-ARCHITECTURE §4.3 and in `il_index.py`:

- the assembly is obfuscated, so **names are not an identity**. `declaringType` + `name` + `arity` is
  a *locator* — `il_index.py` uses it to find the one `MethodDef` row and fails if it is not unique —
  not a guarantee;
- **tokens move when metadata changes.** Adding or removing a method renumbers `MethodDef` rows, so a
  token can match while pointing at something else entirely;
- the **hash is over the exact bytes `CORINFO_METHOD_INFO` hands the JIT** (`ILCode[0 ..
  ILCodeSize)`), which is what the hook actually has in hand when `compileMethod` is called. Matching
  on it is name-independent, token-independent, and build-specific in the way that matters: if a
  method's IL changes, the hash stops matching and the hook refuses to install instead of patching
  the wrong function.

Two further properties of the table are load-bearing. The five hashes are **distinct**, and
`il_index.py` refuses a table in which two targets share one — identical hashes would mean the
matching is broken. And the record's `role` and `citation` fields, together with the `signatureHint`
and one-line `why` carried in `il_index.py`'s `TARGETS` list, are the human anchors of *intent*: the
frame tick is "once per frame, after `Client.DrainColdQueue`, before `UpdateScene`"; spawn is "the
complete threat event, delivered as arguments (no field reads)"; collision is "the local collision
decision — the instant the server is about to be told"; escape is "the client's own nexus entry
point — runs the client's own gates"; and the movement integrator is "the input→position step: it
reads `GameScene.GameInput` and commits `Player.Position`, so a replacement on it can both steer and
measure". That is what a reviewer checks after a patch (see below), not the hashes.

## The hash recipe

Quoted from `targetMethods._recipe` in `hook/known-build.json`; the identical string is `IL_HASH_RECIPE`
in [`hook/tools/il_index.py`](../../hook/tools/il_index.py):

> sha256 of MethodDef.Rva's exact IL instruction bytes: ILCode[0 .. ILCodeSize), little-endian as
> stored. No header, no .locals, no exception-handler sections, and no re-encoding of any kind -- the
> hash is over the bytes as they sit in the image, which are the same bytes CORINFO_METHOD_INFO hands
> the JIT.

Hashing the **raw** bytes rather than a re-encoded or normalised instruction stream is what lets the
two sides agree without either of them owning an IL decoder: the native side hashes the loader's copy
of exactly these bytes, and `il_index.py` hashes the same bytes out of the image, so neither can
disagree with the other about operand widths. That is the whole point of the choice. If the identity
depended on `il_index.py`'s interpretation of the opcodes, a bug in one operand-width table entry
would silently change the identity of a target: the table would regenerate with a different hash,
every file-level check would still pass, and nothing would look wrong. (An earlier draft did
normalise short opcodes to their long forms to survive a re-encoding. It was dropped: the CLI does not
re-encode IL the loader validated, and a patch that genuinely rewrote a method's encoding is exactly
the event this gate exists to catch.)

`ilHashVersion` must match on both sides. `il_index.py` carries `IL_HASH_VERSION` and says of it that
"the native side carries the same constant and refuses to compare a hash across versions" — the
native side must *refuse*, not merely prefer, because a v1 hash and a v2 hash of the same method are
different numbers and comparing them can only produce a false mismatch or a false match. Changing the
recipe means bumping the constant and regenerating the table; a table regenerated under a new version
is a recipe change, not a changed build, and must not be read as one.

## Re-verifying after a game patch

Run these in order. Steps 1–5 re-verify the build that is installed; steps 6–8 are the ones that
apply when the game legitimately updated.

1. **The static gate, first.**
   ```powershell
   .\hook\tools\Fingerprint.ps1
   ```
   Exit 0 is the only acceptable result before installing anything. A failure prints
   `FINGERPRINT FAILED -- N of M checks failed` and names each component with its expected and actual
   value; exit 2 means it could not run (install missing, record unreadable). Pass
   `-GamePath "D:\Games\Darza's Dominion"` if the install moved.

2. **Check which apphost the run is looking at.** If the file's size matched
   `sizeOpenGlVariant`, the gate says so — `which apphost: OpenGL variant -- NOT the analysed build`
   — and compares against the OpenGL pair instead. Only the root apphost's build has been analysed;
   a green OpenGL run is green about the wrong file.

3. **Re-derive the target table without writing it.**
   ```powershell
   python .\hook\tools\il_index.py --check
   ```
   This re-reads the PE's CLI metadata directly (no `ilspycmd`, no `dotnet`, no network), re-hashes
   each target's IL bytes, cross-checks every target against `hook/il/client-5.8.2.il` on RVA, code size
   and parameter count, and exits 1 with `TARGET TABLE NOT TRUSTWORTHY` followed by one line per
   problem. `--check` writes nothing. The tool also has a `--self-test` mode, which checks the reader
   against signatures the documents state independently of the metadata (all four targets' arities
   among them) and reads neither `hook/known-build.json` nor the IL dump.

4. **Prove the method-level gate can still fail.**
   ```powershell
   python .\hook\tools\il_index.py --mutation-test
   ```
   It copies the assembly to a temporary directory, flips one byte in the middle of `collision`'s
   instruction stream (not its header), and requires exactly that target's hash to move while the
   file size is unchanged. `MUTATION TEST PASSED` is the evidence; anything else means the gate is
   broken, not that the build is fine.

5. **Prove the file-level gate can still fail.**
   ```powershell
   powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\hook\tools\Test-FingerprintGate.ps1
   ```
   This copies the assembly, its `runtimeconfig.json` and the two runtime DLLs into a sandbox, flips
   one byte inside `collision`'s IL with the file length preserved, runs `Fingerprint.ps1 -GamePath
   <sandbox>` and requires a non-zero exit. It is the test that closed the hole the first mutation
   test found, where a same-size edit passed a size-only check.

6. **If the game legitimately updated, regenerate the record** — without `--check`:
   ```powershell
   python .\hook\tools\il_index.py
   ```
   On success this rewrites the `targetMethods` block and prints `hook/known-build.json updated:
   targetMethods + assembly.mvid` (it writes `assembly.mvid` when the record does not have one yet).
   Two cautions:
   - it **refuses to write while any problem is outstanding**, and a changed assembly SHA-256 is a
     problem, so the new file identity has to be recorded first (`assembly.size` and
     `assembly.sha256`, and the OpenGL pair if that apphost changed too). `hook/known-build.json` says of
     itself: "Regenerate after every game or update, and record what changed."
   - do not hand-edit the `targetMethods` values; the block says so itself.

7. **The reviewer's job is intent, not hashes.** Accepting the new hashes is not verification. For
   each of the four targets, confirm that the method with that name and arity in that declaring type
   is still **the same hook point**: the frame tick is still the per-frame `Update` that runs after
   `Client.DrainColdQueue` and before `UpdateScene`; spawn is still the 16-argument projectile-spawn
   payload that carries the whole threat event as arguments; collision is still the local collision
   decision that precedes the claim to the server; escape is still the client's own nexus entry
   point. `il_index.py`'s `TARGETS` list carries the `why` and `signatureHint` for exactly this
   reading. A name-and-arity match whose `why` no longer describes the method is a **changed hook
   point**, not a regenerated hash. Tokens and RVAs moving between builds is expected and harmless; a
   role moving is not.

8. **Close the loop.** Re-run the gate and both mutation tests against the regenerated record, and
   confirm `ilHashVersion` is still `1` on both sides.

## What the gate cannot check

These are recorded by `Fingerprint.ps1` itself as known gaps — the run ends with `FINGERPRINT OK --
N checks passed, M known gap(s)` — and a gap is not a pass.

| gap | why, and what answers it |
|---|---|
| **the effective runtime environment** | the gate's own line is `effective runtime environment: cannot be read from a script (check DOTNET_TieredCompilation is unset in the launcher)`. In .NET 9 an environment variable overrides `runtimeconfig.json`, so a stray `DOTNET_TieredCompilation=1` inherited from a launcher defeats the whole design while the file still says `false`. HOOK-ARCHITECTURE §1 records the hazard; §9 check 4 reads the *effective* value in-process and refuses to install if tiering is on |
| **the loaded assembly's MVID** | `the loaded assembly MVID: must be re-checked in-process at attach`. The gate hashes a file on disk; it cannot see which module the running process loaded (HOOK-ARCHITECTURE §9 check 5) |
| **which of the two shipped apphosts is running** | the gate resolves one path and, when the size matches, reports *which file* it read as information. Which apphost is actually running is a property of the process, not of a directory, which is the second reason the assembly fingerprint is re-checked at attach |
| **whether a target has been inlined into its caller** | a method the JIT never reports was either never called or inlined into its caller, and only the JIT compilation stream can tell those apart: HOOK-ARCHITECTURE §9 check 6 requires every target's IL hash to appear in the compilation stream within N seconds and logs which target was missed. No static check of the file can answer it |
| **the target-method IL hashes, when the tooling is unavailable** | if `python` or `il_index.py` is missing, the gate records a gap rather than a pass: the recorded hashes are then checked physically from the file but not re-derived from the metadata. IMPLEMENTATION-PLAN's Phase 0 lists the same set of gaps, and requires the last two to be re-checked in-process at attach (HOOK-ARCHITECTURE §9) |

## Build-specific findings that a maintainer must not "fix"

Each of these was established by measurement, each contradicts either the documentation or the naive
expectation, and each is "obviously wrong" enough that a future reader will want to correct it. All
of them live in [`hook/tools/il_index.py`](../../hook/tools/il_index.py).

### `MoreSects` second size field is not trustworthy in this build

**Finding.** A fat method header with the `MoreSects` flag is documented to carry a second size field
at +12 that covers the header *and* the extra data sections, and the documented rule is to use it.
**This build disagrees.** For `DarzaWindow::Update` the `FlagsAndSize` field declares a 12-byte
header (3 dwords) and the code really is at +12, while the +12 field says 60 — and the 48 bytes it
would skip decode as a plausible but wrong instruction stream, which is exactly the trap: a wrong
offset does not crash, it yields a wrong hash. Across the **1,941 fat+`MoreSects` methods in this
assembly, +12 decodes cleanly 1,202 times against +60's 742, and 739 decode either way**, so the
field cannot be trusted on its own.

**Evidence.** The `MoreSects` note in `method_body()`, which carries those counts; and the
independent witness in `hook/il/client-5.8.2.il`, which records `Header size: 12` and `IL_0000: call void
DarzasDominion.Graphics.DynamicFont::WarmAtlasStep()` for that method (dump line 500932ff), i.e. the
code begins 12 bytes in, not 60.

**Instruction: leave it alone.** `method_body()` resolves the offset by evidence instead of by rule:
when the declared header and the documented alternative disagree, it takes whichever candidate produces
a stream that decodes exactly to `CodeSize`, preferring the **declared** header when both do; a method
that decodes under neither is handed to the caller to be reported rather than guessed at. The
preference is not arbitrary — the declared size is the standard fat-header layout (the header ends
where `CodeSize` ends), and the +12 field is the one that disagrees with it. This is a
**hash-correctness** issue, not cosmetics: the wrong candidate hashes the same number of bytes from the
wrong start, so the digest belongs to no method at all under the right target's name, and every
size-based check still passes. Restoring the documented rule, or hardcoding `+12` because "it works
here", removes the only thing that notices when it does not.

### The metadata table layouts are not the documented ones

**Finding.** `il_index.py` walks the CLI metadata tables itself, and this assembly's row layouts are not
the ones a reader that follows the obvious rules arrives at. What actually had to be fixed, from
`SCHEMAS` and the reader's width rules:

| table | row size | what the reader walks | why the naive reading is wrong |
|---|---|---|---|
| `MethodDef` | **18** | `Rva` **4** + `ImplFlags` 2 + `Flags` 2 + `Name` 4 + `Signature` 4 + `ParamList` 2 | every column is the standard one. The original reader had `Rva` at 2 bytes, which makes the row 16 and puts every subsequent `Name`, `Signature` and `ParamList` two bytes early. The columns that then land on `Name` still resolve to *plausible* strings for most rows, so the misparse was invisible from the table itself and showed up only as a downstream symptom |
| `TypeDef` | **18** | `Flags` 4 + `TypeName` 4 + `TypeNamespace` 4 + `Extends` 2 + `FieldList` 2 + `MethodList` 2 | standard; listed because it is the other table the reader is anchored on |
| `Field` | **10** | `Flags` 2 + `Name` 4 + `Signature` 4 | standard |
| `Param` | **10** | `Flags` 2 + `Sequence` 2 + `Name` 4, **plus one further 2-byte column** | `SCHEMAS["Param"] = [None, None, STR, None]`. This is the one layout here that is a **measurement rather than a reading**: nothing in the code states it, and the documented 8-byte shape is what the reader first used |
| `Assembly`, and the tail of the stream | not byte-exact | `Assembly` does not parse under the documented columns at all, and the tables after `MethodDef` are not byte-exact under the documented layouts | this is why `Assembly.Name` is unreadable (next subsection) and why the MVID comes from `Module` |

The `Param` row was pinned down by requiring the tables *after* it to parse coherently, not by finding a
description of it. With the documented 8-byte row, `Param` ends two bytes per row early and drags every
later table out of step; with 10 bytes, the walk up to `MemberRef` accounts for every byte and then ends
45,994 bytes short of the `#~` stream's end (the appended private data described below). The stride is
what makes `MethodDef.ParamList` land on the right rows, and therefore what makes the arity check work —
so it is load-bearing, and it is corroborated by the arity agreeing with six signatures the documents
state independently.

**Evidence.** The tables the reader is *anchored* on — Module, TypeRef, TypeDef, Field, MethodDef,
Param, MemberRef — agree with the independent census of this same assembly: **23,743 `MethodDef`
rows and 25,105 `Field` rows**, as recorded in [README.md](../../hook/README.md) and
[CLIENT-FINDINGS.md](CLIENT-FINDINGS.md) §0.1 (produced by `hook/work/md_probe.py`). The reader's own
comment is that those tables "account for every byte up to `MemberRef` exactly"; a wrong column width
in one of them would put `MemberRef` somewhere else. The walk is additionally asserted against the
metadata stream: if it ends more than `0x20000` bytes from the end of the `#~` stream, the reader
fails loudly and says a column width is wrong.

The figures, as measured on this build (`il_index.py --self-test` and the walk audit it prints):

| quantity | value |
|---|---|
| `MethodDef` rows / `Field` rows / `TypeDef` rows | 23,743 / 25,105 / 3,584 |
| fat method bodies whose walk consumes the body exactly | 10,738 |
| fat method bodies whose walk does **not** (reported per-target as `ilDecodesCleanly=false`) | 371 |
| tiny method bodies (no walk needed; the code is one length byte) | 12,161 |
| residual bytes between the end of the known tables and the end of `#~` | 45,994 |

The 371 are the honest bound on this reader's instruction walk. They are not a target-side problem: none
of the four targets is among them, and the hash does not depend on the walk — but a patch that moved a
target *into* that set would be reported, which is the point of checking.

**Instruction: leave the sizes alone**, and do not extend the byte-exact walk into the tail. The
layout that matters for the four targets is anchored and independently corroborated; the tail is
explicitly treated as *not* byte-exact, which is why the reader checks its own walk rather than
trusting it. The check is a bound, not a proof: if the walk ends more than `0x20000` bytes from the end
of the `#~` stream the reader fails loudly, and this build's walk ends **45,994 bytes (44.9 KB) short**
of the end — the tables it knows about account for every byte up to `MemberRef`, and the shortfall is
what an obfuscator's private data appended after the tables looks like. It is tolerated and recorded,
rather than papered over by inventing a table to absorb it.

### `Assembly.Name` cannot be read from this build's metadata

**Finding.** Because the `Assembly` table sits in the perturbed tail, the assembly name and version
`il_index.py` prints may be blank, and the MVID does not come from the `Assembly` table at all: it is
read from the `Module` table (row 1, its `Mvid` GUID column), which is how `hook/known-build.json`'s
`assembly.mvid` was produced.

**Evidence.** `assembly_name_and_version()`'s own docstring: the assembly row "sits in the tail,
where this build's obfuscator has perturbed the stream enough that a single row cannot be located
with confidence", so it *probes* the row for a self-consistent `(version, name)` pair instead of
trusting a fixed column layout — and it is "diagnostics only: nothing in the tool's output depends on
it".

**Instruction: leave it alone, and do not chase a blank.** Nothing depends on the name or version:
the gate never reads them, the target table is keyed on the MVID and the assembly SHA-256, and a
blank field in a log line is not a symptom of anything.

### The IL dump's textual nesting cannot be reconstructed reliably

**Finding.** `il_index.py` deliberately does **not** attribute methods to declaring types from the IL
dump. ilspycmd's block layout does not let a class stack be reconstructed reliably: a `.class`
declaration can be followed by `.field`/`.custom` lines before its `{`, and `.property`/`.event`
blocks contain their own `.get`/`.addon` members. The dump is therefore used only for what it states
unambiguously about a method body — its RVA, its code size and its parameter count — while the
declaring type comes from the metadata.

**Evidence.** `scan_il_dump()`'s docstring states the hazard and the deliberate limitation, and
`resolve_target()` states the split: the metadata knows the type and the name, the dump is the
independent witness that the RVA, code size and arity agree.

**Instruction: keep the split.** Attributing a method to the wrong type would be worse than not
answering: a brace-counting reconstruction produces a confident but wrong answer with nothing to
contradict it, whereas the current design reports a target the dump does not contain as *unchecked*
and the caller turns that into a problem. A disagreement between the two sides is reported as a
failure, never smoothed over.

### The instruction walk is a check, never the identity

**Finding.** `code_entry()` exists because some methods carry a jump indirection at the start of
their stream — `br.s +3`, a zero byte, then a second `br.s +0`, with the real body at +5 — and it
matches that whole five-byte shape (`2B <delta> 00 2B 00`) exactly rather than testing for "starts
with `br.s`". The near-miss is real in this build: the frame tick's stream contains
`IL_0030: br.s IL_0035`, `IL_0032: ldc.i4.0`, `IL_0033: br.s IL_0035` — bytes `2B 03 16 2B 00` — which
is the ordinary shape a C# conditional leaves behind (one side `ldc.i4.1` + `br.s`, the other
`ldc.i4.0` + `br.s`, both meeting at `brtrue.s`), not an indirection. Separately, the opcode table
`decode_length()` walks with used to be **one entry short** — `br` (`0x38`) had no row, so everything
after it sat one index low — and the walk could not consume every body; that is fixed, and its own
section below records the measurement that found it.

**Neither of the four recorded targets needs the indirection, and none of them uses it.** Measured
against the dump, each of their streams begins at `IL_0000` with a real instruction — `call void
DarzasDominion.Graphics.DynamicFont::WarmAtlasStep()` for the frame tick (at +12, its declared header),
and `ldarg.0` for spawn, collision and escape — so `code_entry()` returns 0 for all four. An earlier
draft of this directory's own notes attributed the frame tick's RVA to the `2B 03 16` bytes; that was
wrong, and the dump contradicts it. The rule exists for methods that do carry the indirection, not for
these.

**Evidence.** `code_entry()`'s docstring (the matched shape, and `2B 03 16 2B 00` named explicitly as
something that "looks superficially similar but is ordinary code"); the dump lines 500950–500972 for
the frame tick; `decode_length()`'s docstring for the offset statistic.

**Note for the reader.** None of the four recorded targets needs the indirection. Verified against
the dump, each of their streams begins at `IL_0000` with a real instruction — `call void
DarzasDominion.Graphics.DynamicFont::WarmAtlasStep()` for the frame tick, `ldarg.0` for spawn,
collision and escape — so `code_entry()` returns 0 for all four in this build. The rule exists for
the methods that do carry the indirection; do not go looking for one in these four.

**Instruction: leave `code_entry()` alone, and fix `decode_length()` only against the
disassembler.** Do not relax `code_entry()` to a prefix test — that shifts the walk by three bytes for
ordinary code like the sequence above. And do not "fix" `decode_length()`'s operand widths *towards the
hash*: the hash is over the raw bytes and no interpretation of them, and the walk exists only to catch a
body this reader mislocated (the `MoreSects` trap above is the real instance of that). The one thing
that *is* a legitimate repair is the one that was made: a table entry that the IL dump's own instruction
offsets contradict, fixed against that witness and measured over every method the dump describes.

### The opcode table's missing `br`, and how it was found

**The table was one entry short for its whole life.** `OPCODES_1` had no row for `br` (`0x38`), so every
row after it sat one index low: `switch` at `0x44` instead of `0x45`, `isinst` at `0x74` instead of
`0x75`, and on to the end. It went unnoticed because the entries either side of the shift mostly share an
operand width — `br` and `brfalse` are both four-byte branches — so the walk usually landed correctly
anyway, and the four Phase 0 targets all consumed their bodies exactly.

**What found it was the auto-aim target.** `AimbotSystem.FindTarget` is 1580 bytes, contains `isinst`,
and the shifted table walked it off the end: `il_index.py` refused to write the record with
`aimTarget: the instruction walk does not consume the body exactly`, which is the check doing its job —
a target that could not be verified would otherwise have been pinned anyway, because the IL *hash* is
over raw bytes and never needed the walk.

**Measured against the dump before and after.** For each of the 20 418 methods the dump describes (RVA,
declared code size and instruction offsets all present), the body was read and walked, and the walk was
required to (a) visit only offsets the dump lists and (b) consume the body exactly:

| table | all visited offsets are the dump's | body consumed exactly |
|---|---|---|
| before (`br` missing) | 11 699 (57.30 %) | 19 971 (97.81 %) |
| after | **19 667 (96.32 %)** | **20 413 (99.98 %)** |

`python hook/tools/check_opcode_table.py` re-runs that measurement against the table
`il_index.py` currently ships, and exits non-zero if it falls below either threshold. It exists
because the number in the row above is a claim about a table that can be edited, and a claim that
cannot be re-measured is a claim nobody can check.

**The digest never depended on this, and still does not.** `il_hash` is SHA-256 over the exact IL bytes;
no entry in the opcode table can move a target's identity. What the table feeds is `decode_length()`
(the "is this body where we think it is" check) and the `MoreSects` offset choice inside
`method_body()` — which *can* move a chosen body, so the fix was verified to leave all five
pre-existing target hashes **unchanged** rather than assumed to.

## Where the numbers come from

| source | what it provides |
|---|---|
| [`hook/known-build.json`](../../hook/known-build.json) | the verified record: every value quoted above, and the authority the gate reads |
| [`hook/tools/il_index.py`](../../hook/tools/il_index.py) | the four targets' identity. A self-contained PE/CLI metadata reader — no `ilspycmd`, no `dotnet`, no network — that reads the real IL bytes and hashes them. Modes: default (verify and write), `--check` (verify only, write nothing), `--mutation-test` (a one-byte IL edit must move exactly that target), `--self-test` (the reader against signatures the documents state) |
| [`hook/tools/Fingerprint.ps1`](../../hook/tools/Fingerprint.ps1) | the static gate: tiered compilation, IL-only status, `ManagedNativeHeader`, the assembly's size **and SHA-256**, the `clrjit` vtable's code-slot count, both runtime DLL versions, and each target's IL bytes at its recorded RVA |
| [`hook/tools/Test-FingerprintGate.ps1`](../../hook/tools/Test-FingerprintGate.ps1) | the mutation test of the gate itself: a copy with one byte flipped inside a target's IL, same file length, must be refused |
| [`hook/tools/Test-JitVtable.ps1`](../../hook/tools/Test-JitVtable.ps1) | the instrument behind the `jit` rows: finds `getJit` in the export directory, recovers `g_CILJit`, and dumps the vtable slots. The four-slot layout and the slot names are recorded in HOOK-ARCHITECTURE §4.1 |
| [`hook/tools/Test-ReadyToRun.ps1`](../../hook/tools/Test-ReadyToRun.ps1) | reads the COR20 `ManagedNativeHeader` and reports IL-only versus ReadyToRun — the instrument behind `managedNativeHeaderRva` and `mustBeIlOnly` |
| `hook/work/md_probe.py` (from this directory, `../../work/md_probe.py`) | the .NET metadata table census: 23,743 `MethodDef` rows and 25,105 `Field` rows for this assembly, as recorded in README.md and CLIENT-FINDINGS.md §0.1 |
| `hook/il/client-5.8.2.il` | the evidence file: an `ilspycmd -il` dump of this build, 2,218,925 lines. Its first line is `// IL code: DarzasDominion`; it records no version of the tool that produced it |

**The dump is cross-checked, not trusted.** `il_index.py` uses it only to locate the targets and to
cross-check what the metadata reader found — RVA, code size and parameter count — and reports a
disagreement as a failure rather than smoothing it over. A target the dump does not contain is
reported as unchecked, and the caller turns that into a problem. The identity of a target never comes
from the dump.

Nothing in this document is a substitute for running the commands in "Re-verifying after a game
patch".

```

`docs/hook/IMPLEMENTATION-PLAN.md`:

```md
# Implementation plan

This is the deliverable: **what to build, in what order, and how to know each step worked.**

The supporting research is [CLIENT-FINDINGS.md](CLIENT-FINDINGS.md) (the client, verified),
[TIMING.md](TIMING.md) (the measured window), [CLIENT-MAP.md](CLIENT-MAP.md) (the exhaustive
reverse-engineering map), [HOOK-ARCHITECTURE.md](HOOK-ARCHITECTURE.md) (how the hook is installed),
[DODGE-ALGORITHM.md](DODGE-ALGORITHM.md) (what it computes), [JAVA-BRIDGE.md](../bridge/JAVA-BRIDGE.md) (how it
reports), [VERIFICATION.md](VERIFICATION.md) (how each phase is proved, and how it can fail) and
[RISKS.md](RISKS.md).

---

## 0. The shape of the answer, up front

The premise the work started from was *"what if the auto-nexus never needed to be triggered?"* The
research says that premise is **half right, and the useful half is not the half it looks like.**

**What is true.** A hook placed at the client's own collision decision occupies a window the reactive
rule structurally cannot. Measured: the server's `GmHealthUpdate` that reflects a hit arrives
**+55.5 ms median (+98.1 ms p90)** after the client resolved that hit, because the reading is a
*notification of damage already applied*, not a warning. The hook's advantage over the reactive rule
is that whole interval plus one frame — **not** the escape round trip, which both designs pay.

**What is not true.** "Never needing to be triggered" implies preventing damage generally. That is
not achievable, and the measurement says why: **74 % of measured HP falls (571 of 775) have no
client-side hit claim at all.** The client only ever claims hits it resolves as its own collision —
and the only claim packets in the whole assembly are `GmHit` (projectiles), `GmAllyHit`,
`GmSweepHit`/`GmPlayerSweepHits` (sweeps) and `GmLaserHit`/`GmPlayerLaserHit` (beams). Damage from
**AoE and bombs produces no claim at all** (`Entity.HitBy(AoeData)`, `Entity.cs:2203`, contains no
`SendPacket`), because it resolves on a timer server-side. So the hook helps exactly where the client
is the first to know — projectiles with a client-visible approach — and does nothing for AoE, bomb
detonations, damage-over-time ticks, or point-blank spawns.

**So the plan is shaped to dodge first and to escape last.** The deliverable is the *dodge*: where the
client is the first to know a bullet is coming, the hook **moves the player out of the way** rather
than ending the run. The client's own `World.RequestEscape()` remains, as the **floor** rather than a
phase of its own — it is reached at exactly one point in the decision
([DODGE-ALGORITHM.md](DODGE-ALGORITHM.md) §7 gate 6), when the projected damage over the horizon is
lethal **and no admissible move avoids it**.

**That merge is the ordering decision of 2026-10-13, and the reasoning is recorded here because it
reverses the plan's original shape.** A predictive nexus is still a nexus: it ends the run, and the
reported frustration is being forced to leave at all. The escape-only phase that used to sit at 3 was
therefore judged of questionable value on its own, and its decision folded into the dodge as the last
gate — one sensor, one snapshot, one frame budget, one place where the two controllers can disagree.
The relay bridge that used to be Phase 5 is now **Phase 4** and is unchanged by any of this: it is
additive to both, and nothing in Phase 3 waits on it.

What that costs is that the largest risk now sits inside the phase that matters: the dodge rests on
the **movement question** (RISKS §2a) — the one thing in this design with no precedent in the
reference engine and no measurement in the captures. The mitigation is structural rather than
optimistic: the question is answered by a spike that uses **no dodge logic at all**, and it is run
before a solver is written (Spike 3.1). If it fails, the plan's honest stop is documented in §3
rather than improvised at the end.

### 0.1 Why the premise is nonetheless worth building on

Three measured facts make the hook decisively better than the current rule, and they are the ground
the dodge stands on:

1. **The current rule can act on stale HP.** The recorded case: an escape injected on a 1 % reading
   **151 ms after HP had already reached zero** (`nexus-20261005-023129-2000.jsonl`). The hook is
   seeded from the same `Player.Health` but advanced by its own predictions, so it cannot be in that
   state.
2. **The current rule cannot distinguish "a hit landed" from "a hit is coming".** With one number it
   must be conservative in the direction that costs runs. The hook knows the bullet, so it can
   distinguish them — which is what lets the dodge be aimed at a predicted path rather than triggered
   by a number, and what stops the escape from firing on the aftermath.
3. **The dodge is genuinely achievable here.** It was not achievable through packets: the packet
   stream never re-broadcasts a projectile's position, so a packet-only dodge is dead reckoning with
   unbounded error (`hook/work/auto-dodge-feasibility.md` §2). In-process, the true position is one field
   read away, and the reference engine's own architecture confirms that every good part of its dodge
   sits downstream of exactly that read.

---

## 1. Workstreams and phases

Five phases. Each has a **spike** (does the mechanism work at all?) and a **deliverable** (is it
built?), and each is gated on the previous one's exit criteria. The estimates are order-of-magnitude
for a single developer working with the existing `drelay` codebase.

| phase | question it answers | risk of the unknown | estimate |
|---|---|---|---|
| **0** | what exactly are we targeting, and can we prove it has not changed? | very low | 1–2 days |
| **1** | can native C++ code get into this process, early, and survive? | **high** | 3–5 days |
| **2** | can we observe the truth, and does our model of it match reality? | medium | 1–2 weeks |
| **3** | **can we move the player out of the way — and escape only when we cannot?** | **highest** | 3–6 weeks |
| **4** | does the relay see the hook, and is that useful? | low | 3–5 days |

**Five phases, because two of the six merged.** Phases 0–2 are the de-risking half and are done
(Phase 0 but for one live experiment that does not gate the hook); Phase 3 *is* the project — the
dodge, with the escape as its floor — and it is the only phase that carries the movement question.
Phase 4 is additive and can slip indefinitely without touching Phase 3.

**Phase 3 is entered only after Phase 2's numbers have been read**, because that is the M6 decision
point, and it is the one place in the plan where stopping is the honest move (§4). Everything before
it exists to make that stop cheap. Note the change of shape: the old plan could stop at a predictive
nexus and still ship something. With the escape folded in as a floor instead of a phase, **a stop
after Phase 2 ships nothing new** — the reactive auto-nexus remains the status quo — so at that point
the deliverable is the measurement itself, and it has to be good enough to stand alone.

---

## Phase 0 — Ground truth, and a build gate

**Goal.** Turn the research into an executable, repeatable check that the target is what we think it
is. This phase produces no hook; it produces the thing that stops the hook from being dangerous later.

### Deliverables

1. ✅ **`hook/tools/Fingerprint.ps1` + `hook/known-build.json` — BUILT.** Runs nine-plus static checks and
   exits non-zero on any mismatch: the tiered-compilation setting, the assembly's IL-only status and
   content hash, the `clrjit` vtable's code-slot count, and both runtime DLL versions. It resolves
   `getJit` from the export directory, recovers `g_CILJit` from the function prologue, and reads the
   vtable itself — so it needs no external tools and no hardcoded RVAs.

   **It was mutation-tested, and the testing found a real hole.** The first version checked the
   assembly *size*, and flipping a single byte of the assembly left every check passing while the
   file's length was unchanged. That is exactly the failure the gate exists to prevent. A SHA-256
   check was added and the mutation now fails loudly with the expected and actual hashes. The lesson
   is recorded in `hook/known-build.json` itself, because it is the kind of thing a future reader would
   otherwise "simplify" away:

   ```powershell
   .\hook\tools\Fingerprint.ps1                    # exit 0 = safe to install
   .\hook\tools\Fingerprint.ps1 -GamePath "D:\Games\Darza's Dominion"
   ```

   Three things it *cannot* check, reported as known gaps rather than passes: the effective
   `DOTNET_*` environment (a `.NET 9` environment variable overrides `runtimeconfig.json`, so a stray
   `DOTNET_TieredCompilation=1` would defeat the whole design), the loaded assembly's MVID, and the
   target-method IL hashes. The last two must be re-checked **in-process at attach**
   ([HOOK-ARCHITECTURE.md](HOOK-ARCHITECTURE.md) §9).

2. ✅ **`hook/tools/il_index.py` + the populated `targetMethods` block — BUILT.** Resolves the four
   targets to an exact byte identity and writes it into `hook/known-build.json`: for each target,
   `(declaring type, name, arity, metadata token, RVA, IL size, IL hash)`.

   It is a **metadata reader, not a text scraper**. It walks the PE's CLI metadata tables
   itself — no `ilspycmd`, no `dotnet`, no network — so the hash is computed over the exact
   `MethodDef.Rva` bytes the JIT will hand the hook, and the IL dump is used only as an
   independent cross-check. Three things it establishes beyond "it runs":

   - **The identity is a SHA-256 of the raw IL bytes**, not of a re-encoded instruction
     stream. The native side hashes `CORINFO_METHOD_INFO.ILCode[0..ILCodeSize)` and needs no
     IL decoder at all, so a wrong operand-width table in this tool cannot silently change
     which function the hook patches.
   - **Every target is cross-checked against the IL dump** on three independent values — RVA,
     code size and parameter count — and a target the dump cannot confirm is reported as *not
     checked*, not as a pass.
   - **The table is deterministic**: two runs produce byte-identical output.

   Four findings from building it are load-bearing and are recorded so that a future reader
   does not "simplify" them away (all four are in `docs/hook/HOOK-BUILD-MATRIX.md`): this build's
   fat-header `MoreSects` size field is **not trustworthy** (a wrong choice there yields a
   plausible-looking but wrong hash); the metadata tables are **not the documented layouts**
   (`MethodDef` is 18 bytes per row, not 16); `Assembly.Name` is unreadable and the MVID is
   taken from the `Module` table instead; and the IL dump's textual nesting **cannot** be
   reconstructed reliably, so targets are resolved from metadata and the dump only
   cross-checks.

   ```powershell
   python .\hook\tools\il_index.py --check            # verify, write nothing
   python .\hook\tools\il_index.py                    # verify + update the record
   python .\hook\tools\il_index.py --mutation-test    # prove the gate can fail
   ```

3. **A pinned constants file** generated by `hook/tools/poolresolve.py` — **deliberately not
   produced.** The values are recovered and reproducible (`poolresolve.py` resolves them from
   the IL and the decrypted pool), but the design rule is *call, don't compute*
   ([DODGE-ALGORITHM.md](DODGE-ALGORITHM.md) §6, §9): the speed law is **called**
   (`PlayerFunctions.TilesPerSecond`, with live status tiers), damage is **called**
   (`Entity.GetDamageTaken`), and trajectories are **called** (`ProjDesc.GetPosition`). A
   frozen constants file would be a second source of truth for numbers the hook must never use
   directly, and its most likely use — deriving a move budget from a nominal speed — is the
   specific bug [CLIENT-FINDINGS.md](CLIENT-FINDINGS.md) §5.3 warns about. The resolved values
   stay where they are read: in `poolresolve.py`'s output and in the documents.
4. ✅ **`docs/hook/HOOK-BUILD-MATRIX.md` — BUILT.** The human-readable half of `hook/known-build.json`:
   the verified build and what breaks if each pinned value changes, the four targets, the hash
   recipe, the re-verification procedure after a patch, what the gate cannot check, the four
   build-specific findings above, and where every number comes from.
5. **The server-authority question — now partly answered, and worth one cheap experiment.** The
   research left this explicitly blocking: *does the server re-simulate hits, or does it trust the
   client's `GmHit` claim?* (`CLIENT-MAP.md` §10.1). Subsequent measurement settled the important half:
   the client **does** send the claim (`GmHit`, id 102, with the local player as `ObjectId` in 161 of
   580 captured packets), **but 74 % of HP falls have no claim at all** — so the server resolves most
   damage independently. That rules out "suppress the claim" as an architecture, which is a result.

   What it does not settle is whether a claim the server *does* receive is *necessary* for the damage
   it accompanies. That distinction no longer changes the design (we anchor on the collision either
   way), so it drops from blocking to interesting. **The experiment is still worth one afternoon**,
   because the answer is useful to RISKS §2b's scope accounting and because it needs no hook: the
   relay is already the man in the middle, so **drop the outbound `GmHit` for exactly one hit and
   observe whether the server still decrements Health.**

   **This is the one Phase 0 item still open, and the only one that needs a live session.**


### Exit criteria

- ✅ `hook/tools/Fingerprint.ps1` exits 0 on the installed build and prints one line per component.
  *met for the 5.8.2 / .NET 9.0.20 build: 15 checks pass, 2 known gaps — and the four target IL
  hashes are now **verified** rather than merely reported. The gate re-hashes each target's
  instruction stream straight out of the assembly and separately requires that `il_index.py`
  regenerate the same table, so the two halves must agree.*
- ✅ **The gate provably can fail — at both levels.** *File level: flipping one byte of the
  assembly (same file size), or flipping `TieredCompilation` to `true`, makes it exit 1 with the
  expected/actual pair named. Method level: `hook/tools/Test-FingerprintGate.ps1` copies the install to
  a sandbox, flips one byte inside a target's IL, and asserts that the gate exits non-zero naming
  **that target's** IL hash while the other three still pass. That distinction is the point: a
  file-level check cannot say which method moved, and "which method moved" is what decides whether
  the hook may install.*
- ✅ The target table lists all four primary targets with **distinct** IL hashes, each
  cross-checked against the IL dump on RVA, code size and parameter count.
- ✅ Deliberately corrupting a copy of the assembly (one byte in a target's IL) makes the table
  regeneration **fail to match**, proving the gate works at the *method* level and not only the
  file level: `il_index.py --mutation-test` reports exactly one target's hash as changed.
- ⬜ The server-authority question has a definitive answer from a controlled `GmHit`-drop trial,
  recorded with the session log that proves it.

### Why this is Phase 0 and not an afterthought

The existing `drelay` documentation makes the argument better than this plan can: three separate
reversals in that project found the decompiled field list disagreeing with the wire, and the lesson
recorded there is *"a decode must consume a captured packet to its exact last byte"*
(`docs/hook/INJECTION.md` §1.1). The hook's equivalent is that a method fingerprint must match the
loaded assembly exactly. Getting this wrong in a hook does not produce a wrong log line; it produces
a patch on the wrong function in a live process.

---

## Phase 1 — Get in, and stay in

**Goal.** Prove the injection and early-load mechanism before designing anything that depends on it.

**Risk: high.** Everything downstream assumes native code can be resident before the first frame and
before the target methods are JITted. If that fails, the whole approach needs re-planning.

> **Status: built, confirmed live, and closed 2026-10-12.** The three artefacts
> (`Drelay.Hook.dll`, `Drelay.Bootstrap.dll`, `Drelay.Launcher.exe`) build clean and every check that
> does not need a running game passes. The live runs have happened too: injection happens before
> `Main`, runtime validation passes, all four targets are matched by IL hash, the frame tick is
> patched, the hook reads live state from the real game, **Exit 2a's log-denial test passed all four
> of its assertions**, and the **hour-long endurance run** completed with no fault recorded and
> 198 586 successful frame reads over 209 897 frame calls. The two verdict lines that read FAIL are
> instrument faults — a `$null` exit code under Windows PowerShell 5.1 (fixed in both runners) and a
> single 323 µs sample that the overflowed frame ring cannot place in time. The accounting is
> [PHASE1-VERIFICATION.md](PHASE1-VERIFICATION.md) §11;
> [PHASE1-HANDOFF.md](PHASE1-HANDOFF.md) is the long record of how it got there and
> [PHASE1-SCOPE.md](PHASE1-SCOPE.md) §6 separates what is verified from what is not.

### Spike 1.1 — injection, with no hooking

- Bootstrap that runs **before the game's `Main`** and writes a line recording: its own path,
  the resolved game directory, the `DarzDominion.dll` MVID, and `getJit()`'s address.
- Two candidate mechanisms to try, in the order given in [HOOK-ARCHITECTURE.md](HOOK-ARCHITECTURE.md) §3:
  a controlled-environment launcher with `CREATE_SUSPENDED` (preferred; needs no writes to the game
  directory), and app-directory proxy DLL + `DOTNET_STARTUP_HOOKS` (needs a write to the install).
- **Success**: the line appears in the game's log directory *before* the game's own first log line,
  and the MVID matches the expected build.

### Spike 1.2 — the JIT detour, observing only

- Detour `compileMethod` per [HOOK-ARCHITECTURE.md](HOOK-ARCHITECTURE.md) §4, with all four
  disciplines (call real first, re-entrancy guard, last-error save/restore, `__try`).
- Log every compilation as `(token?, IL size, IL hash, native entry, native size)` to a CSV.
- **This spike validates three unverified assumptions at once**, and each is worth stating:
  1. does the vtable-slot-2 GUID check work on this build?
  2. does `getMethodDefFromMethod` actually live at the documented slot, or at the older one?
  3. is the `nativeEntry` we capture the address that will actually execute (i.e. does the EE copy
     after we return)?
- **Success**: the CSV contains all four target methods, matched by IL hash, with stable addresses
  across two runs. (Stable addresses are expected because tiering is off — an *unstable* result would
  mean the `TieredCompilation: false` assumption is wrong, which is the single most important thing
  this spike can discover.)

### Spike 1.3 — one detour, one field

- MinHook-patch **one** target (the frame tick) with a detour that reads exactly one float from the
  world and appends it to a file.
- **Success**: plausible values at ~60 Hz for 30 minutes of play, including zone transitions, a
  forced GC, and an alt-tab. No crash, no visible frame hitch.

### Deliverable — the hook skeleton

`Drelay.Hook.dll` (C++/x64) + `Drelay.Bootstrap` (managed), with:
- the startup self-check list from [HOOK-ARCHITECTURE.md](HOOK-ARCHITECTURE.md) §9, implemented as
  code and run on every start;
- the target table consumed from Phase 0, with a hard refusal on mismatch;
- the field-offset resolution pass, run every launch, logging every resolved offset;
- an off switch that is honoured before any patch is applied.

### Exit criteria

- The game runs for an hour with the hook loaded and **all four targets patched**, with no crash and
  no measured frame-time regression above the budget.
  *The design point is **60 Hz (16.7 ms per frame)** — the operator will cap FPS in the game's own
  settings, and the high-rate/uncapped limit test is deferred. Justification: the hook has been
  measured running under an **uncapped ~200 Hz frame loop** at the title screen (~4.9 ms per frame),
  so 60 Hz is the conservative design point, not the observed worst case.*
  *Open decision, not taken here: only `frameTick` is patched today, deliberately — a detour body must
  match the target's signature, and the other three have no Phase 1 behaviour to run
  ([PHASE1-SCOPE.md](PHASE1-SCOPE.md) §2.4). Either this criterion is amended to "the one target with
  Phase 1 behaviour patched", or the other three get pass-through detours.*
  **Closed 2026-10-12 as amended**: the criterion is read as "the one target with Phase 1 behaviour
  patched", which is what `frameTick` is, and the hour ran with it patched and no fault recorded
  ([PHASE1-VERIFICATION.md](PHASE1-VERIFICATION.md) §11.6). Phase 2 gives the other three their
  bodies, and its own exit criteria name them.
- **Exit 2a — a destroyed log target costs evidence, never the game.** With the hook running and
  patched, the evidence path is denied to the hook **by a stated mechanism**: a second process holds
  `hook.log` open with sharing disabled, which is the mechanism every observed failure has had (a
  scanner or a reader). *Renaming or deleting the file is not a test while the hook holds its own
  handle — Windows keeps the file alive, or the hook simply recreates it on the next pass.* The run
  must then show all four:
  1. **the game is unaffected**: it runs to completion and exits the way it does in an untouched run;
  2. **the frame cost is unchanged**: `frames.csv`'s `elapsed_us` distribution matches an untouched
     run's — the evidence path is off the frame path and must stay off it;
  3. **the kill was felt**: `hook.log.append-failed` exists, naming the `errno`, the win32 error and
     the path the hook actually tried to open; and, when the lock is applied before the evidence
     files are written, `summary.txt` carries `log appends : N failed pass(es)` with `N ≥ 1`. **A run
     with neither is a run whose control never fired** (handoff §8's third question);
  4. **a transient kill costs no line**: once the lock is released, the lines written before it appear
     in `hook.log` — the read cursor advances only on a successful write, so the retry is the
     mechanism, and the test asserts it rather than assuming it.

  *Not tested. The failure mode is not hypothetical and the instruments already exist: the run
  `hook\obj\live-runs\20261010-014016-p11352` logged one `ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION` (errno 13, win32
  32, `lines pending: 0`) and recovered every line, and handoff §10 records ~371 failed appends in the
  run whose launcher tail held the handle. What is missing is a test that denies the path
  deliberately and asserts those four properties.*
  **Met 2026-10-12**: `hook/tools/Run-Exit2a-LogDenial.ps1`, run from the operator's shell
  (`hook\obj\cases\exit2a-logdenial\`, run `20261012-030308-p19828`). All four properties hold —
  `phase 1 complete`, no fault event, the cost unchanged (9 µs worst after the first, against the
  baseline's 2 µs), `hook.log.append-failed` with `errno 13 / win32 32`, `log appends : 113 failed
  pass(es)`, and `log lines : 66 written, 0 overflowed` with 72 lines present. The lock was taken
  during the collection delay and its denial proven with a refused write probe. The verdict's one
  FAIL is the `$null` exit code of §11.3. See [PHASE1-VERIFICATION.md](PHASE1-VERIFICATION.md) §11.2.

- **Exit 2b (Phase 4) — a relay that dies mid-session changes nothing.** The bridge is observation:
  a missing, stalled or dead relay must not change the hook's behaviour by one instruction, and the
  hook must never wait on it ([JAVA-BRIDGE.md](../bridge/JAVA-BRIDGE.md) §8, [RISKS.md](RISKS.md) §2d).
  *Moved to Phase 4's exit criteria, because it cannot be tested here and is not Phase 1's: the relay
  is Phase 4 and absent, its **absence** is the status quo — every run so far is a no-relay run — and
  what needs proving is the relay dying **after** attach.*
- Starting the hook against a deliberately different build **refuses and logs why**, and the game
  runs normally.
  *Satisfied: `hook/tools/Test-PeReader.ps1` covers the deliberately tampered MVID, and run 1 of
  `hook/tools/Test-Injection.ps1` covers the fingerprint mismatch — the run is refused with both values
  named.*

---

## Phase 2 — Observe, and find out whether the model is true

**Goal.** Build the sensor, and use it to answer the question that decides whether the dodge is worth
building: **does our prediction of a collision agree with the game's?**

**This phase changes nothing about the game.** It is read-only, it is the largest single de-risking
step in the plan, and it produces the ground truth that every later phase is tuned against.

> **Status: closed by operator decision on 2026-10-13, with one measurement carried forward.** The
> execution plan, the decision rule for the mechanism Phase 1 left open (`ProjDesc.GetPosition` and
> the live projectile set must be touched **on the game's thread**, which a call detour into managed
> code cannot do), the instrumentation this phase needed first, and the fallback if the mechanism
> test failed are all in [PHASE2-SCOPE.md](PHASE2-SCOPE.md). Its §7 restates these criteria against
> their actuals, and the close rests on two explicit waivers rather than on the criteria being met:
> the sampler's p99 cost (**"ignore performance concerns for now"** — the cost work belongs with the
> solver that shares the frame, which is now Phase 3) and the false-negative accounting, which the
> session that produced it over-counted by asking the collision predicate on every entry instead of
> every `true` (§4.15). That last number is the one open measurement, and Phase 3's dry-run trial is
> where it is closed out.

### Deliverable 2.1 — the threat set

- Spawn hook: `Projectile.ProcessProjectileData` → add a record keyed on `(GameId, startTime)`,
  reading **only arguments** ([DODGE-ALGORITHM.md](DODGE-ALGORITHM.md) §3.2).
- Frame tick: re-read each live bullet's position; apply the two-strike retirement with a min-age
  grace; invalidate on pool reuse.
- **Test T3** (`RISKS.md` §Test list): force a pool reuse and assert no record inherits.

### Deliverable 2.2 — the trajectory sampler

- Resolve `ProjDesc.GetPosition`'s concrete slot once; call it for a fixed 30 ms grid out to the
  horizon ([DODGE-ALGORITHM.md](DODGE-ALGORITHM.md) §4.2).
- Anchor every sample set on the live position each frame.
- Implement the linearity gate, and log when it says a trajectory is **not** linear — that log is the
  direct evidence for how often curved shots occur in real play, which currently is unknown.

### Deliverable 2.3 — the ground-truth comparison

**The most valuable artefact in the whole project.**

- Hook the collision decision (`Projectile.HitCharacter`) and, **for every call that returns
  `true`**, log: the bullet identity, the frame, `World.ClientTime`, the player position, the bullet
  position, the computed `r_eff`, and whether our own sensor had **predicted** an intersection with
  this bullet, and if so **how many milliseconds of warning** it gave.
- **The `true` is not a detail, and getting it wrong cost a session.** `HitCharacter` is a per-frame
  *predicate*: `Projectile.Update` calls `Hit()` on every live projectile every frame, and the answer
  decides whether the hit resolves (`Projectile.cs:1505,1514`; `CLIENT-FINDINGS.md` §4 records that it
  "returns true iff the bullet is being consumed by the hit"). Logging every *entry* counts questions
  instead of decisions — the 2026-10-12 20:42 session logged 418 328 of them against 48 resolved hits,
  and every frame a bullet spent near the player became another false negative. **The event this
  deliverable is about is the `true`; the entries are not evidence.**
- Also log bullets that hit that we never predicted, and bullets we predicted that never hit.

This gives four numbers that decide everything:

| measurement | what it decides |
|---|---|
| **how much warning we had** (distribution) | whether there is time to move — the input to Phase 3's dodge budget and to the timing of its escape floor |
| **false negatives** (hit, not predicted) | whether the model is complete enough to be relied on |
| **false positives** (predicted, no hit) | whether the dodge will be over-cautious; directly the `#ghost` rate |
| **the per-frame cost** (p50/p99) | whether the Phase 3 solver fits the budget at all |

### Exit criteria

- Over several hours of real play, the prediction agrees with the game's own collision decision on
  the great majority of hits, and every disagreement is explicable by a named cause (a curved
  trajectory, a homing re-target, a pool-reuse race, a >horizon flight).
- The sensor's p99 per-frame cost is inside the budget with room for the solver.
- **The linearity-gate log has told us what fraction of real bullets are straight**, which is the
  number that decides how good a dodge can be.

*As closed on 2026-10-13: the third criterion is met — **0.695** of sampled trajectories were straight,
over 406 077 linear and 178 611 curved sample sets — the first is the measurement the phase was gated
on but its false-negative count is an over-count from a wrong event set, and the second is waived for
now and moved into Phase 3 with the solver that shares the frame
([PHASE2-SCOPE.md](PHASE2-SCOPE.md) §4.15, §7).*

### Why this phase is not optional

Phase 2 is where the project can fail *cheaply*. If the sensor cannot predict collisions, no solver
will help, and the honest answer is to **stop before Phase 3** rather than to build a dodge on a model
that does not match reality. Building the solver first would hide a sensor problem inside a tuning
problem, which is exactly the failure mode that makes dodges feel haunted.

**Stopping here now means stopping for real.** Under the old ordering the consolation prize was a
predictive nexus that shipped on its own; the merge removed that, so a stop after Phase 2 leaves the
reactive auto-nexus as the status quo, and the deliverable is the measurement itself — which is why
§4's decision point is stated as a decision and not as a checkpoint.

---

## Phase 3 — Dodge, with the escape as its floor

> **Status: entered 2026-10-14, and Spike 3.1 is ANSWERED YES as of 2026-10-14 04:08.**
> [PHASE3-HANDOFF.md](PHASE3-HANDOFF.md) is the measurement and the next step; the execution plan,
> the corrected spike order and the measurement that reshapes the phase are in
> [PHASE3-SCOPE.md](PHASE3-SCOPE.md). What exists now: a **fifth pinned target** (the movement
> integrator, `World.cs:12666`) with a managed replacement on its entry, a per-frame actuator that
> writes `GameScene.GameInput` (the mechanism this section ranks first), an opt-in and bounded
> launcher switch for it, and `hook/tools/steering_report.py` to read the result against the relay's own
> wire evidence. **The live sweep of run `20261014-040859-p22748` moved the player under hook control
> in eight commanded directions: the value read back from `MoveAngle` equalled the value written on
> every logged frame (worst `0.0000000 rad`, 1428 of 1951 frames moved, heading residual ≤ 2°,
> mean cos 0.995), and the per-frame displacement (0.133–0.146 units at 16.680 ms) agrees with the
> resolved `3.5 + 5.0·(SPD+10)/75` law and with §5.2's offline step distribution.** The one witness
> still outstanding is the wire's: no relay log was attached, so `GmKicked` has not been observed
> *absent* — the operator reports no disconnect, and illegal movement is disconnected quickly. That
> does not gate the dodge; it gates the claim, and it is one command
> ([PHASE3-HANDOFF.md](PHASE3-HANDOFF.md) §3.1, §7). **Two corrections to this section's text are
> load-bearing and are recorded rather than quietly dropped:** (1) the "cheapest possible way to
> learn whether the server validates movement" it names — injecting a plausible `Move` from the
> relay — cannot answer Spike 3.1, because the relay cannot reach the actuator this design chose and
> the question is not whether the server validates movement (the operator settled that) but whether
> the hook can steer through the client's own input path; [PHASE3-SCOPE.md](PHASE3-SCOPE.md) §3 is
> the argument, and the proxy keeps the one job that is genuinely its own. (2) The
> **movement-boundary search** this section asks Spike 3.1 to run is **not** run by deliberate
> overspend, for the reasons in §3 and §"Exit criteria" of [PHASE3-SCOPE.md](PHASE3-SCOPE.md): `b =
> TilesPerSecond × frameSeconds` is a legal move by construction, so the design never needs to know
> where the cliff is, and the per-frame figure it does need is now measured
> ([PHASE3-HANDOFF.md](PHASE3-HANDOFF.md) §1.4). The search stays available as an explicit, opt-in
> experiment.

**Goal.** Not needing the nexus, in the cases where that is possible — and calling it only when
nothing else is.

**This is the merged phase, and the merge is concrete.** The move and the escape are not two features
with two triggers; they are one decision with two outcomes, taken once per frame
([DODGE-ALGORITHM.md](DODGE-ALGORITHM.md) §5, §7):

| outcome | when |
|---|---|
| **move** | an admissible move exists that avoids lethal projected damage (gates 4–5) |
| **escape** | the projected damage over the horizon is lethal **and no admissible move avoids it** (gate 6) |
| nothing | everything else, logged with the reason it did nothing (gates 0–3, 7) |

**Why it is one phase.** A predictive nexus is still a nexus: it ends the run, and the frustration
that started this work is being forced to leave at all. Escape-only was judged of questionable value
as a standalone phase (operator decision, 2026-10-13), and the two share one sensor, one snapshot and
one frame budget — building them apart would have meant building the same plumbing twice and then
reconciling two controllers in the same frame, which is a **verified** hazard rather than a
hypothetical one ([RISKS.md](RISKS.md) §3d).

**Risk: highest.** Not the algorithm — the algorithm is well specified, and
[DODGE-ALGORITHM.md](DODGE-ALGORITHM.md) §12 is explicit about what transfers from the reference
engine and what must not be copied — but the **movement question** ([RISKS.md](RISKS.md) §2a), which
is the one thing in this whole design with no precedent in the reference and no measurement in the
captures. Spike 3.1 exists to answer it before any solver code is written.

### Phase 3 prerequisite — scope decisions, already taken

Two decisions remove work from this phase, and both are recorded because they change what "done"
means:

1. **AoE and bomb damage is out of scope by operator decision.** It is left to the player to dodge
   manually. That closes the coverage gap this plan previously treated as a required task — but it
   **promotes intent preservation to a requirement** ([DODGE-ALGORITHM.md](DODGE-ALGORITHM.md) §5.7):
   a dodge that overrides the player's steering takes away the tool they need for the channel it does
   not cover. An AoE volume may be a *score* input; it must never be an *admission* filter.
2. **Terrain is available, not hypothetical.** The client's own collision grid is
   `private byte[,] World.<grid>` (`World.cs:4318`), fed by `GmTiles` and written at `World.cs:9677`.
   Admission rules 2 and 3 read it directly ([CLIENT-FINDINGS.md](CLIENT-FINDINGS.md) §5.4), so the
   "running blind" degradation is a fallback for a failed offset resolution rather than an expected
   state.

**Movement validation is also reframed.** The server does validate movement, but the check is
**distance per game tick** — so the design's per-frame budget, derived from the game's own
`TilesPerSecond × frameSeconds`, is the constraint that matters, and it is an arithmetic question
rather than an architectural one ([RISKS.md](RISKS.md) §2a).

### Spike 3.1 — can we move at all? (do this before writing a solver)

This spike uses **no dodge logic whatsoever**. It answers one question: *can the hook cause the
player to move in a direction the server accepts?*

Three mechanisms, in order of legitimacy ([CLIENT-FINDINGS.md](CLIENT-FINDINGS.md) §5.2):

| mechanism | how | what to watch for |
|---|---|---|
| **input steering** (preferred) | write `GameScene.GameInput.MoveAngle` / `.Moving`, which `World.cs:12690-12692` consumes one line later | the client generates the position, its own speed law, its own collision and its own timestamped move records — so the outbound stream is legitimate **by construction**. Watch for `GmKicked` (id 185) with a movement reason |
| **`MovingTowards`** | the client's own server-sanctioned move-to-a-point facility, `World.cs:12733-12750` | is it usable without a `GmMoveTowards` from the server? Unknown; a one-line experiment |
| **position write** | **do not** | corrupts `Player.TPS` and the move history the outbound packets are built from (`World.cs:12756-12783`); the reference engine's warning about raw writes causing server snap-backs is the same failure in another engine |

**The existing `drelay` proxy can help here, with no hook at all.** It is already the man in the
middle; injecting a plausible `Move` and watching for a kick is a test the proxy can run today, and
it is the cheapest possible way to learn whether the server validates movement. **Do this first.**

**Success criterion**: the player moves under hook control for a sustained period, the server does
not kick, no snap-backs, and the dodge device's own movement accounting (`Player.TPS`) stays sane.
Because the validation is a distance-per-tick check, the spike should deliberately probe the
**boundary**: find the largest per-tick magnitude that is still accepted, and confirm the design's
budget sits inside it with margin.

> **Measured 2026-10-14, and the boundary probe is deliberately not run.** The sustained movement
> happened, in eight directions, for 1951 frames; the distance-per-tick question is answered from the
> other end — the client's own accepted `GmMove` telemetry (1.44 units per 200 ms typical, 1.96 at
> p99, [PHASE3-SCOPE.md](PHASE3-SCOPE.md) §5.2) and now the client's own per-frame integrator
> (0.133–0.146 units per 16.680 ms frame, [PHASE3-HANDOFF.md](PHASE3-HANDOFF.md) §1.4), both inside
> the resolved law. **Deliberate overspend is a live-character cost for a number the design does not
> use**: `b = playerSpeed · frameSeconds` is a legal step by construction, so the cliff is not on the
> path. The kick is still unwitnessed on the wire and is the one thing this criterion leaves open
> ([PHASE3-HANDOFF.md](PHASE3-HANDOFF.md) §3.1).

**If this fails**: **the dodge does not exist, and with it the point of the project.** The escape
floor of Deliverable 3.4 is the only behaviour left, and the merge decision above already recorded
that escape-only is of questionable value on its own — so the default is to stop and document, and
shipping the floor by itself would be a deliberate operator choice rather than a fallback this plan
assumes. Steel yourself for that outcome before starting, because it is a real possibility and the
honest response is to stop rather than to escalate to more invasive techniques.

### Spike 3.2 — the solver, offline

> **DONE, 2026-10-14.** The solver, the trace recorder and the offline harness exist and are green on
> five synthetic scenarios; the seven defects the harness found are recorded with their symptoms.
> **[SPIKE3.2-OFFLINE-SOLVER.md](SPIKE3.2-OFFLINE-SOLVER.md)** is the handoff, including the one
> outstanding item — a recorded session, which is the only thing that can settle T7.

The decision is a pure function of a plain-data snapshot ([DODGE-ALGORITHM.md](DODGE-ALGORITHM.md)
§2). That property exists **so that the solver can be tested without the game.** Build the snapshot
