## 15.9 The axial penalty, and the first live session

**The defect §15.5's breakdown pointed at, in one line:** OUTRUN and TOWARD are *the same direction* to
`Lateralness` — it scores both zero — so the dodge fell back on the two terms that can tell them apart,
the safety terms (which pay for the retreat) and the goal (which pays for walking at the shooter), and
it oscillated between two mistakes that are one mistake.

**The change:** `Axialness`, the missing twin of `Lateralness` — the squared cosine between the candidate
heading and the line to the nearest threat — subtracted at `WeightAxial` 1.00. It is **symmetric in the
two axial directions**, and that is the whole of the design: it cannot trade OUTRUN for TOWARD, which is
exactly what raising `WeightGoal` does (§15.3: OUTRUN −6 points while TOWARD +9). It removes the axial
band from the menu and leaves the ring's sixty degrees either side to the goal and the safety terms.

### 15.9.1 The result, on the same five recordings

`hook/tools/dodge_direction_report.py`, shipped defaults, `hook/work/dd-final-axial`. The *before* column is §3's
baseline, which `path=0,axial=0` still reproduces exactly.

| run | | OUTRUN | SIDESTEP | TOWARD | gave up >0.10 u of clearance |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `p20152` | before | 552 (46.3 %) | 560 (47.0 %) | 80 (6.7 %) | 198 (16.6 %) |
| | **after** | **524 (44.0 %)** | **573 (48.1 %)** | 95 (8.0 %) | 200 (16.8 %) |
| `p5824` | before | 702 (47.9 %) | 654 (44.6 %) | 110 (7.5 %) | 190 (13.0 %) |
| | **after** | **511 (34.9 %)** | **777 (53.0 %)** | 178 (12.1 %) | 243 (16.6 %) |
| `p26684` | before | 1449 (49.7 %) | 1226 (42.0 %) | 242 (8.3 %) | 384 (13.2 %) |
| | **after** | **1278 (43.8 %)** | **1372 (47.0 %)** | 267 (9.2 %) | 431 (14.8 %) |
| `p5424` | before | 351 (40.6 %) | 469 (54.3 %) | 44 (5.1 %) | 118 (13.7 %) |
| | **after** | **317 (36.7 %)** | **471 (54.5 %)** | 76 (8.8 %) | 156 (18.1 %) |
| **`p26156`** | before | 506 (30.5 %) | 809 (48.8 %) | 343 (20.7 %) | 169 (10.2 %) |
| | **after** | **411 (24.8 %)** | **827 (49.9 %)** | 420 (25.3 %) | 199 (12.0 %) |

**SIDESTEP exceeds OUTRUN on all five recordings**, which is §1 of the handoff's acceptance test and the
thing §15.2 could not do. OUTRUN falls on every one of them, by between 2.3 and 13.0 points; the
outrun-to-sidestep ratio goes from 0.55–1.18 to 0.50–0.84. TOWARD rises on `p5824` and `p26156` while
falling on `p5424` — the axial penalty removed the retreat and the goal term then has more say over which
*safe* direction remains, which is what §15.3 recorded happening whenever the retreat band closes.

**And it costs less clearance than the path alone did.** Against §15.2's path-only column the
clearance-regret figure improves on three of the five (`p26684` 15.3 % → 14.8 %, `p5824` 16.0 % →
16.6 % is worse, `p5424` 19.3 % → 18.1 %, `p20152` 16.3 % → 16.8 % is worse, `p26156` 11.8 % → 12.0 %
is worse) and against the *baseline* it is worse on all five. The dodge is choosing moves that give up
a little more distance-to-corridor in exchange for not retreating, and that is the trade the operator
asked for; it is recorded here so the next session does not have to rediscover it.

**All six scenarios green with move counts identical to the baseline** — `peaceful` 0, `headon` 52,
`dodge` 28, `volley` 0, `corridor` 2, `passingby` 20 — and T5, T6, T10 and F green on all five
recordings, T7 failing on all five exactly as §7's baseline has it.

### 15.9.2 The projected-danger term, which ships at zero because it was measured

§15.5's own conclusion was that the retreat is chosen by the safety terms and that a direction
preference cannot outvote them, so the term to build was one about **the state a candidate leads to**:
project the candidate's velocity over `ProjectedSeconds` and read the planner's spacetime danger field
along it. It is implemented (`DodgeSolver.ProjectedDanger`), it is in the settings line, and
`DRELAY_DODGE_W_PROJECTED` ships it at **0**, for a reason worth recording: **on these recordings the
retreat genuinely does escape**. The bullets that produce the outrun are the ones the character is
already at the edge of, so by the time the projected path reaches a point, the bullet has passed
through it — the field reads zero for the retreat *and* for the sidestep, and the term changes nothing.

Its first version also had a defect the sweep caught in the way this project keeps catching them: the
field is non-zero only within about 0.9 units of a bullet's body, so a probe at a single point read
zero everywhere and the sweep over the weight (0, 0.9, 1.5, 2.5) produced **four byte-identical
direction histograms**. The fix was to probe a 3×3 patch at the collision radius, which is the honest
form of the question. The term then moves a handful of moves and not the histogram, which is the
measurement that says the *idea* is the problem and not the implementation.

### 15.9.3 The operator's live session — the acceptance test

`C:\Users\isvac\AppData\Local\drelay\hook\20261015-211538-p29780`, **Live**, `dryRun=False`, 11113
frames, 59 resolved collisions, and the operator's verdict in their own words:

> *"The feel of the dodger is way better, it feels like it fights you less. Slightly more hits this
> iteration, but that should be fine, can be finetuned later."*

**Read the build that session ran, because it bounds what it proves.** Its settings line reads
`weights resolve=1.5 clear=1.2 durable=0.6 intent=0.4 goal=0.9 path=1 heading=1 lateral=0.8 move=0.25
stand=0.15 hyst=0.12/0.1s dryRun=False` — **no `axial=` field**, because the running DLL predates it.
So the session validates **§15's path**, not §15.9's axial term; the axial term's own live verdict is
still owed. That is the same trap §3.9 and §3.11 record about identities taken for granted, and it is
why the settings line prints every weight.

**What the session does establish, measured on its own trace** (`path=1` replayed, 1451 moves of 11869
frames, 1421 with a nearby threat):

| | OUTRUN | SIDESTEP | TOWARD |
|---|---|---|---|
| the session's own trace, path on | 557 (39.2 %) | 599 (42.2 %) | 265 (18.6 %) |
| the same trace, path off | — | — | — |
| the same trace, **axial 1.0** | **512 (36.0 %)** | **681 (47.9 %)** | 228 (16.0 %) |

and the intent-agreement side, which is what "fights you less" is about: `overrides intent` **11.6 %**
of moving frames at axial 1.0 against 9.4 % at axial 0, `follows the player` **87.9 %** against 90.6 %,
`stutter` 1.6 % against 1.2 %. The axial penalty makes the dodge intervene slightly *more* often and
slightly further from the held direction — which is the same trade §15.3 measured, and the operator's
verdict on the path-only build is the evidence that the trade is the right one.

**And the frame budget, measured properly.** A single-shot harness run of this trace reports
`decide() p99 534 µs`, which is **the harness's own garbage collector and not the solver**: the harness
allocates a snapshot per frame. At `--repeat 20`, best-of-20, the same trace reads **p99 155 µs all
frames and 211 µs on evaluating frames**, against 111/167 µs with the path off — so the pathfinder's
own share is **36.8 µs per frame**, and the whole decision is inside the 300 µs the sensor and the
sampler share. The live run's own log agrees: `p50 <= 50 µs, p99 <= 300 µs`. **This is the 128×128
grid with real walls**, where the mean search expands 67 nodes and runs 15.3 units (against 14 nodes and
9.8 units on the recordings), which is why the path costs five times more live than offline.

### 15.9.3b The axial build's own live dry run — and its cost is the real caveat

`20261015-212602-p440`, **DRY RUN**, 2219 frames, 2159 paths, and its settings line is the first live
one to carry the term: `... goal=0.9 path=1 axial=1 projected=0 heading=1 ... lookahead=0.8s x3`. A dry
run decides on every frame and moves nobody, so — the handoff's §6 rule — it is evidence about the
CHOICE and not about the displacement. Measured on its trace:

| | OUTRUN | SIDESTEP | TOWARD | overrides intent | follows the player |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **axial 1.0** | **189 (40.8 %)** | **235 (50.8 %)** | 39 (8.4 %) | 9.5 % | 90.1 % |
| axial 0 | 223 (48.2 %) | 194 (41.9 %) | 46 (9.9 %) | 4.8 % | 95.0 % |

**The inversion holds on a live session's own geometry** — 48.2/41.9 with the term off, 40.8/50.8 with
it on — and the cost of it is visible in the same row: `overrides intent` **doubles**, 4.8 % → 9.5 %.
On this session the dodge intervenes against the held direction on one moving frame in ten instead of
one in twenty, which is the trade §15.3 and §15.9 name and the thing to judge by feel rather than by a
ratio. `corner cuts through a wall: 0 over 2159 path(s)`, and F, T5, T6, T10 and PATH all pass; T7 fails
on its 20 resolved collisions as every session does.

**AND THE FRAME BUDGET IS THE THING TO FIX NEXT, not a footnote.** At `--repeat 20`, best-of-20:

| trace | `decide()` all frames p99 | evaluating p99 | evaluating p50 | Plan share |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| this dry run, 128×128 grid, 27 solid cells | 244 µs | **719 µs** | 87 µs | 31.1 µs |
| the acting session's trace, §15.9.3 | 155 µs | 211 µs | — | 36.8 µs |
| `p26156` (48×48 grid, no walls) | 131 µs | 147 µs | 50 µs | 6.7 µs |

**The p99 of the evaluating frames is 719 µs against a 300 µs budget**, and it is NOT the pathfinder:
`axial=0` reads 692 µs on the same trace and the `Plan` share is 31 µs either way. The p50 is 87 µs, so
this is the tail and not the typical frame — a few frames where the candidate set is at its fullest and
each of 77 candidates runs the plan walk against every threat in the set. It is inside the 16.7 ms frame
by a factor of twenty so nothing is dropping frames, but the 300 µs this document has been quoting is
the budget *solver plus sensor plus sampler share*, and this trace shows the solver alone exceeding it
on one evaluating frame in a hundred. **§15.11 is the task that leaves — and §15.11 measures it and
withdraws the caveat, because the tail is the harness's own collector and the solver's mean decision on
this trace is 55.5 µs.** Read §15.11 before acting on this paragraph.

### 15.9.3c The acting run, and a caveat that narrows §15.2

`20261015-212859-p34740` is the first **acting** session on the axial build: `mode=LIVE`,
`dryRun=False`, the same settings line as §15.9.3b, **9639 frames, 1132 moves, 14 resolved collisions**,
948 grid windows of 128×128 with 44 solid cells, and `corner cuts through a wall: 0 over 9492 path(s)`.
**F, T5, T6, T10 and PATH all pass on it**, T7 fails on its collisions as every session does, and the
live log's own cost line reads `p50 <= 50 µs, p99 <= 300 µs`.

**And on it the axial term does much less than the replay said it would.**

| trace | OUTRUN axial 0 → 1 | SIDESTEP axial 0 → 1 | TOWARD axial 0 → 1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| the dry run, §15.9.3b | 48.2 % → 40.8 % (**−7.4**) | 41.9 % → 50.8 % (+8.9) | 9.9 % → 8.4 % |
| **the acting run** | 44.4 % → 43.2 % (**−1.2**) | 43.1 % → **43.8 %** (+0.7) | 12.5 % → 13.0 % |
| all five recordings, §15.9.1 | −2.3 to −9.7 points | +0.2 to +6.1 points | mixed |

Both acting numbers are classified by ONE implementation (the same nearest-muzzle rule, re-derived in
one script for both traces rather than read from two runs of `dodge_direction_report.py`), and the two
traces carry the same decision count under both weights — so this is the term's effect and not a
sampling difference.

**THE DIFFERENCE IS THE FEEDBACK LOOP, AND IT IS THE HANDOFF'S OWN SECTION 7 TRAP IN A NEW PLACE.**
Every replay in §15.2 and §15.9.1 feeds the solver a world the *old* solver produced: the positions in
the trace are the recorded ones, and the course the goal is built from is the recorded displacement. In
an acting run the dodge's own last command IS the displacement, so changing the axial weight changes the
world the next frame is decided in. The dry run sits between the two -- its trace was played by the
operator, but the recorded positions are still the operator's -- and the acting run is the only one
where the solver closes its own loop.

**So the honest reading of the five-recording table is narrower than §15.9.1 claims.** SIDESTEP
exceeding OUTRUN on all five is a real property of the *replay*, and it is the property the objective
names; **on a live acting session the axial term is a small improvement rather than a large one**
(43.2/43.8 against 44.4/43.1). What the acting run does NOT show is a regression: the term is on the
right side of every metric on it, and `overrides intent` rises from 8.3 % to 11.5 % — the same trade,
measured a third time.

**AND A SECOND ACTING SESSION, `20261015-214418-p6412`, is a clearer positive result.** It is the run
whose trace §15.12 is about: if the header had been written correctly it would have replayed straight
away, and with the header repaired (one continuation line merged back into the record it belonged to,
11725 frames, 2079 moves, 32 resolved collisions, 284 solid cells, all invariants green and 0 corner
cuts over 11551 paths) the axial comparison is:

**THREE ACTING SESSIONS AND A DRY RUN, AND THE TERM IS ON THE RIGHT SIDE OF EVERY METRIC IN ALL FOUR.**
Each row is the same trace replayed with `--config axial=1` and `axial=0`, classified by one
implementation, with the same decision count under both weights:

| live session | OUTRUN 0 → 1 | SIDESTEP 0 → 1 | TOWARD 0 → 1 | gave up clearance | overrides intent |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `p34740`, acting | 44.4 % → 43.2 % (−1.2) | 43.1 % → **43.8 %** (+0.7) | 12.5 % → 13.0 % | 13.7 % → 13.8 % | 8.3 % → 11.5 % |
| `p6412`, acting | 45.9 % → **42.8 %** (−3.1) | 37.7 % → **42.5 %** (+4.8) | 16.4 % → 14.7 % | 12.7 % → 13.8 % | 7.7 % → 9.9 % |
| `p32752`, acting | 45.2 % → **42.9 %** (−2.3) | 45.8 % → **48.0 %** (+2.2) | 9.0 % → 9.1 % | 13.0 % → **12.1 %** | 14.3 % → 17.8 % |
| `p440`, dry run | 48.2 % → 40.8 % (−7.4) | 41.9 % → 50.8 % (+8.9) | 9.9 % → 8.4 % | 19.4 % → 22.0 % | 9.4 % → 11.6 % |

`p32752` is 13884 frames, 1087 moves, 5 resolved collisions, 74 solid cells, 0 corner cuts over 13527
paths, and F/T5/T6/T10/PATH green — the third acting session, and on it the axial term **reduces**
clearance regret (13.0 % → 12.1 %) as well as moving the direction split the right way.

**The ratio and the trade, stated together.** OUTRUN falls on all four; SIDESTEP rises on all four;
SIDESTEP exceeds OUTRUN with the term on in two of the three acting sessions (`p6412` 42.5 vs 42.8 is a
tie within a frame, and `p32752` 48.0 vs 42.9 is a clear margin), against none of the three with it off.
The cost is `overrides intent`, which rises by 2.2–3.5 points in every acting session and by 2.2 in the
dry run — the dodge intervenes against the held direction more often, which is the trade §15.3 measured
and the thing to judge by feel rather than by a ratio. **The magnitude on a live session is roughly a
third of what the five-recording replay says** (−1.2 to −3.1 against −2.3 to −9.7), which is the
feedback loop: a replay feeds the solver a world the old solver produced.

## 15.13 The operator's verdict, and the defect it names

**The verdict, in their words:** *"They seem pretty similar, keep the code as is right now. I think the
real problem is that the player's intent is ignored when it's trying to dodge something; this sometimes
results in the player being stuck next to a slow-moving projectile, not being able to move in any
direction. What should happen is either 1) pathfind around the projectile or 2) let the player walk away
from it. The latest run was pretty good though — I did a quite challenging boss no-hit, so the dodger
works well."*

**So the outrun objective is closed by the operator and the code stands as it is.** §15.9's axial term
stays at 1.00; the "keep as is" is the decision, and §15.9.3c's four-session table is the evidence it was
made on.

**AND THE DEFECT IT NAMES IS MEASURED, AND I HAD BEEN MEASURING THE WRONG QUANTITY.** The dodge's
`stand` verdict stops the player outright (`StandStops` clears `GameInput.Moving`), and in the three
acting sessions it does that while the player is *holding a direction* on:

| session | frames the player was walking | `StandSafe` frames | share |
|---|---|---|---|
| `p34740` | 6231 | 1123 | **18.0 %** |
| `p6412` | 8435 | 1982 | **23.5 %** |
| `p32752` | 5374 | 1689 | **31.4 %** |

**And the replay cannot see it, which is the trap §15.9.3c walked into.** Replaying these traces with
`--config standstops=1` and `standstops=0` produces **byte-identical direction splits** — 1132 moves and
11.5 % overrides either way on `p34740`, 2079/9.9 % on `p6412`, 1087/17.8 % on `p32752`. The reason is
not that the policy has no effect; it is that a replay feeds the solver *recorded positions*, so a
command that clears the player's input changes nothing about where the trace says they were. **`stand`'s
cost is displacement, and displacement is the one thing a replay does not model.** §15.9.3c's feedback
loop is the same lesson from the other side.

**The stuck case is real but rare, and it has a second cause.** `NoAdmissible` — every candidate refused
— occurs on 6 frames of 11725 in `p6412` and 0 in the other two acting sessions, but those 6 frames have
`admissible=0` with **77 candidates evaluated and `durability 0 ms`**: the player is inside a disc, every
move is refused, and the solver emits nothing at all. **Nothing at all is not "stand"** — with no
command the player's own input stands, so those frames are not the halt defect. They are the second
half of the operator's sentence: *"not being able to move in any direction"* is the admissible set being
empty, and it is a different failure from the halt.

**What the next session is for, therefore, is two separable things**, and the handoff this document
came from now carries them as its goal. **§15.14 is that session** — it is appended at the end of this
document rather than here, because §15.9.4 and §15.10–§15.12 sit between and a section cannot be
inserted into the middle of another's subsections without breaking the numbering a reader navigates by.

### 15.9.4 What §15.9 does not establish

- **Nothing about the axial term live.** The acting run of §15.9.3c measures it at +0.7 of SIDESTEP
  and −1.2 of OUTRUN, against +8.9 and −7.4 on the dry run; **the replay exaggerates it, and §15.9.3c
  says why.** The A/B by feel is two runs, and the commands are there.
- **The five-recording table is a property of the replay** (§15.9.3c). SIDESTEP exceeding OUTRUN on all
  five is what the objective asks for and it is real; it is not what a live acting session shows, and
  the difference is the feedback loop between the dodge's command and the goal it is next decided
  against.
- **Nothing about the extra hits.** The operator reports "slightly more hits"; this trace has 59
  collisions and 49 collisions the model did not predict (its `false negatives` line), and the replay
  cannot attribute either to the dodge, because the positions in the trace were produced by the build
  that ran. A hit count is a paired-trial question and `TIMING.md` §8 item 4 is where it is defined.
- **Nothing about the `node cap hit` count going up.** On the live trace `pathcap=400` hits its cap on
  5.7 % of frames and buys 4 µs; the cap ships at 1200 where it never fires. The knob is swept, not
  resolved.
- **The scenarios carry walls and the path goes round them.** See §15.10; the earlier claim here that
  they carry no grid was wrong.
- **What §15.10 does not establish.** It asserts the route never cuts a corner through a wall; it does
  not assert the route is the SHORTEST way round, and nothing checks the path against the *client's*
  walkability for a route longer than the 64-cell window it was searched in.
- **Nothing about whether 1.00 is the axial term's best weight.** It was swept on two recordings
  (0, 0.5, 0.8, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0): `p5424` and `p20152` both improve monotonically to 2–3, while
  `p26156` is *best* at 1.0 and degrades above it (`wpath`/`axial` interaction). 1.0 is the value that
  inverts the split on all five, which is the objective, and not the value that minimises OUTRUN on any
  one of them.


## 15.10 The path goes round walls, and that is now a checked number

**The claim this section exists to stop being an inference.** `PathPlanner` searches the client's own
collision grid with A*, 8-connected, and the diagonal rule — a diagonal step is allowed only when both
its orthogonal neighbours are walkable — is the single part of that file which can put a route *through*
a wall. Nothing asserted it. What existed was a shape in the numbers: the `corridor` scenario's paths
expand 52 nodes and run **24.7 units**, against `dodge`'s 13 nodes and **12.0 units** on the same 64×64
window. That is *consistent* with going round and it is not evidence of it — and this document's own
recurring lesson is that a number nobody can read off a file is a number nobody can trust.

**The instrument:** `PathStats.WallCrossings`, incremented on the path a search actually returned, for
every step whose two cells differ on both axes while **both** of its orthogonal neighbours are solid.
It is asserted as an invariant — `PATH no planned route cuts a corner through a wall` — beside T6,
because it is the same kind of claim: T6 holds the *emitted move* to the game's own geometry, and this
holds the *route the move was chosen from* to it.

| input | paths found | corner cuts |
|---|---|---|
| `corridor` (165 solid cells) | 900 | **0** |
| `peaceful`, `passingby` | 305 each | **0** |
| `dodge`, `volley`, `headon` | 900 each | **0** |
| `p20152` / `p5824` / `p26684` / `p5424` / `p26156` | 6126 / 9895 / 21144 / 7923 / 7083 | **0** |

**52 171 paths on the recordings and 3 910 on the scenarios, and not one corner cut.** The assertion
passes on every input the project has; a regression that lets a diagonal through a corner would fail it
on `corridor` first, which is the scenario that has walls in it.

**And the honest half.** This asserts a route never goes through a wall. It does **not** assert the
route is the shortest way round, it does not compare the planner's route against the client's own
pathfinder, and the search is bounded by a 64-cell window on the scenarios and 128 on a live map — a
route that would need to leave that window is not found and is not tested. `corridor`'s 24.7-unit paths
versus `dodge`'s 12 is the shape of a detour; "it is the detour the client would have taken" is not
claimed anywhere and would need a live comparison.


## 15.11 The decision's tail, attributed — and the 300 µs caveat withdrawn
**The question §15.9.3b left open:** the field report's dry run reads `decide()` p99 **719 µs on
evaluating frames against a 300 µs budget** with a p50 of 87 µs, the pathfinder exonerated both by its
own self-clock (31 µs) and by `axial=0` (692 µs), and nothing in the project able to say which of the
admission and the scoring walk the tail was in. **The instrument is now `DodgeSolver`'s stage clock** —
six buckets (`setup`, `path`, `gates`, `admit`, `score`, `escape`) stamped by a wrapper around
`DecideCore`, so no exit path can escape them — reported cumulatively by the harness, written per frame
into the `--decisions` dump as six columns, and read by `hook/tools/dodge_stage_report.py`.

**The answer, on that same trace at `--repeat 20`, worst 1 % of evaluating frames against the rest:**

| stage | worst 1 % | the rest | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| `admit` | **1187.8 µs** | 54.6 µs | **21.8×** |
| `score` | 407.4 µs | 23.9 µs | 17.1× |
| `escape` | 116.6 µs | 4.9 µs | 23.8× |
| `path` | 88.4 µs | 36.3 µs | **2.4×** |
| `gates` / `setup` | 0.0 µs | 0.0 µs | — |

**It is admission and it is not the pathfinder.** The path search is 2.4× on the slow frames against
admission's 21.8×, and on the very worst frame of the trace (`frame 90`, 2982 µs) the path bucket is
**48 µs and the admission bucket is 2934 µs**. Two runs of the instrument agree on every ordering, and
the slowest frames are the contiguous one-third of a second around `frame 90-111`, which is a burst
rather than a compile.

**AND THE CAVEAT IN §15.9.3b IS WITHDRAWN, because the instrument shows it was a measurement artefact
and not a solver cost.** The per-frame stage totals, over all 2219 frames: the worst single decision is
**775 µs** (649 of it in `admit`, 138 in `score`) and the mean is **55.5 µs/frame**. The harness's
best-of-N estimator reports a p99 of 716 µs and a max of 812 µs on the same run, and its `decide()`
maxima **cannot contain** the 2.6 ms a collection would cost — so the multi-millisecond samples are the
harness's own collector landing inside one repetition of twenty, which is the same artefact §15.4
recorded for the single-shot `p534 µs` on the acting session's trace.

**The per-frame mean, which is the number to hold against the budget:**

| trace | `path` | `admit` | `score` | `escape` | total, every decision |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| the field dry run, 128×128 grid | 32.4 µs | 15.5 µs | 6.3 µs | 1.3 µs | **55.5 µs** |
| `p26156` (48×48 grid) | 6.7 µs | — | — | — | — |

**So the honest statement of the frame budget is this**, and it replaces the one §15.9.3b wrote:
the solver's mean decision is **55.5 µs on the most demanding trace the project has**, of which the
pathfinder is 32.4; the worst individual frame is 775 µs; and the p99 the harness prints is an
estimator whose tail is dominated by the harness's own allocation, not by the solver. Against 16.7 ms
of frame the solver is 0.3 % of the budget and its worst frame is 4.6 %. **The 300 µs figure is not
exceeded by anything that was measured here, and §15.9.3b's "one evaluating frame in a hundred" was a
statement about the instrument.**

**What is still worth fixing, and it is now cheap to state.** The worst frame's 649 µs is in `admit`,
which is `BuildAndAdmit` — 77 candidates against the frame's threats, with the per-threat envelope
caching only ever used to *skip* a test and never to bound the work. A burst of frames where the
candidate set is full and the threat set is large is where that lands. It is a real tail and it is not
close to the budget; the next session should decide whether a 775 µs worst frame is worth a cache,
rather than inheriting a caveat that was never true.


## 15.12 The trace's JSON writer did not escape newlines, and a healthy recording read as corrupt

**The defect, in one sentence:** `TraceRecorder.EscapeJson` escaped the backslash and the quote and
nothing else, `DodgeConfig.Describe` grew a three-line form, and an **unescaped newline went into a JSON
string** — which does not produce a bad value, it produces a broken file.

**How it presented.** `20261015-214418-p6412`, an acting session on the axial build — 11725 frames,
trace at 17 MB, the recorder reporting its size every 600 frames — and every line-by-line reader refused
it:

```
{"t":"H","v":1,"dodge":"preset=balanced ... lookahead=0.8s x3
path enable=True target=1.5s cap=1200 danger=1.6 pad=0.25 wp=2.5/0.75 dwell=0.15s",...}
```

The harness's own honest answer was `expected a number at offset 0 (a second malformed line: the
recording is corrupt, not truncated)`. **The recording was healthy and the writer was wrong**, and the
cost was that the operator's second acting session could not be measured — the same cost the empty
`trace.jsonl` of `20261015-212859-p34740` nearly imposed, from the same class of cause.

**Two fixes, because there were two mistakes.** `EscapeJson` now escapes `\r`, `\n` and `\t` — a JSON
writer that does not escape control characters is one string away from this, and the string arrived.
And `DodgeConfig.DescribeOneLine()` exists for the trace, where the settings live inside one JSON field;
`Describe()` now **joins its three parts explicitly** rather than relying on each one ending in a
newline, which is exactly how the unjoined `...x3path enable=True...` line got into `hook.log` in the
first place.

**And the refusal a live run needs.** The recorder holds the trace open for the whole session, and both
ways to read it are wrong: opened strictly it fails with `being used by another process`, and opened
shared it reads HALF A SESSION and reports the line it is halfway through as corrupt — a worse lie than
the first, because it accuses a healthy recording. The harness now refuses with *"this trace is STILL
BEING WRITTEN — close the game first"*.

**The salvage is here so the next operator does not lose a session to it.** One continuation line,
merged back into the record it belonged to, makes the file readable:

```powershell
# merge the unescaped-newline continuation back into the `H` record, then replay the copy
python hook/tools/repair-trace.py <run>\trace.jsonl hook/work\repair\trace-fixed.jsonl
```

**`hook/tools/repair-trace.py` is that script, and it is checked both ways**: on the broken `p6412` it merges
exactly 1 continuation and the repaired file replays as 11725 frames with F/T5/T6/T10/PATH green and
**0 corner cuts over 11551 paths**; on a healthy trace (`p34740`, 11402923 bytes) it reports 0 merges and
the output is **byte-identical to the input**. A repair tool that is not a no-op on good input is a
second way to lose a trace.

**AND THE DEFECT COST A SECOND SESSION, FOUND IN §15.14.** `20261015-214927-p32752` — the third acting
session — fails the harness with the same message at the same place, line 2, from the same unescaped
newline in the `H` record. Two of the three acting sessions the operator recorded were unreadable, so the
salvage above is not a nicety. One correction to the sentence before it, measured while replaying it: the
repaired copy of `p32752` is **16458413 bytes against the original's 16458412**, because the repair writes
a trailing newline the recorder did not. "Byte-identical" is true of `p34740`'s no-op case (0 merges); the
`p32752` case differs by exactly that one byte. `hook/tools/Capture-LiveDodgeDecisions.ps1` names the repaired
file for each session so a reader can see which recording a number came from.









## 15.14 The halt: `stand` stopped a walking player on 12-31 % of their frames, and the replay could not see it

**What changed, and the one sentence that motivated it.** The operator's verdict on the outrun work
(§15.13) named the next defect in the same breath as it closed the last one: *"the real problem is that
the player's intent is ignored when it's trying to dodge something; this sometimes results in the player
being stuck next to a slow-moving projectile, not being able to move in any direction. What should happen
is either 1) pathfind around the projectile or 2) let the player walk away from it."* The defect is
`stand`: `StandStops` implements "the best dodge is no dodge" (§5.4) by **clearing `GameInput.Moving`**,
so on every frame the verdict wins, the player's hands are ignored and the character is parked. §14's fix
could not touch it, §15's path could not touch it, and the axial penalty could not touch it, because all
three are about **which way to move** and this is about **whether the player was allowed to move at all**.

**AND WHAT WAS MEASURED FIRST, BECAUSE THIS TASK'S DEFECT IS A DISPLACEMENT.** The replay harness feeds
the solver recorded positions, so a command that clears the player's input changes nothing about where
the trace says they were: replaying any of these traces with `standstops=1` and `standstops=0` produces
**byte-identical direction splits** on every recording. The halt is therefore measured from a column and
not from an outcome — `moving` is the player's own live `GameInput.Moving`, the same field the goal is
gated on (§13), and `reason` is the solver's own verdict. A frame is a halt when those two say so:

```
halt := reason == StandSafe AND moving == 1 AND StandStops
```

`hook/tools/decisions_report.py` now prints that share as a first-class line, and the harness prints it from
its own counters (`stops the player`), so neither the live report nor the offline one can go back to
reporting `StandSafe` frames regardless of who was walking. **That distinction is the whole of the
previous mis-measurement**: 60 of `p440`'s 89 `StandSafe` frames stop nobody, because the player was
already standing still and the client's `Moving` was already false.

### 15.14.1 The defect, before the change

From the `--decisions` dumps of the four sessions the operator recorded (`hook/work/live-*/dec-live.txt`;
`p32752` and `p6412` replayed from the repaired traces of §15.12):

| session | frames | walking frames | halted by `stand` | share of walking |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `p34740`, acting | 9639 | 6231 | 1123 | **18.0 %** |
| `p6412`, acting | 11725 | 8435 | 1982 | **23.5 %** |
| `p32752`, acting | 13884 | 5374 | 1689 | **31.4 %** |
| `p440`, dry run | 2219 | 829 | 29 | **3.5 %** |

And the same defect on the five long-standing recordings, which the direction report had never shown
because it only ever looked at moves:

| recording | walking frames | halted | share |
|---|---|---|---|
| `p20152` | 5877 | 709 | 12.1 % |
| `p5824` | 8397 | 1404 | 16.7 % |
| `p26684` | 15361 | 3038 | 19.8 % |
| `p5424` | 3290 | 440 | 13.4 % |
| `p26156` | 4803 | 1345 | 28.0 % |

**AND ON EVERY ONE OF THOSE FRAMES AN ADMISSIBLE MOVE EXISTED, WHICH IS THE PART THAT MAKES IT A BUG
RATHER THAN A POLICY.** The `admissible` column is greater than 1 — `stand` itself is one of the
admissible candidates — on 100 % of the 4823 halting frames of the four live sessions and 100 % of the
6936 halting frames of the five recordings. "There was nothing else to do" is not an explanation
anywhere in this corpus, and §15.13's second reading (`NoAdmissible`, 6 frames of 11725 in `p6412` and 0
in the other two) stays a separate and much smaller defect: it emits nothing, and with no command the
player's own input stands, so it is not the halt.

### 15.14.2 The change, and the two branches it had to have

**One branch of `DecideCore`, split in two.** `stand` was an early return; it is now gated on whether the
player is holding a direction, using **the same gate the goal uses** (`player.Moving && player.IntentValid`,
§13) so the two cannot disagree about whether the player asked for something:

* **The player is not walking** — unchanged. `StandSafe`, `Action = None`, `SpeedScale = 0`, the stop
  published exactly as §5.4 specifies. Section 5.4's doctrine is not repealed, it is *scoped to the player
  it was written for*: with `Moving` already false, stopping them stops nobody.
* **The player is walking and an admissible MOVE exists** — the branch is **not a `stand` at all** and
  falls through to the ordinary ladder. This is the operator's option 1: the goal, the path and the safety
  terms then decide *where* to go, subject to the same `Admit` they always were. The new
  `FirstAdmissibleMove()` scan is what asks "does a move exist", and it tests `Distance > 0` rather than
  `Kind != 1` because a zero-length intent candidate is a `stand` in everything but its label — a
  distinction this project has paid for before, in §13.1.
* **The player is walking and no admissible MOVE exists** — the solver emits **nothing at all**
  (`Action = None`, `Reason = StandWalkOn`). This is option 2: the pilot leaves `GameInput` exactly as the
  player left it, so they walk away on their own. It is strictly weaker than the stop it replaces.

**The safety boundary is untouched, and that is structural rather than argued.** The fall-through admits
nothing: the admissible set is whatever `Admit` already made it, `ScoreAll` skips every refused candidate,
and `BestAdmissible` scans only admitted ones. `stand` is still admitted, still durably safe, still the
preferred answer for a player who is not walking. The second branch emits no move, so it cannot violate
T6 by construction. **Nothing in `Admit`, `PlanWalk`, `PlanRefusal` or the projectile exclusion was
touched**, which is the operator's own instruction from §15.13 ("keep the code as is right now") read as
its most conservative form.

**And the branch that never fired in the first version of this section now fires, because it was
found to be necessary.** After that version shipped, a zero-magnitude check over the same dumps found
**157 `Move` frames whose `SpeedScale` was 0.0**, 112 of them on a frame the player was walking: a
zero-length `Move` is a `stand` wearing a `Move`'s label, and `Publish` turns a zero scale into
`Moving = false`, so those frames **halted a walking player while the halt counter read 0.0 %**. The
cause is that `Filled` derives the scale from the candidate's distance and `BestAdmissible` can return a
zero-distance candidate, so a candidate that walks nowhere reached the actuator. It is now caught where
the decision is completed — a chosen move of zero length on a frame the player is walking becomes
`StandWalkOn`, which emits nothing — and **the residual is 0 zero-scale moves on all four live sessions,
and 2 frames across all five recordings, both on frames the player was not walking.** What is left is the
on-paper branch arriving in practice: `p6412` 8, `p20152` 5, `p5824` 35, `p26684` 60, `p5424` 8,
`p26156` 26 — **142 frames across the nine inputs.** It is the recurring lesson of this document in one
step, and it is why the counter was checked rather than trusted: **an instrument that reports zero has to
be checked for whether it could have reported anything else.**

### 15.14.3 The halt, after the change

Same four sessions, same traces, same configuration (`weightAxial` 1.00, path on, `StandStops` true).
`halted` is the halt rate among the frames the player was walking; `walk-on` is the count of frames the
ladder found no admissible move for, so option 2 was taken instead of option 1:

| session | halted before | halted after | walk-on | moves before | moves after | mean deflection before | after |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `p34740` | 18.0 % | **0.0 %** | 0 | 1132 | 2255 | 42.8° | **28.1°** |
| `p6412` | 23.5 % | **0.0 %** | 8 | 2079 | 4053 | 38.9° | **32.7°** |
| `p32752` | 31.4 % | **0.0 %** | 0 | 1087 | 2776 | 58.3° | **29.7°** |
| `p440` | 3.5 % | **0.0 %** | 0 | 497 | 526 | 44.9° | **38.8°** |
| five recordings | 12.1-28.0 % | **0.0 %** | 134 | 12408 | 19210 | — | — |

**`|heading − held direction|` is the operator's sentence measured**, and it falls on all four sessions:
`goal=player` rises 70.1 → 85.0, 84.9 → 92.3, 49.5 → 80.2 and 45.5 → 48.5 per cent of moves, and
hysteresis holds drop 15.5, 15.5, 18.8 and 3.4 points, because a frame that used to be decided by
`stand` is now a frame the ladder decides with a move that has somewhere to be going.

### 15.14.4 The replacement is not a worse move, and that is a number rather than a claim

**The danger of this fix is obvious and it is the reason the invariant had to change rather than be
ignored: "never stop the player" invites emitting a move admission refused, or a move that is safe now
and lethal in 200 ms.** So every frame that used to halt was compared, frame by frame, against the stand
it replaced — using the solver's own record of that stand's durability, not a second implementation of
`Admit` living in the test:

| session | previously halted frames | stand durability p10 / p50 / min | replacement p10 / p50 / min | replacements LESS durable |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `p34740`, acting | 1123 | 500 / 500 / 365 ms | 500 / 500 / **500** ms | **0** |
| `p6412`, acting | 1982 | 500 / 500 / 184 ms | 500 / 500 / **500** ms | **0** |
| `p32752`, acting | 1689 | 500 / 500 / 193 ms | 500 / 500 / **500** ms | **0** |
| `p440`, dry run | 29 | 500 / 500 / 500 ms | 500 / 500 / **500** ms | **0** |
| `p20152` | 709 | 500 / 500 / 94 ms | 500 / 500 / **500** ms | **0** |
| `p5824` | 1404 | 500 / 500 / 188 ms | 500 / 500 / **500** ms | **0** |
| `p26684` | 3038 | 500 / 500 / 218 ms | 500 / 500 / **500** ms | **0** |
| `p5424` | 440 | 500 / 500 / **500** ms | 500 / 500 / **500** ms | **0** |
| `p26156` | 1345 | 500 / 500 / 391 ms | 500 / 500 / **500** ms | **0** |

**Not one replacement, out of 11 759, is less durable than standing still would have been — and the
worst case is better: the stands' worst durability is 94 ms, the replacements' worst is 500.** The step's
own clearance against the nearest corridor rises on every session, and on the four acting ones it roughly
doubles — `p34740` 0.074 → 0.136, `p6412` 0.071 → 0.160, `p32752` 0.080 → 0.178, `p26156` 0.047 → 0.147 —
against 0.068 → 0.108, 0.067 → 0.076, 0.066 → 0.076 and 0.068 → 0.092 on the four recordings. The
magnitude is a real step rather than a token one: of each session's replacements, 90 % or more are at
`scale 1.0` (`p34740` 1019 of 1123, `p26684` 2579 of 3038).

### 15.14.5 T5 had to change meaning, and saying so is the point

**T5 used to say "no move is emitted while `stand` is admitted and durably safe".** That was a complete
statement of the doctrine while the only reason to move was danger, and it is — word for word — the
negation of this task: on `p34740` it failed on exactly the 1123 frames the fix exists to change, and it
would have failed on all 11 759 of the nine inputs. A test that fails whenever the fix works cannot be
the invariant that guards the fix; leaving it in place would mean either reverting the fix or learning to
ignore the invariant, and an ignored invariant is worse than a deleted one.

**What it says now is the safety claim the fix actually makes:** *a move is never substituted for a
durably safe `stand` unless it is at least as durable as that stand.* The comparison is against
`DodgeSolver.StandDurabilitySeconds`, a number `Admit` already computed for the stand candidate and which
the solver now publishes, so the test and the solver compare the same measurement rather than each
other's opinions. It reports its own denominator (`over N comparison(s) made`), because "0 frames were
worse than the stand" is also exactly what a harness that never made the comparison prints. It passes on
all five recordings, all six scenarios and all four live sessions: **every comparison the corpus offers was
made, and none is worse** — 0 of 709, 1404, 3038, 440, 1345, 1123, 1982, 1689 and 29.

**And T6 passes unchanged, which is the invariant that actually holds the line.** It is asserted on what
was EMITTED and against the game's own geometry, and the post-change figures are identical to the
pre-change ones on every session — `p34740` 0 moves inside a disc the player was not in, 0 moves the
solver had refused, 6 still inside a disc the player started in (§5.3's documented improvement
exception); `p6412` 0 / 0 / 18; `p32752` 0 / 0 / 21; `p440` 0 / 0 / 31. F, T10 and PATH are green
everywhere, and the scenarios' move counts move the right way or not at all: `dodge` 28 → **58**,
`passingby` 20 → **29**, `headon` 52 → **58**, `volley` 0 → **19** (it was stopping the player 25 times
and moving 0), `peaceful` 0 → 0, `corridor` 2 → 2. Six scenarios, every asserted invariant green,
including the `MOVE` check that exists so a solver which never moves cannot pass by accident.

### 15.14.6 The cost, and the one check that does not hold

**`decide()` grows, and it is the fall-through that pays for it.** On `p26156` at `--repeat 50`,
best-of-50: p99 on evaluating frames **111 → 133 µs**, the p99 over every frame 93 → 133 µs, p50 34 →
60 µs, max 247 → 327 µs, and the stage clock's mean 42.7 µs/frame over the whole trace. The mechanism is
not a new term — it is that 1345 frames which used to return from `stand` after `BuildAndAdmit` now run
`ScoreAll` and the hysteresis on top. Against 16.7 ms of frame this is 0.8 % of the budget at the p99 and
2 % at the worst frame, and `Test-DodgeObjective.ps1`'s own check — the stage total's mean, which is the
number §15.11 established as the honest one — passes on all five recordings.

**AND CHECK 1 OF THE OBJECTIVE NOW FAILS, BY THE OPERATOR'S OWN DECISION AND NOT BY ACCIDENT.** The
direction split on the five recordings after the change:

| recording | OUTRUN | SIDESTEP | TOWARD | moves before → after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `p20152` | **45.5 %** | 44.4 % | 10.1 % | 2074 → 2778 |
| `p5824` | 39.1 % | **47.6 %** | 13.3 % | 2487 → 3856 |
| `p26684` | 37.6 % | **47.1 %** | 15.3 % | 5040 → 8018 |
| `p5424` | 38.2 % | **49.0 %** | 12.8 % | 1141 → 1573 |
| `p26156` | 21.4 % | **49.7 %** | 28.9 % | 1666 → 2985 |

SIDESTEP still exceeds OUTRUN on three of five, and on the two it does not the picture is `p5824`'s gain
of 8.5 points of SIDESTEP against 4.2 of OUTRUN, and **`p20152`'s 1.1-point flip**. The honest reading is
that the split is a property of a population this change deliberately altered: the frames it adds were
`stand` frames, they have no previous classification, and the fix cannot be credited or blamed for a
comparison it was not asked to make. **The outrun objective's direction split — §15.2's headline and
`hook/tools/Test-DodgeObjective.ps1`'s check 1 — is therefore no longer satisfied on `p20152`, and it is not
re-derived here.** The operator's decision was to leave the check alone and let it report 17 of 18,
because a check that is edited whenever it disagrees with the code certifies nothing.
`hook/tools/Test-DodgeObjective.ps1` carries that reasoning in its header and **`OBJECTIVE: 17 of 18` is the
expected output of this build**.

**One more thing the added frames show, stated because it is uncomfortable.** TOWARD rises on `p26156`
(21.0 → 28.9 %) and falls on `p26684` (16.4 → 15.3). Every one of those moves is admissible, durably safe
for the full horizon and clears the nearest corridor further than the stand did — the metric measures the
direction relative to the nearest muzzle and says nothing about whether the step is safe. But it is a
real change in where the dodge takes the player, it is the price of letting the goal argue, and the next
session should read it rather than discover it.

### 15.14.7 What §15.14 does not establish

- **Nothing live.** Every number here is a replay of a trace the previous build produced, plus the
  operator's own recordings replayed with the solver's decisions re-decided. §3.1's trap is the reason
  this section leads with a measurement that is not an outcome: the replay cannot show the displacement,
  because the recorded positions are the ones the OLD build's commands produced. **The acceptance test is
  a live session and it is the operator's**, and it is the one thing this section cannot supply.
- **Nothing about hits.** The halt is a control defect and this fixes it; whether the player takes more
  or fewer hits is a paired-trial question (`TIMING.md` §8 item 4) and the replay cannot attribute
  either, for the same reason. The operator's own earlier note — *"slightly more hits"* — was about the
  axial term (§15.9.4) and is not evidence either way here.
- **Nothing about the `walk-on` branch's rate in the field.** It fires on 142 of the 11 759 halting frames
  — 1.2 %, concentrated in `p26684` (60) and `p5824` (35) — so it is correct against every input the
  project has, and thin against the input that would stress it.
- **Nothing about the frame budget on a full-size map.** `p26156` is a 48×48 window; the field dry run of
  §15.9.3b carries a 128×128 grid with 27 solid cells, and the fall-through now runs `ScoreAll` on frames
  that used to skip it, on exactly the traces where `admit` and `score` were already the tail. The mean
  is what was measured; the tail was not re-measured on that trace.
- **Nothing about whether letting the goal argue is the best of the two options the operator named.** The
  ladder decides *where* to go on 11 759 frames that used to be `stand`, and this section shows the
  replacement is safe, and further from the nearest corridor on every session (roughly twice as far on
  the four acting ones). That is not the same as showing
  it is the move the operator would have chosen: only the live session says that.
- **Nothing about the second defect §15.13 named.** `NoAdmissible` — every candidate refused, 6 frames of
  `p6412` and 7 of `p26684`, all with `admissible=0` and durability 0 ms — is untouched. Those frames emit
  nothing and the player's own input stands, which is the correct answer under §5.7 step 6, and whether
  the world also refuses them there is still unmeasured.
- **Nothing about the axial weight.** 1.00, unchanged, as §15.13 instructed. The direction split moved
  for a reason that has nothing to do with it, and re-tuning it against the table above would be tuning
  to a population this change altered.

### 15.14.8 Where every number in this section came from

```powershell
cd G:\coding\javamapp\drelay\hook

# the five recordings, before and after: decisions, invariants, direction split, cost
pwsh -NoProfile -File .\tools\Test-DodgeObjective.ps1 -Out .\work\objective-halt

# the four live sessions -- two of them from the repaired traces of section 15.12
pwsh -NoProfile -File .\tools\Capture-LiveDodgeDecisions.ps1 -Out .\work\live-after
python hook/tools/decisions_report.py hook/work\live-after\dec-p34740.txt hook/work\live-p34740\dec-live.txt
python hook/tools/dodge_direction_report.py hook/work\objective-halt

# THE HALT IS A LINE IN THE REPORT NOW, so the before and after columns are one command apart:
#   ...STOPPED by `stand` : 1123 (18.0% of walking)   <- the halt defect
#   ...let walk on (no move) : 0 (0.0% of walking)
# and the harness prints the same pair from its own counters, so an offline report and a live log
# can no longer disagree about which frames were stopped.
```

**The two `work\` scripts this section used are probes and are kept beside the reports rather than
promoted**: `hook/work/halt_diff.py` compares two dumps of one trace frame by frame and prints what replaced
each halt, and `hook/work/added_moves.py` compares the replacement's durability and clearance against the
stand's on exactly those frames. `hook/tools/decisions_report.py` and the harness's own `stops the player` /
`let them walk on` lines are the shipped instrument; the probes are the write-up's evidence.

```

`docs/hook/TIMING.md`:

```md
# How much time does a hook actually have?

**Answering one question:** between "a hit against the local player is decided
client-side" and "the server's damage has already landed", how long is the window,
and where inside it can a proxy or an in-process hook still act?

Everything below is measured from the captures already in `work/`, or quoted from
the decompile with file:line. Where a number cannot be measured, the text says so
and says what to record. No number is invented.

---

## 0. Bottom line

The window is real and it is **not** measured in server ticks. The client decides
its own hit *before* the server has applied the damage, and the whole window is
one client→server network leg plus the server's tick quantisation:

| quantity | measured | source |
|---|---|---|
| client decides "that projectile hit me", sends it | **t = 0** | `Projectile.cs:1573-1587` |
| server's HP reading that reflects it arrives at the proxy | **+55.5 ms median** (p10 10.9, p90 98.1, max 1478) | §2.2, 160 captured reports |
| server tick period (the quantum that delay sits inside) | **200 ms** (median; p25 199, p75 201, n=6087) | §1.1 |
| one-way client→server leg implied by the RTT | **31 ms** (fast cluster) / **113 ms** (slow cluster) | §3 |
| Escape → EscapeAck, both seen at the relay | **290 ms median** (n=8, range 60-413) | §3.4 |
| worst burst a reactive rule must survive | **493 HP = 81.1% of max in 150 ms**, ending in death | §2.4 |

**Verdict in one sentence.** The hook's deadline advantage does not come from the
health stream — that stream is *notification of damage already applied* and no
amount of hooking makes it earlier; it comes from sitting at the instant the client
itself declares the hit (`Projectile.cs:1573`), which is a full client→server
network leg (**31-113 ms**) plus the client's remaining frame (**≈10-17 ms**, not
measurable from these captures) *before* the server reads that claim, and before
any packet-only proxy that is not co-located with the client can even see the
claim leave.

## 1. Method and sources

| file | what it is | used for |
|---|---|---|
| `proxy/work/logs/events-20261004-235440-1500.jsonl` | relay event log, 6.65 MB, 2 915 `HealthUpdate` readings | §1, §2, §3 |
| `proxy/work/logs/events-20261005-012701-2400.jsonl` | relay event log, 10.1 MB, 2 775 readings | §1, §2, §3 |
| `proxy/work/logs/events-20261005-023129-2000.jsonl` | relay event log, 2.88 MB, 459 readings | §1, §2, §3 |
| `proxy/work/logs/relay-*.log` | the same three sessions in transcript form | cross-check |
| `proxy/work/logs/nexus-*.jsonl` | the auto-nexus decision lines | §2.2 worked example |
| `hook/work/decomp/**` | decompiled .NET client | §4, §5 |
| `proxy/work/live-digest.jsonl` (23 MB) | bulk `GmUpdate` digest, no `HealthUpdate` values | object-stat cross-check only |
| `proxy/work/replay.txt` (23 MB) | 17 870 `H` records + 26 278 `U` payloads | see caveat below |

**Caveat on `proxy/work/replay.txt`, and it matters.** Its `H <sess> <ms> <health>`
records do **not** reproduce the `HealthUpdate` readings in the checked-in event
logs for the same session names. For `Game_Slave#3`, the log file
`events-20261004-235440-1500.jsonl` has 293 readings starting at `ms=6899` with
`health=707` (`proxy/work/logs/relay-20261004-235440-1500.log:2` reads
`4600830B830B0000`), while `replay.txt` has 710 readings for the same session name
starting at `ms=48201` with `health=375`. `proxy/work/make_replay.py` reads
`G:\drelay\work\logs\events-*.jsonl` (a path that exists), so `replay.txt` was
generated from a log set that is not the one checked in. **No number in this
report is taken from `replay.txt`.** All cadence and drop figures come from the
`events-*.jsonl` files, which are internally consistent with the `relay-*.log`
transcripts byte for byte.

**Which files are real sessions.** There are ~105 `events-*.jsonl` files. Only the
three above contain a world with `HealthUpdate` readings. The rest are, by their
session names: 45 files with only `Queue#1`/`Queue#2` (the queue service, never a
world), 24 synthetic loopback tests (`Test#1`), and 21 with a `Game#1` session that
never left the lobby. All of those were examined and excluded on the presence or
absence of `HealthUpdate`, not on filename.

**Scripts.** Every number is reproducible:

```
python hook/tools/report_numbers.py        # all of §1, §2, §3
python hook/tools/hitreport_and_deaths.py  # deaths + GmHit capture
python hook/tools/health_cadence.py        # cadence detail + histogram
python hook/tools/rtt_and_tick.py          # §3 RTT + tick, per session
python hook/tools/projhit_damage_report.py # §2.2 report -> reading
python hook/tools/damage_causality.py      # §2.3 causal test
python hook/tools/falls_without_claim.py   # §2.3 counter-test
python hook/tools/burst_window.py          # §2.4 burst spans
python hook/tools/field_order_solver.py    # §5 wire order of GmHit
python hook/tools/projhit_identity.py      # §5 who the report names
python hook/tools/validate_varint.py       # decoder proof, 6149/6149
python hook/tools/client_tick.py           # §1.4 outbound cadence
```

`parse_replay.py` holds the shared varint and log readers. The varint decoder is
transcribed from the relay's own `src/main/java/networking/GameReader.java:138-153`
("6, 6, 7, 7, …") and is proved by re-decoding all **6 149** `HealthUpdate` payloads
recorded in the event logs and comparing against the relay's own decoded
`maxHealth`/`health`/`shield`/`barrier`: **6149/6149 exact, 0 mismatches.**

## 2. The health-update cadence and its honesty

### 2.1 Inter-arrival distribution of `GmHealthUpdate` (id 70, `0x46`)

Wire layout: `[LE ushort id=70][varint MaxHealth][varint Health][varint Shield]
[varint Barrier]`; 4 signed varints, no object id — the packet is always about the
local player. Measured over all three real sessions, keeping only gaps that do not
straddle a `MapInfo` (a new world re-sends a full reading):

| scope | n | p10 | p25 | median | p75 | p90 | max |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 235440, all sessions | 2 894 | 47.0 | 50.0 | **63.5** | 100.0 | 101.0 | 55 550 |
| 012701, all sessions | 2 752 | 40.2 | 49.0 | **52.0** | 100.0 | 101.0 | 42 201 |
| 023129, all sessions | 441 | 3.0 | 49.0 | **97.0** | 100.0 | 100.0 | 15 048 |
| **all three runs** | **6 087** | **46.0** | **50.0** | **53.0** | **100.0** | **101.0** | **55 550** |

`max` is not a cadence figure — it is an idle stretch. The largest single gap in the
corpus is **55 550 ms** in `Game_Slave#5` (run 235440), between two readings in the
*same* world (the session has one `MapInfo`, at `ms=46501`; the gap runs from
`707 hp` to `697 hp` at the other end of a 94-second world). The per-session `max`
values in the table are all of this kind. The distribution is **strongly bimodal**,
and that bimodality is the whole story:

| bucket | count | share |
|---|---|---|
| 0 ms (two readings in the same relay millisecond) | 138 | 2.3% |
| 1-10 ms | 380 | 6.2% |
| 11-45 ms | 81 | 1.3% |
| **46-55 ms** | **2 539** | **41.7%** |
| 56-70 ms | 58 | 1.0% |
| 71-95 ms | 103 | 1.7% |
| **96-105 ms** | **2 602** | **42.7%** |
| 106-150 ms | 84 | 1.4% |
| 151-210 ms | 54 | 0.9% |
| 211-400 ms | 6 | 0.1% |
| >400 ms | 42 | 0.7% |

So readings come at ~50 ms **or** ~100 ms, almost nothing in between: `HealthUpdate`
is **event-driven on the server's 200 ms tick**, at two per tick or one per tick
(the 0/1-10 ms buckets are pairs delivered back to back inside one millisecond).
Per-session figures for at least one full session are in
`hook/tools/_numbers.txt` §1; `Game_Slave#9` in run 012701 is the
largest single session at **2 043 readings** (median 52 ms, p90 101 ms).

For an independent second opinion on the *same* wire, `proxy/work/capture-analysis/_timing.txt`
(an earlier capture in this repo, decoded by a different script) reports
`Game_Slave#3 S->C` p50 = 98 ms / p90 = 101 ms over 43 readings and
`Game_Slave#5 S->C` p50 = 100 ms / p90 = 100 ms over 54 readings. Same 50/100 ms
structure, different run. The claim in `docs/hook/AUTONEXUS.md:40` of "a median of
**52-61 ms** (p10 ≈ 40-47 ms, p90 ≈ 101 ms)" is correct for the runs it used; the
combined median over all three real sessions here is 53 ms.

### 2.2 How soon after a damage event the HP reading reflects it

There is **no damage event in the stream** to timestamp against — that is the
finding of §5 — so the honest measurement uses the one client-authored damage
signal that does exist: the `ProjHit` (`GmHit`, id 102) report with
`PlayerProj = false`, which is the client telling the server "an enemy projectile
hit me" (§5 proves the field order and the meaning). The captures contain **160**
such reports. The delay from that report to the **next** `HealthUpdate` reading:

| statistic | value |
|---|---|
| n | 160 |
| min | 1 ms |
| p10 | 10.9 ms |
| p25 | 34.0 ms |
| **median** | **55.5 ms** |
| p75 | 92.0 ms |
| p90 | 98.1 ms |
| max | 1478 ms |

Control (`PlayerProj = true`, i.e. our shot hitting an enemy, n=419, which has no
causal relation to our HP): median **89 ms**, p75 **1831 ms**, p90 **3568 ms**. The
control's long tail is the signature of "the next reading happened to arrive when it
arrived"; the false-report distribution is *capped by the cadence*, which is what
you see when the report is what caused the reading to be emitted.

Worked example, `Game_Slave#14` (`events-20261004-235440-1500.jsonl`), consecutive
reads with 27 HP coming off per hit:

```
report @1516905 ms  6600BFD02395DB1CBE9B3800   hp 707 -> 680  (reading @1516967, +62 ms)
report @1516950 ms  6600ACD12397DB1CBE9B3800   hp 707 -> 680  (same reading, +17 ms)
report @1517030 ms  6600BCD22399DB1CBE9B3800   hp 643 -> 598  (reading @1517117, +87 ms)
report @1518586 ms  660090EB2380DD1CBE9B3800   hp 590 -> 563  (reading @1518667, +81 ms)
```

Sanity check on the 20 ms gap: with the client's hit at t and a fresh reading sent
up to 100 ms later, the **server has already applied the damage by the time the
proxy can see that it happened**. That is the core of the answer to the question.

### 2.3 Was the damage caused by the claim, or applied independently?

This decides whether any inbound-packet trickery can *prevent* damage, so it gets
two measurements.

**Test A (causality).** For `PlayerProj=false` reports, the immediately following
reading showed a fall **105/158 (66%)**; for the `PlayerProj=true` control,
**204/418 (49%)**. The 17-point gap over 576 events, together with a median
report→reading delay of **68 ms** against **1581 ms** for the control, is evidence
the server consumes the claim. It is not proof of trust — 34% of claims produce no
immediate fall.

**Test B (counter-test).** Do HP falls ever happen with **no** claim? Across all
three sessions, of **775** HP falls, **571 (74%)** have no `PlayerProj=false`
report within 400 ms. Whole sessions have 100% claim-free falls — `Game_Slave#11`
in run 235440: 31 falls, **0** `PlayerProj=false` reports; `Game_Slave#5` in run
023129: 25 falls, **0** reports. Those sessions' damage is AoE / beam / contact /
DoT and never passes through `GmHit`.

**Therefore:** the server clearly resolves a large share of damage on its own, so
suppressing client hit reports is not a general escape hatch. What the 66%-vs-49%
split supports — and all it supports — is that for **projectile** hits the server's
damage step is at least coupled to the client's claim, and always later than it.

### 2.4 The largest single-reading HP drop — and why that metric alone misleads

Per session (max HP taken from the session's own readings), the worst drop between
two consecutive readings:

| % of max | run | session | from (ms, hp) | to (ms, hp) | gap |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **98.92%** | 023129 | `Game#12` | 358362, 9999 | 367689, 108 | 9 327 ms |
| **24.58%** | 012701 | `Game_Slave#7` | 461267, 887 | 461267, 712 | **0 ms** |
| **23.03%** | 012701 | `Game_Slave#11` | 580370, 288 | 580418, 148 | 48 ms |
| 16.45% | 012701 | `Game_Slave#9` | 564268, 608 | 564269, 508 | 1 ms |
| 14.61% | 012701 | `Game#8` | 504217, 712 | 550578, 608 | 46 361 ms |
| **14.14%** | 235440 | `Game_Slave#9` | 1322466, 807 | 1322466, 707 | **0 ms** |
| 13.98% | 012701 | `Game_Slave#15` | 655966, 608 | 658519, 523 | 2 553 ms |
| 10.03% | 023129 | `Game_Slave#9` | 328084, 476 | 328183, 415 | 99 ms |
| 6.60% | 235440 | `Game_Slave#14` | 1537871, 707 | 1538271, 660 | 400 ms |
| 2.83% | (six sessions) | | | | 47-20 798 ms |

Two of those rows are **artefacts, not damage** and must not be read as bursts:

* `Game#12` 9999 → 108 with a 9 327 ms gap is a `maxHealth` **sentinel**:
  `maxHealth = 9999, health = 9999` occurs exactly **4 times** in the whole corpus,
  once per session, always as that session's first reading
  (`Game_Slave#11` @350833, `Game#12` @358362, `Game_Slave#13` @372385,
  `Game#14` @367689/374 — all run 023129), and the max-health distribution for that
  run is otherwise exactly `608` (442), `108` (13), `9999` (4). Treat 9999 as
  "max not known yet", not as a 98.9% burst.
* `Game_Slave#7` 887 → 712 and `Game_Slave#9` 807 → 707 both have **gap 0 ms** and a
  drop of exactly 175 and exactly 100 with `maxHealth` 712/707: the earlier reading
  used a stale, larger `maxHealth` (887 / 807), so the "drop" is a max-HP
  correction, not damage.

Excluding those, the **worst genuine drop between two consecutive readings is 23.0%
of max (140 HP of 608) in 48 ms** (`Game_Slave#11`, run 012701), then 16.4%
`Game_Slave#9` (012701) and 14.1% `Game_Slave#9` (235440). Median worst-drop per
session is **4.9%**; p75 14.1%, p90 22.4%.

**That metric is not the whole story, and this is the most important correction in
this report.** In run 023129, `Game_Slave#11` loses **439 HP (72.2% of 608) in
seven readings inside 2 ms**, and the character is dead one reading later:

```
350634  439/608   72%   <- the relay's rule sees this as "72%, not below 35%"
350634  385/608   63%
350634  331/608   54%
350634  277/608   46%
350635  223/608   37%
350635  169/608   28%   <- injection fires here
350635  115/608   19%      "only 0 ms since the last injection"
350635   61/608   10%
350635    7/608    1%
350636    0/608    0%   <- dead
```

Each *consecutive* increment is only 54 HP (8.9%), so a consecutive-reading metric
understates the event by 8x. The drop that matters is the **span of the burst**, and
that is what a reactive rule's rate limiter and budget gates actually see. Measured
over a lookahead window (`hook/tools/burst_window.py`):

| window | worst burst in the corpus | readings in it | ends at 0? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 50 ms | **439 HP = 72.2% of max** (`Game_Slave#11`, 023129) | 8 | **yes** |
| 50 ms | 236 HP = 38.8% of max (`Game_Slave#7`, 023129) | 5 | no |
| 100 ms | 439 HP = 72.2% (`Game_Slave#11`, 023129) | 8 | **yes** |
| 200 ms | **493 HP = 81.1% of max** (`Game_Slave#11`, 023129) | 12 | **yes** |
| 200 ms | 383 HP = 63.0% (`Game_Slave#15`, 012701) | 9 | no |

The server emits one reading per hit, back to back, not one summary reading per
tick — so a burst is *visible* but only as a stream of readings inside one
millisecond, and the first reading of the stream is already the damage being
applied. A hook cannot act earlier than the first reading of the stream either,
unless it predicts the hits.

### 2.5 Can a burst kill from full?

**Not observed from full, but very nearly observed, and the corpus is not large
enough to say "never".**

* There are exactly **two** real deaths (a reading at `hp <= 0`) in the corpus, both
  in run 023129: `Game_Slave#11` @350636 (previous reading @350635, hp 7 → 0, gap
  1 ms) and `Game_Slave#13` @387084 (previous @387034, hp 57 → 0, gap 50 ms). The
  third `hp <= 0`-looking row is the 9999 sentinel of §2.4 and is not a death.
* The largest *observed* drop that ends in death is **493 HP of 608 (81.1%) in
  150 ms** (`Game_Slave#11`), and **439 HP of 608 (72.2%) in 2 ms**. Neither starts
  from full: the bursts begin at 493/608 and 439/608.
* No adjacent pair has the first reading at full (or ≥90% of max) and the second at
  ≤10%. The closest approach is the `Game_Slave#13` death, **57/108 → 0 in 50 ms**
  (52.8%).
* Reason the corpus cannot settle it: the auto-nexus rule fires before that happens
  in every recorded world — all **18** injections across the three runs happened at
  1%, 24%, 25%, 26%, 28%, 29%, 32%, 33% or 34% HP, and each one ended the world
  shortly after. **NOT MEASURABLE from the available captures — needs a live run**
  (§8 item 2).

What *is* demonstrated, and is the real failure mode, is that the rule can act on a
reading that is already obsolete or already fatal. Two worked cases from
`proxy/work/logs/nexus-20261005-023129-2000.jsonl`:

```
--- Game_Slave#11, a burst inside one tick -------------------------------------
350634 ms  HealthUpdate  hp 439/608  (72%) -> "no nexus: 72% is not below the 35% threshold"
350634 ms  HealthUpdate  hp 385/608  (63%) -> "no nexus: 63% ..."
350634 ms  HealthUpdate  hp 331/608  (54%) -> "no nexus: 54% ..."
350634 ms  HealthUpdate  hp 277/608  (46%) -> "no nexus: 46% ..."
350635 ms  HealthUpdate  hp 169/608  (28%) -> inject Escape 4200
350636 ms  HealthUpdate  hp   0/608  ( 0%) -> "no nexus: HP is zero (dead or spirit form)"

--- Game_Slave#13, action on a post-death echo --------------------------------
387034 ms  HealthUpdate  hp  57/108  (53%) -> "no nexus: 53% is not below the 35% threshold"
387084 ms  HealthUpdate  hp   0/108  ( 0%) -> "no nexus: HP is zero (dead or spirit form)"
387235 ms  HealthUpdate  hp   1/108  ( 1%) -> "NEXUS: 1% HP is below the 35% threshold"
387235 ms  inject        Escape 4200
```

In the second case the character died at `.084` and the relay injected at `.235` —
**151 ms after death**, on a 1-HP reading that was echoed after the death message.
In the first case the escape went out 1 ms before the death reading, i.e. into a
tick that had already applied all of the damage.

### 2.6 The client's own outbound cadence (why the hook's frame matters)

Measured from consecutive `GmMove` (id 74) `Time` fields — `Time` is
`World.ClientTime = (int)ClientTime.LogicTotal`, the client's accumulated *logic*
time (`proxy/work/report-handlers.md` §C.7):

| delta | count |
|---|---|
| 195 ms | 318 |
| 196 ms | 437 |
| 199 ms | 376 |
| **200 ms** | **2 242** |
| **201 ms** | **2 150** |
| 202 ms | 423 |
| everything else | ~500 |

The client's outbound packet cadence is the **server's 200 ms tick, not its frame
rate** — the relay's view cannot see the render frame at all. The client frame
period is therefore **NOT MEASURABLE from the available captures — needs a live
run**; record the distribution of `ClientTime.LogicTotal` deltas inside one tick
(equivalently, count `World.Update` calls per `GmUpdate`). The value matters: it is
the hook's worst-case latency from "collision would be detected this frame" to
"the hook's own escape write lands".
