## 3. Round-trip time

### 3.1 What is measured vs inferred

Everything in this section is **observed at the relay**, i.e. at the same
observation point a packet proxy occupies. It is therefore a direct measurement of
what a proxy gets, and only an upper bound on what the client's NIC sees.

Three clocks are present, and they answer different questions:

| pair | what the delta really is | n | median |
|---|---|---|---|
| `CheckPing` (106, C→S, empty) → `CheckPingAck` (107, S→C, empty) | close to a true application round trip: request goes out, server answers directly | 776 | see below |
| `Ping` (92, S→C) → `Pong` (72, C→S) | the **relay's own observation skew**, not the network — the client answers the server's ping within a millisecond | 1 555 | **0 ms** (p90 1 ms, max 5 ms) |
| `Escape` (66, C→S, `4200`) → `EscapeAck` (158, `9E0001`) | one round trip **plus** the server's decision, both endpoints observed here | 9 | **290 ms** |

`Ping`→`Pong` measuring 0 ms is itself the proof that the relay sees both
directions of a session with negligible internal skew, so the other two pairs are
network/server time, not relay time.

### 3.2 `CheckPing` → `CheckPingAck`

The distribution is **bimodal by destination, not noisy**, and the split is stable
across all three runs. Sessions map to destinations via each run's `RETARGET` lines:

* every `Game#NN` → `3.71.176.153:6411` or `18.145.215.213:6411`
* every `Game_Slave#NN` → `18.145.161.25:6410`

that mapping holds without exception in all three runs
(`relay-20261004-235440-1500.log`, `relay-20261005-012701-2400.log`,
`relay-20261005-023129-2000.log`).

| cluster | n | min | p10 | p25 | median | p75 | p90 | max |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Game_Slave#NN` (6410) | 583 | 29 | 44.0 | 51.5 | **63.0** | 74.0 | 99.6 | 304 |
| `Game#NN` (6411) | 193 | 176 | 187.0 | 198.0 | **226.0** | 277.0 | 320.8 | 380 |

Per-session medians inside the fast cluster: 46-86 ms
(`Game_Slave#17` 46.0, `Game_Slave#13` 50.0, `Game_Slave#11` 58.0,
`Game_Slave#7` 59.0, `Game_Slave#14` 61.5, `Game_Slave#9` 64.0,
`Game_Slave#5` 65.0). Inside the slow cluster: 188-314 ms (`Game#10` 188.0,
`Game#8` 198.5, `Game#4` 219.5, `Game#6` 235.0, `Game#2` 267.0).
**The clearest counter-example is an intra-run inversion.** Both sessions dial the
same destination under this grouping, yet in run 012701 `Game_Slave#3` measures a
**68.5 ms** median (n=4) while `Game_Slave#5` measures **203.5 ms** (n=20) — and in
the other two runs it is the other way round (`Game_Slave#3` also shows 219.0 ms in
235440, while `Game_Slave#5` shows 61.5 / 51.0 ms in 235440 / 023129). So the
fast/slow split is not purely a property of the `6410` vs `6411` route; the same
route varied by run. The relay has no route-level instrumentation to explain it, so
this is recorded as unexplained run-to-run variance, and the two cluster medians
(63.0 ms and 226.0 ms) are quoted as the observed range of the two legs rather than
as fixed constants.

**Inferred, one-way:** halve the RTT, since the two directions are unmeasured
individually. **31 ms** for the fast cluster (31.5 = 63.0/2), **113 ms** for the slow
one (113 = 226.0/2). Stated as an inference, not a measurement: the asymmetry is
unknown, and a relay sitting between client and server cannot separate the two legs.
Given the run-to-run variation just noted, treat 31-57 ms as the plausible one-way
range for a well-connected client and 90-113 ms for the `6411` route.

### 3.3 Server tick

Measured independently as the arrival cadence of `GmUpdate` (id 1) on the
server→client stream:

| run | n | p10 | p25 | median | p75 | p90 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 235440 | 2 636 | 198.0 | 199.0 | **200.0** | 201.0 | 202.0 |
| 012701 | 3 161 | 198.0 | 199.0 | **200.0** | 201.0 | 202.0 |
| 023129 | 1 831 | 199.0 | 200.0 | **200.0** | 200.0 | 201.0 |

Exactly 5 Hz, matching the reference engine's `kServerTickSec = 0.2f`. One further
consequence, from `proxy/work/report-handlers.md:406-407`: `GmUpdateAck.Time` is
`LastClientTime`, i.e. the **previous** tick, so the server's round trip and its
tick quantisation are both present in anything the client acks.

### 3.4 `Escape` → `EscapeAck`, and what it implies for the deadline

Every pair where both ends were observed at the relay (9 events; the other injections
in these runs ended a world, so the ack never came):

| run | session | Escape @ | EscapeAck @ | delta |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 235440 | `Game#4` | 41 861 | 42 140 | 279 ms |
| 235440 | `Game_Slave#20` | 1 821 721 | 1 822 019 | 298 ms |
| 235440 | `Game_Slave#3` | 37 297 | 37 357 | **60 ms** |
| 235440 | `Game_Slave#5` | 140 319 | 140 609 | 290 ms |
| 235440 | `Game_Slave#9` | 1 402 991 | 1 403 404 | 413 ms |
| 012701 | `Game#8` | 531 753 | 532 016 | 263 ms |
| 012701 | `Game_Slave#3` | 52 937 | 53 074 | 137 ms |
| 023129 | `Game_Slave#11` | 357 450 | 357 726 | 276 ms |
| 023129 | `Game_Slave#13` | 404 193 | 404 481 | 288 ms |

median **290 ms**, range 60-413 ms. The 60 ms and 137 ms pairs sit *below* the same
session's RTT cluster, which is consistent with the server answering a client packet
that arrived just before a tick boundary — i.e. the ack is quantised by the 200 ms
tick, so it is an upper bound on the round trip rather than a clean estimator of it.
`docs/hook/AUTONEXUS.md:44` reports "245-305 ms" for the same quantity in its own run;
the 9-pair ensemble here is consistent with that.

**Deadline arithmetic.** Let the server apply damage to the local player at its own
clock time `T`. Anything the client fires at real time `t` is processed by the
server at the first tick boundary at or after `t + one_way`:

```
T_earliest_effect = next_tick_boundary( t + one_way )
necessary condition for arriving before the server's damage step:
    t + one_way  <  T
```

Substituting the measured values, with `one_way ≈ 31 ms` (fast cluster, inferred):

* To influence the tick that applies damage, a packet must leave the client
  **≥ 31 ms before `T`**, and on average **31 + 100 = 131 ms** before `T` because the
  tick grid is unknown from outside and uniform (200 ms grid, mean half-period 100 ms).
* The relay-observed `Escape`→`EscapeAck` of **290 ms** is the full `2 × one_way`
  plus server-side decision and tick quantisation, and is the number to use when
  asking "does the escape beat the next damage": an escape emitted at `t` is
  *answered* ~290 ms later, and the server has had a tick boundary in between.
* The current reactive rule acts **on** a `HealthUpdate`, i.e. at `t ≈ T + one_way`
  (the reading is generated after the damage is applied). It is therefore always
  **one one-way leg + up to one tick too late to prevent anything** — it can only
  react to damage already taken.

---

## 4. The client's own hit timing

### 4.1 When the client decides a hit, and where the code is

`hook/work/decomp/DarzasDominion.Darza.Game.Objects/Projectile.cs`, `HitCharacter()`
(called from `Hit()` at `:1505`, which is called from `LateUpdate` at `:1246`):

```csharp
// Projectile.cs:1514-1517
private bool HitCharacter()
{
    int clientTime = World.ClientTime;       // the client's own logic clock

// Projectile.cs:1573-1587
    if (DistanceSquared(World.Player.Position) < num2 * num2 && 0 == 0
        && CanHitEntity(World.Player.GameId, clientTime) && 0 == 0)
    {
        bool num3 = RegisterEntityHit(World.Player.GameId, clientTime);
        World.Player.HitBy(this);            // cosmetic: damage numbers, flash, sfx
        if (Prefs.close_menus_on_damage && 0 == 0) base.Scene?.OnDamage();
        Client.SendPacket(new GmHit
        {
            Time = clientTime,               // <-- the client's clock
            ProjectileId = GameId,
            ObjectId = World.Player.GameId,  // <-- targets the LOCAL PLAYER
            PlayerProj = PlayerOwned         // <-- false for an enemy shot
        });
        if (num3 && 0 == 0) return ... 1 ... != 0;
    }
```

and the caller:

```csharp
// Projectile.cs:1246
else if ((Desc.Telegraph <= ... 7 || (double)num >= Desc.Telegraph * ... 24)
         && Hit() && 0 == 0)
{
    Remove();
    return;
}
```

`num2` is set at `:1597` (`num2 = World.Player.Radius + Radius;`) or at `:1555`
(`num2 = MathF.Max(num2, (float)Desc.Proximity);`). The test is a circle overlap
against `World.Player.Position` — the client's **locally predicted** position, not
the server's.

### 4.2 Is the collision test cosmetic, or ahead of the server?

**It runs ahead of the server, and it is also cosmetic — both at once, and that is
the whole point.**

* It is a **claim**, not a resolution: it emits `GmHit` to the server (`:1581`,
  `:1687`, and `AoeBomb.cs:287,323`) and never writes the outcome to HP. The client
  derives a *predicted* damage number only for display, inside
  `Entity.HitByProjectile` (`Entity.cs:2459`), which ends in
  `World?.ShowDamageMessage(...)` (`Entity.cs:2566-2580`) and `PlaySfx`, using a
  locally computed `GetDamageTaken(...)`. Nowhere there is `Health` written.
* It therefore runs **at the client's local collision instant**, which precedes the
  server's own resolution by at least the client→server leg (`one_way`, §3), and by
  more if the server re-checks against the authoritative position from its last
  received `Move`.
* `World.ClientTime` — the timestamp the client puts in the claim — is the client's
  own logic clock (`World.cs:9505  ClientTime = (int)time.LogicTotal;`), not a
  server clock, which is why a proxy can use `GmHit.Time` only as a client-side
  ordering key.

### 4.3 Does anything in the client ever decrement `Player.Health`?

**Confirmed: no. Only the `GmHealthUpdate` handler ever sets `Player.Health` to a
server value, and nothing decrements it.** Evidence: an exhaustive search of the
whole decompile for assignments to `Health`/`Player.Health`.

Searches run (via `grep`, over all `*.cs` in `hook/work/decomp`):

```
\.Health\s*(-=|\+=|=)        -> 34 matches, all enumerated below
Health\s*[-+]=               -> 4 matches, all `target.Health += source.Health`
                                (item tooltip stat aggregation, not gameplay)
```

The complete set of writes to a `Health` field in the client:

| file:line | write | gameplay? |
|---|---|---|
| `DarzasDominion.Darza.Game/World.cs:16001-16116` (specifically `:16055`) | `world.Player.Health = gmHealthUpdate.Health;` inside the registered `HealthUpdate` handler | **the only authoritative writer** |
| `World.cs:16052` | `world.Player.Health = 0;` on the `PlayerDead` branch of the same handler | death only |
| `World.cs:7905` | `Player.Health = 0;` in the local `PlayerDead` path | death only |
| `World.cs:481`, `:484` | the decompiler's duplicate closure copy of the same handler | same code |
| `...Objects.Entities/Player.cs:4951` | `Health = stat.GetShort();` in `Player.ProcessStat`, `case StatsType.Hp` | spawn / refresh, **not** per hit |
| `...Objects.Entities/Entity.cs:148`, `:168` | `Health = 25;` in base ctor / `Reset()` | initialisation |
| `...Objects.Entities/Entity.cs:431`, `:435` | `Health = stat.GetLong() / GetInt()` in `Entity.ProcessStat` | spawn / refresh for non-player entities |
| `...UI.Desktop.Tooltips/DesktopItemTooltip.cs:10033`, `...UI.Mobile.Tooltips/MobileItemTooltip.cs:9251` | `target.Health += source.Health;` | tooltip affix aggregation |
| `...Data.Affixes/AffixData.cs`, `AffixPointMath.cs`, `ItemData.cs`, `ItemQuality.cs`, `ArmorTraits.cs`, `Affixes/AffixPoints.cs`, tooltip classes | `Health` | data/UI fields on *other* types |

Neither `Entity.HitBy(Projectile)` (`:2198`), `Entity.HitBy(AoeData)` (`:2203`),
`Entity.HitBy(int, ...)` (`:2339`) nor `Entity.HitByProjectile(Projectile)`
(`:2459`) assigns to `Health`, and neither does `Projectile.HitCharacter`. The
per-hit path is **purely presentational on the client**.

Two consequences, both load-bearing for the design:

1. A hook cannot "see the damage before the client does" in `Player.Health` — the
   value is the server's, delivered already-applied. The earliest client-side
   knowledge is the **collision test** at `Projectile.cs:1573`, not the HP number.
2. Conversely, the hook does not need to guess at HP: `Player.Health` at any moment
   is exactly the last `GmHealthUpdate` value, so a hook's prediction can be seeded
   from the authoritative number and then differ from it only by the damage it has
   not yet seen. That is a much better footing than a proxy's, which must infer HP.

---

## 5. What the client tells the server: `ProjectilesAck` / hit reports

### 5.1 There is no packet whose payload is a "damage taken" value

Exhaustive check. I enumerated every class in
`hook/work/decomp/DarzaGameNet.Packets.Game.Client/` (117 classes) and extracted every
public field plus the `hehe(n)` lookup index from `Type =>`. **No client→server
packet carries an HP, health, damage or shield field.** The complete field lists are
in the tool output of
`python -c "..."` run over that directory (the pick: `GmHit` = `Time, ProjectileId,
ObjectId, PlayerProj`; `GmAllyHit` = `Time, ProjectileId, ObjectId`;
`GmPlayerLaserHit` = `Time, LaserId, ObjectId`; `GmSweepHit` = `Time, SweepId`;
`GmProjectilesAck` = `ProjectileId, Time, Position`). Searched for the words
`Health`, `Hp`, `Damage`, `Shield` across `DarzaGameNet.Packets.Game.Client/*.cs`:
the only hits are enum members and unrelated classes.

`GmHealthUpdate` (id 70) is **server→client only** — there is no client class for
id 70. So the direction is unambiguous: HP travels from server to client and never
the other way.

### 5.2 `ProjectilesAck` (id 64, client→server) — positional/clock, not damage

`DarzaGameNet.Packets.Game.Client/GmProjectilesAck.cs` (`Read` at `:55`,
`Ack => true` at `:17`): fields in order **`ProjectileId`, `Time`, `Position`**.
Exactly one send site in the whole client, `World.cs:10989`, inside the drain of
`GmProjectiles`:

```csharp
// World.cs:10989, quoted in proxy/work/report-handlers.md §C.1
Client.SendPacket(new GmProjectilesAck
{
    ProjectileId = _ECF0_F129_ED83_ECC8_F588.ProjectilesId,
    Time = ClientTime,
    Position = Player.GamePoint        // <-- the client's own position
});
```

So every `GmProjectiles` (id 86) from the server is answered with "this is where I
am, at this clock" — which is *why* the server can resolve a projectile's geometry
against the client's position one tick later, and why the client's hit claim
(`GmHit`) is plausible to the server. It carries **no damage**. Captured counts in
the 012701 run: 4 221 `Projectiles` / 4 221 `ProjectilesAck`, i.e. always paired.

### 5.3 `ProjHit` (id 102, class `GmHit`) — the nearest thing, and it does exist

`proxy/work/report-handlers.md:374` lists id 102 `ProjHit` among the enum members with
"no packet class at all", then `:377` infers it is `GmHit.cs` (pool index 212, used
by no other class). The captures confirm the inference and fix the field order by
brute force rather than by reading the obfuscated state machine:

`hook/tools/field_order_solver.py` tries all 24 permutations of
`{Time, ProjectileId, ObjectId (varint), PlayerProj (bool)}` against all **580**
captured `ProjHit` payloads. Result: exactly **6** orderings consume every payload
exactly (the three varints are byte-indistinguishable from each other), all with
`PlayerProj` in the last position. Time-monotonicity within a session — `Time` must
be non-decreasing — breaks the tie at **99.5%** for `Time` first against **87.2%**
for the alternatives:

```
ProjHit  =  Time(varint) -> ProjectileId(varint) -> ObjectId(varint) -> PlayerProj(bool)
```

This is *not* the order the decompiler prints for `GmHit.Write`
(`Time -> PlayerProj -> ProjectileId -> ObjectId`, `GmHit.cs:20-57`): that method is
a flattened `while(true) switch(num)` state machine and the printed source order is
not the wire order. The measurement wins.

`PlayerProj` is **not** always true, and that is the discovery:

| PlayerProj | count | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `true` (419) | 72% | the client's own projectile hit an enemy — `Projectile.cs:1687` |
| `false` (161) | 28% | the client's **non-owned** projectile hit the target it names — `Projectile.cs:1581` |

and the target it names is the **local player**:

* In every session where `PlayerProj=false` reports exist at all, the ObjectId is a
  single value: `Game_Slave#14` → 460542 (9x) and 1361 (10x);
  `Game_Slave#11` → 456799 (11x); `Game_Slave#15` → 457237 (16x);
  `Game_Slave#17` → 457492 (13x); `Game_Slave#7` (012701) → 453757 (32x);
  `Game_Slave#9` (012701) → 456719 (9x); `Game_Slave#11` (023129) → 460338 (14x).
* `hook/tools/projhit_identity.py` cross-references that id against the
  per-object `StatsType.Hp` (int16) values the server streams in `GmUpdate`:
  `Game_Slave#9` ObjectId **458799** appears as an object with an Hp stat in
  **120** `GmUpdate` packets, and **120/120** of those Hp values match a
  `HealthUpdate` reading within 2 HP; `Game_Slave#9` (023129) ObjectId **459766**:
  **15/15**. That is the local player.
* `GmMapInfo` (id 5) is what carries `PlayerId` (`GmMapInfo.cs:18`, read at `:287`,
  matched at `World.cs:10142`), but the relay does not decode the field into its
  event log, which is why the cross-reference above had to go through the Hp stat.

**So, plainly:** the client *does* tell the server when it has been hit — not with a
damage number, but with a collision claim naming the local player's object id, the
projectile id, and the client's own clock. That packet is `GmHit` / `ProjHit`
(id 102) with `PlayerProj = 0`. The design brief's belief that "there is no
damage-report packet" is **refuted for projectile hits**, and **confirmed for
everything else**: there is no AoE/beam/contact/DoT equivalent, and no packet
anywhere in the client→server direction carries a damage or HP value (§5.1).

### 5.4 The search that establishes the negative

Run over `hook/work/decomp/DarzaGameNet.Packets.Game.Client/*.cs` (117 files) and
`hook/work/decomp/**/*.cs`:

```
pattern: \.Health\s*(-=|\+=|=)          -> 34 matches (all in §4.3's table)
pattern: Health\s*[-+]=                 -> 4 matches, item tooltips only
pattern: new GmHit|GmHit\b|new GmProjHit|GmProjHit
        -> 5 matches: Projectile.cs:1581, :1687, AoeBomb.cs:287, :323, GmHit.cs:6
pattern: class GmProjHit                -> no match (no such class)
enum enumeration of GmPacketType        -> no client class exists for id 70
```

### 5.5 Capture counts for completeness (run 012701, from the relay's own log)

| packet | direction | count |
|---|---|---|
| `Projectiles` (86) / `ProjectilesAck` (64) | S→C / C→S | 4 221 / 4 221 |
| `ProjHit` (102) | C→S | 484 |
| `AllyHit` (174) | C→S | 756 |
| `HealthUpdate` (70) | S→C | 2 775 |
| `Update` (1) / `UpdateAck` (83) | S→C / C→S | 3 184 / 3 182 |
| `Aoes2` (161) / `Aoes2Ack` (?) | S→C / C→S | 252 / 252 |

Note the near-1:1 pairings (`Projectiles`/`ProjectilesAck`, `Update`/`UpdateAck`,
`Aoes2`/`Aoes2Ack`) and the *asymmetric* hit traffic: 484 `ProjHit` against 2 775
health readings, i.e. **83% of HP changes are not accompanied by any client hit
claim** — the same 74% (400 ms window, all three runs) that §2.3 Test B reports.

## 6. The deadline arithmetic, as a table

Time is measured from **the first instant the client could know**, which §4 shows is
the local collision test (`Projectile.cs:1573`), not the HP number. `one_way` is the
inferred 31 ms (fast cluster, §3.2); the slow cluster's 113 ms and the measured
`Escape`→`EscapeAck` of 290 ms (§3.4) are quoted where they change the answer.
"Packet-only proxy" means a proxy at the relay's observation point; "in-process hook"
means code inside the client process.

| threat | first client-side knowledge → impact | what a packet-only proxy can do | what an in-process hook can do | can an escape plausibly arrive in time? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Single slow projectile** (visible approach, e.g. 300+ ms of flight) | `GmProjectiles` announces `Position` + `Angle`; speed and lifetime are **not on the wire** and must come from object data. Client collision at impact − 0. | See the shot at spawn; act at spawn + its own processing (~1 ms, §2.4's relay took 0 ms-1 ms decision). Cannot see the bullet's true later position (no re-broadcast). | Evaluate the true swept path against the real player position and hit radius **every frame**, and write the escape the same frame the danger becomes real. | **Yes, comfortably.** Any escape sent ≥ 31 ms + tick offset before impact lands; a 300 ms flight leaves ≥ 200 ms of margin even at 290 ms ack. |
| **Fast projectile** (crosses the player's hitbox in < one frame of travel, e.g. >20 tiles/s) | the client's collision test at impact − 0; the hit report leaves at impact + 0. | Sees `ProjHit` only *after* the client has already been hit; the server reading follows **+55.5 ms median** later (§2.2). Effectively reactive-only. | Detect the *predicted* intersection on the previous frame(s) — the swept-segment test is arithmetic the client already has all the inputs for. Gains the whole report→reading interval, **55.5 ms median / 98.1 ms p90**. | **Yes if the hook predicts** (it buys 55-98 ms plus one frame); **no if it waits for the collision**, because the claim is already in flight and the server has already read it. |
| **Point-blank spawn** (enemy fires from inside the player's hitbox) | t = 0 *at* the collision; there is no earlier frame at which the projectile had a different position. | Nothing before the claim; nothing after. | At best one frame: the hook still learns only when the collision test runs. | **No.** The damage is decided in the same frame the first knowledge exists; **NOT MEASURABLE from the available captures — needs a live run** to confirm the frame period (record `ClientTime.LogicTotal` deltas per tick, §2.6). |
| **AoE that lands on the player's tile** | `GmAoes2`/`GmAoes` announces the AoE; `AoeProjectile` carries `Target`, `Value` (damage), `Radius`, `Delay` (`proxy/work/report-handlers.md` §C.3) — **a telegraph in the packet stream**, unlike a bullet. | Best case in the whole protocol for a proxy: exact impact tile, exact damage, and a `Delay`. Relay-inject the escape on arrival of the AoE packet. | Same information, ~1 frame earlier, plus access to the live tile/occupancy state (a proxy must infer blocking). | **Yes, if the Delay is non-zero** — measured AoE delays are not in these captures: **NOT MEASURABLE from the available captures — needs a live run** (record `AoeProjectile.Delay` vs. the `HealthUpdate` fall). AoEs with `Delay = 0` are point-blank rows. |
| **Damage-over-time / beam** (laser, sweep, tick damage) | `GmLaserRetarget` (271) / `GmLaserHit` (364) / `GmLaserRetarget` handler queues; `GmPlayerLaser` (68) carries `Position` + `Angle`. | A proxy can see the beam exists but not its current hit state; and §2.3 Test B shows whole sessions whose damage never produces a `ProjHit` (0 claims for 31 and 25 falls). | Can test beam-vs-player geometry per frame and escape on the first frame of intersection, before the first tick of damage. | **Partly.** The first tick is preventable if the hook is one frame ahead; subsequent ticks are **not** — once the server is ticking damage, no escape beats the next tick. |
| **Melee / contact hit** *(does not exist - operator-confirmed, and no damage site in the decompile requires it; retained only as the "no client involvement" control case)* | t = 0 at the collision; there is no telegraph in the packet stream at all (no `ProjHit` is generated for contact damage in any captured session). | Nothing. The proxy's first signal is the reading, **+55.5 ms median** after the collision. | Same t = 0, but the hook can act in the same frame instead of one network leg later. | **No**, and specifically: the server's own collision test (its `PopulateEnemies` analogue) applies damage with no client involvement, which is exactly the 74% of falls with no claim in §2.3. |

Every row's "can it arrive in time" test uses the same inequality from §3.4:
the escape must leave the client at least `one_way` (31 ms fast / 113 ms slow)
before the server tick whose damage step matters, and the tick grid is uniform
200 ms, so budget the **mean 100 ms of tick quantisation** on top.

---

## 7. The honest conclusion

### 7.1 What the hook actually fixes

**Fixed — the reaction latency after knowledge.** The current reactive rule's
decision path costs ~0-1 ms (`decisionLatencyMs`, seen as 0 in
`proxy/work/logs/nexus-20261005-023129-2000.jsonl`), so the rule is already
latency-optimal *given its input*. The input is the problem. A hook replaces
"wait for the server to tell me I was hit" with "I know the instant the client
resolves the hit". Three effects, and they are **not** additive because two of them
are alternatives to the same baseline:

* **vs. the reactive rule: +55.5 ms median (p90 +98.1 ms).** That is the measured
  collision → reflecting-reading interval (§2.2). It is decision time the hook has
  and the reactive rule does not. It is *not* gained again from any network term
  below — the reactive rule already writes its escape 0-1 ms after its reading.
* **vs. a remote (cloud/relay) proxy: +31 ms (fast cluster) / +113 ms (slow
  cluster).** A proxy that is one network leg away has not even *seen* the client's
  hit claim when the hook has already acted on its own collision test. Same frame,
  different place in the network.
* **vs. a co-located proxy that parses outbound traffic: at most one frame,
  ≈0-17 ms, and only by predicting.** This is the hardest comparison and the one
  worth stating plainly, because it is where the packet-only design is strongest.
  Such a proxy can read the `GmHit` claim the moment the client writes it, which is
  essentially the same instant the hook learns of the collision — so the hook's
  *action* gains only the remainder of that frame. Its real advantage is
  **knowledge**, not action: it can run its own swept test on the previous frame and
  be ready *before* the collision exists, which buys the **55.5 ms median / 98.1 ms
  p90** of §2.2 as prediction headroom rather than as notification. A proxy cannot
  do this: it has the spawn packet but not the live projectile position or the live
  player hit radius — `hook/work/auto-dodge-feasibility.md` §2 tabulates both as absent
  from the stream ("Current (later) position: **NO. Never re-sent**"; "Size / hit
  half: **NO (derived)**") — so its swept test would run against dead-reckoned
  geometry.

Sum against the reactive rule, for the fast cluster, taking the maximum rather than
the sum of overlapping terms: **≈55.5 ms median of extra decision budget, ≈98 ms at
p90**, plus one frame if the hook predicts rather than reacts.

**Fixed — acting on knowledge that is true rather than stale.** §2.5's worked
examples are the concrete cases. The relay fired on a 1-HP reading echoed **151 ms
after the character had died**; and in the other death it fired at 28% into a burst
that had already taken 439 HP (72.2%) off the bar in 2 ms. A hook seeded from
`Player.Health` (which §4.3 shows is exactly the last server value) and advanced by
its own collision predictions cannot be in either state.

**Fixed — threats with a client-visible approach.** Slow projectiles, fast
projectiles (by prediction), telegraphed AoEs, and the first tick of a beam. These
are the rows of §6 marked "yes".

### 7.2 What remains physically impossible

Not "hard" — impossible, for the reasons already in the data:

1. **Any burst whose damage does not pass through a client-visible collision.** 74%
   of measured HP falls have no client hit claim at all (§2.3 Test B: 571 of 775).
   For those, the server is the only witness and the `HealthUpdate` is the first
   signal anyone gets. The corpus contains one such burst of **493 HP = 81.1% of
   max inside 150 ms, ending in death** (§2.4).
2. **Point-blank spawn** (and, were it to exist, melee/contact - it does not). t = 0 is the collision; there is no
   frame in which earlier knowledge exists.
3. **Every damage tick after the first tick of a beam/DoT.** Once the server is
   ticking damage, an escape must traverse `one_way` + tick quantisation to change a
   decision that is already being made.
4. **Preventing damage by suppressing the client's hit claim.** §2.3: 34% of claims
   produce no immediate fall and 74% of falls have no claim, so the server plainly
   resolves damage without the claim; suppressing `ProjHit` would blind the server to
   some hits and remove none of the ones that matter.

### 7.3 Quantified improvement over the reactive rule

| metric | reactive rule (measured) | hook (arithmetic from the above) | improvement |
|---|---|---|---|
| time from local knowledge to decision | 0 ms after the *reading*; the reading is itself **+55.5 ms median / +98.1 ms p90** after the collision | ≤ 1 frame after the collision (≈10-17 ms) | **≈55-98 ms**, plus one frame |
| time from local knowledge to packet on the wire | 0-1 ms after the reading (§2.4); **+31 ms of network** before the server can act on it in the fast cluster | same frame as the collision; **+31 ms network** from the client's NIC | **≈31-113 ms** against a non-co-located proxy |
| HP percentage the rule cannot see | between consecutive readings: median worst-drop per session **4.9%**, p75 **14.1%**, p90 **22.4%**, worst **23.0% in 48 ms**. Across a burst: worst **72.2% in 2 ms** and **81.1% in 150 ms**, the latter ending in death | unchanged — this is an input limitation, not a latency one, unless the threat has a client-visible approach | **0%** for claim-free damage; **the whole burst** for predicted projectiles |
| largest observed post-death action | injected `Escape` on a 1% reading **151 ms after `hp` reached 0** (`nexus-20261005-023129-2000.jsonl`, `.084` → `.235`); in the other death, the escape went out 1 ms before the `hp 0` reading, into a tick that had already applied 439 HP (72.2%) of damage | cannot act on stale HP | **≈151 ms** of provably-avoidable error |

The "0%" row is the honest centre of the answer: the hook's advantage is entirely a
*latency* advantage inside the window between the client's collision test and the
server's damage step, and that window exists **only for damage the client is the
first to know about**. Where the server is the first witness, no hook helps, and the
measured cadence — 53 ms median, 100 ms p75, event-driven on a 200 ms tick — is the
floor on how bad that can be.

---

## 8. What to record in the next live run

Each of these is a number this report marked NOT MEASURABLE. All are wire-observable
without new instrumentation beyond what the relay already writes:

1. **Client logic-frame period.** Log `ClientTime.LogicTotal` from two consecutive
   `Update`/`Attack`/`Move` frames *within one server tick* (currently the relay
   records only the last `Time` per packet). What to record: the histogram of
   intra-tick `LogicTotal` deltas; it is the hook's worst-case in-frame latency.
2. **A kill that starts from a full bar.** Log every `HealthUpdate` and, for each
   pair whose earlier reading is ≥90% of max and later reading is 0, the whole packet
   window between them. One occurrence settles §2.5. (The *within-tick* burst case is
   already measured — §2.4 — but the corpus contains no burst that began at full HP.)
3. **`AoeProjectile.Delay` vs. the `HealthUpdate` fall.** Decode `Delay` and `Radius`
   from `GmAoes2` (id 161) and pair it with the first falling reading. That is the
   telegraph budget for the AoE row of §6.
4. **Whether an escape can beat a hit that is already claimed.** Inject an escape
   *and* log the `ProjHit` claim, so the escape's position in the
   claim→measurement window is known rather than inferred. The relay already
   timestamps both; what is missing is a deliberate paired trial.
5. **One-way asymmetry.** A `CheckPing`/`CheckPingAck` pair measures only the sum.
   To separate the legs, compare the relay's timestamp for a known server-origin
   event (`GmPing`'s embedded timestamp) against the client-bound arrival — the
   relay currently discards the `GmPing` time field (`hex 5C00 6E7B02176F22DF08`).

```

`docs/hook/VERIFICATION.md`:

```md
# Verification playbook

How to prove the hook works, and — more importantly — how to find out when it does not.

The companion documents are [IMPLEMENTATION-PLAN.md](IMPLEMENTATION-PLAN.md) §2 (the test list) and
[RISKS.md](RISKS.md) §4 (the two-controller integration test, which is the one test that belongs to
neither the offline suites nor the wire checks and is reproduced in §5.1 below). Where that material
defines the suites, this document is the **procedure**: what to run, in what order, and what a pass
actually licenses you to believe.

The design principle throughout is the one the existing `drelay` project already established for its
packet work: **a test must be able to fail in the direction that matters.** `docs/hook/INJECTION.md` §1.6
explains why the injection tests assert against literal bytes rather than round-trips — a round-trip
passes even when both directions share the same wrong idea of the format. The hook has the same
failure mode available to it: a prediction harness that compares the model against itself will pass
forever.

So every test below names **the wrong answer it can produce**, not just the check it performs.

---

## 1. The layered strategy, and what each layer can and cannot establish

A dodge's *quality* cannot be proven by tests — the reference engine's own safety audit says
*"live gameplay remains unverified"* for much of its newest code. What testing can establish is
narrower and still valuable: that the sensor tells the truth, that the solver obeys its own safety
rules, and that the hook does not harm the game.

| layer | runs where | establishes | **cannot** establish |
|---|---|---|---|
| **L0 — static gate** | offline, seconds | the target is the build we built for, **method by method** — all four detour points still have the IL hashes the hook will match on | anything about runtime behaviour |
| **L1 — offline unit/invariant** | offline, milliseconds | the solver's safety invariants hold over recorded and synthetic snapshots | that the snapshot resembles a real fight |
| **L2 — model agreement** | live, read-only | the predictor agrees with the game's own collision test | that agreeing implies good dodging |
| **L3 — in-game A/B** | live, acting | the hook beats the baseline on a measured metric | that the metric generalises past the sample |
| **L4 — end-to-end wire** | live, both processes | the hook's decisions reached the server | anything the server does not report |

The layers are ordered by cost and by how much they can mislead. **L2 is the pivot**: it is the only
layer that can tell us whether the model is right, and everything after it is tuning. Build L2 before
the solver.

---

## 2. L0 — the static gate

Run before every session. It is seconds of work and it is what turns "the hook crashed the game" into
"the hook refused to install and said why".

```powershell
# One command. Exits 0 when it is safe to install, 1 on any mismatch.
.\hook\tools\Fingerprint.ps1

# A different install, e.g. the OpenGL apphost or a second machine:
.\hook\tools\Fingerprint.ps1 -GamePath "D:\Games\Darza's Dominion"
```

Its expected values live in [`hook/known-build.json`](../../hook/known-build.json), which is a **record** rather than a
policy: it is regenerated whenever a game or runtime update is accepted, and the diff is the audit
trail of what changed.

**Expected output on the verified build** (5.8.2, .NET 9.0.20, clrjit 9.0.2026.41315) — abbreviated
to the checks whose *shape* matters here; the gate prints all fifteen:

```
TieredCompilation off        False        False        PASS
target framework             net9.0       net9.0       PASS
assembly not ReadyToRun      0            0            PASS
assembly size                50216960     50216960     PASS
assembly SHA-256             B3418153...  B3418153...  PASS
JIT vtable code slots        4            4            PASS
coreclr.dll version          9.0.2026.41315  9.0.2026.41315  PASS
clrjit.dll version           9.0.2026.41315  9.0.2026.41315  PASS
target frame tick IL hash    CF8779CF...  CF8779CF...  PASS
target spawn IL hash         8A7928BD...  8A7928BD...  PASS
target collision IL hash     D6F353B8...  D6F353B8...  PASS
target escape IL hash        6E3B9F4C...  6E3B9F4C...  PASS
target IL hashes             4 targets re-derived by il_index.py, all matching   info
```

The four target-IL checks are the ones added when Phase 0 was completed, and they are the load-bearing
pair: the gate **re-hashes each target's instruction stream out of the assembly itself** (so a changed
method is caught with no other tooling), and it separately requires `hook/tools/il_index.py` to regenerate
the identical table from the metadata (so the two independent readers must agree).

Two checks it deliberately does **not** claim to make, reported as gaps rather than passes:

| gap | why a script cannot close it | where it is closed instead |
|---|---|---|
| the effective `DOTNET_*` environment | a `.NET 9` environment variable overrides `runtimeconfig.json`, so a launcher-inherited `DOTNET_TieredCompilation=1` would defeat the whole design | the launcher builds a controlled environment block; the hook reads the effective setting in-process ([HOOK-ARCHITECTURE.md](HOOK-ARCHITECTURE.md) §9) |
| the loaded assembly's MVID | the script reads a file, not a process | the hook re-checks at attach |

**Falsification test for L0 itself — and it has now found two bugs, one in the gate and one in the
tool behind it.** The gate was first mutation-tested by flipping one byte of the assembly while leaving
its length unchanged: the **first version passed**, because it checked size rather than content. A
SHA-256 check closed that. The second round went one level deeper — flipping a byte *inside a target's
IL* — and that is where the real find was: `il_index.py` was reading the wrong 48 bytes for
`DarzaWindow::Update`, because this build's fat-header `MoreSects` size field is not trustworthy. The
wrong bytes decoded as a plausible instruction stream, so nothing looked broken; only the
disassembler comparison exposed it. Both tests are now permanent:

```powershell
python .\hook\tools\il_index.py --mutation-test          # method-level, no sandbox copy
python .\hook\tools\il_index.py --self-test              # reader vs. documented signatures
powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File `
    .\hook\tools\Test-FingerprintGate.ps1                # the gate vs. mutated target IL
```

The last one asserts that the gate names **the specific target whose IL moved** while the other three
still pass. That distinction is the point: a file-level failure cannot tell you which method changed,
and "which method changed" is what decides whether the hook may install at all. **This is the test for
the test**, and it is why "the gate passes" is not by itself evidence of anything.

The full re-verification procedure, and the build-specific findings a maintainer must not "simplify"
away, are in [`docs/hook/HOOK-BUILD-MATRIX.md`](HOOK-BUILD-MATRIX.md).

**What L0 cannot tell you:** whether the running process loaded the bytes it checked. That is what the
in-process MVID check is for.

---

## 3. L1 — the solver's invariants, offline

The solver's decision is a **pure function of a plain-data snapshot** ([DODGE-ALGORITHM.md](DODGE-ALGORITHM.md)
§2). That property exists specifically so this layer is possible. Feed it:

- synthetic snapshots (hand-built volleys with known answers);
- **replayed snapshots from L2's logs**, which is where the value is, because they are real fights.

### The invariants to assert

Each of these is a property that can be checked mechanically, and each names the failure it catches.

| # | invariant | the wrong answer it catches |
|---|---|---|
| I1 | `stand` is never rejected while the player is durably safe for the full horizon | the dodge moving for no reason, which is how a dodge gets a player killed |
| I2 | no admissible candidate is inside a bullet's disc at its own arrival time | the primary safety violation |
| I3 | the chosen heading does not change while it stays admissible and no alternative beats it by the hysteresis margin | 60 Hz oscillation — the player vibrating instead of moving |
| I4 | **hysteresis cannot lock a heading that has become unsafe** | an over-eager anti-jitter turning into a death — the failure I3's fix introduces |
| I5 | a candidate is never emitted with a magnitude above the per-frame legal budget `b` | a move the server can reject |
| I6 | temporal clearance is never credited past the point the prediction is trusted | a blind tail scoring as "clear for 600 ms" |
| I7 | a re-rented `Projectile` never inherits a dead bullet's record | "the dodge reacts to bullets that do not exist" |
| I8 | the solver's cost stays inside its slice as candidate count scales | the frame budget |
| I9 | **with the computed speed at or below zero, no move is emitted at all** and the decision reports "immobile" | a dodge the player physically cannot execute — `Paralyzed` zeroes the speed law, and so may any future effect |
| I10 | the emitted magnitude scales with the game's own speed law across every `Slowed` tier | a nominal-speed dodge that overspends the budget exactly when the player is debuffed, and looks wrong to the server |
| I11 | **an AoE volume never removes a candidate; it may only affect its score** | the dodge overriding the player's manual AoE dodge, which is the one thing accepted scope depends on it not doing ([DODGE-ALGORITHM.md](DODGE-ALGORITHM.md) §5.7) |
| I12 | walkability never rejects a cell the client's collision grid reports as walkable | a stale or wrongly-indexed terrain grid silently fencing the player in |

I3 and I4 are deliberately in tension and must both hold. Testing only I3 produces a dodge that
commits to a heading that has become lethal; testing only I4 produces one that jitters.

I9 and I10 are the two that a naive harness skips, because both require driving the solver with a
speed it did not choose. They are exactly the cases where a dodge is most likely to be wrong in a way
that matters, because they coincide with the player being least able to compensate.

**What L1 cannot tell you:** whether the snapshot is *representative*. A solver can satisfy every
invariant on synthetic data and behave badly in a real 40-bullet fight. That is what L2 is for.

---

## 4. L2 — the model-agreement measurement (the pivot)

**This is the most important test in the project, and it changes nothing about the game.** It is
read-only, and it produces the four numbers that decide whether any of the rest is worth building.

### The procedure

1. Hook the frame tick and the collision decision. **Do not hook the spawn yet** — first prove the
   simplest version works.
2. Every frame, run the sensor over the live threat set and record, per bullet, the earliest
   predicted intersection time with the player's swept path.
3. On every `Projectile.HitCharacter` call **that returns `true`** — the method is a per-frame
   predicate and most of its entries answer "no" — record: the bullet identity, the frame,
   `World.ClientTime`, the player position, the bullet position, the computed `r_eff`, and **whether
   the sensor had predicted this bullet, and with how much warning**.
4. Also record the bullets the sensor predicted that **never** hit.
5. Play for several hours across varied content. The log is the deliverable.

### What to compute from it

| metric | definition | decides |
|---|---|---|
| **warning distribution** | for each hit the sensor predicted, `predictedImpactTime − firstPredictionTime` | whether there is time to move — the input to Phase 3's dodge budget and to the timing of its escape floor |
| **false-negative rate** | hits that happened but were never predicted, per hit | whether the model is complete enough to rely on |
| **false-positive rate** | predictions that never became hits, per prediction | how over-cautious the dodge will be; this *is* the ghost rate |
| **cost** | p50/p99 per-frame microseconds | whether the Phase 3 solver fits the budget at all |
| **linearity census** | the fraction of live bullets whose sampled path passes the linearity gate | how good a dodge can possibly be |

### Interpreting it honestly

| result | meaning | action |
|---|---|---|
| low false negatives, useful warning, cost inside budget | the model is sound | proceed to Phase 3 |
| high false negatives | the sensor is **missing threats**, which is the dangerous direction | stop; find the cause before building anything |
| high false positives | over-cautious; will refuse safe cells | tune the horizon and the trust prefix; acceptable to ship only if the false positives are explicable |
| warning ≈ 0 | **the whole premise fails** for this content | stop at nothing; document and re-plan |
| cost over budget | the solver cannot run | reduce candidate count, or cull harder before sampling |

**The falsification test that matters:** take the false negatives and explain every one by a *named
cause* — a curved trajectory, a homing re-target, a pool-reuse race, a flight longer than the horizon,
a bullet spawned inside the player. **If any false negative has no named cause, the model is not
understood and must not be trusted.** That sentence is the acceptance criterion for L2.

**What L2 cannot tell you:** whether *acting* on the prediction improves outcomes. A perfect
predictor with a bad solver, or with movement the server rejects, changes nothing. That is L3.

---

## 5. L3 — the in-game A/B

### The baseline must be a measured session, not an impression

Record a baseline run with the hook's acting disabled, then a run with it enabled, on comparable
content. Compare **death rate in claim-bearing cases** — that is, deaths where L2's log shows the
client declared the hit — because including claim-free deaths dilutes the signal with cases the hook
structurally cannot affect ([RISKS.md](RISKS.md) §2b).

### The Phase 3 trial specifically

The acting decision is verified differently from the sensor, because it needs live state and cannot be
replayed. The procedure is a **deliberate paired trial**, and the existing relay already has both
halves of it (`TIMING.md` §8 item 4):

1. run in dry run; log the exact moment the hook *would* have moved, the moment it *would* have
   escaped, and the reason it chose each;
2. pair that against the relay's `HealthUpdate` trace and against the death, if there was one;
3. join the hook's `escape` event with the relay's `EscapeAck` on `World.ClientTime`
   ([JAVA-BRIDGE.md](../bridge/JAVA-BRIDGE.md) §5.3), which measures the end-to-end escape latency that neither
   side can produce alone.

**The acceptance criterion is an accounting, not a rate:** every death in the trial must fall into
exactly one of two buckets — *"no warning existed"* (a claim-free fall, expected for ~74 %) or
*"warning existed and the dry-run decision would have survived the horizon"*. **A death in neither
bucket is a bug**, and a third bucket labelled "unclear" is a failed trial.

**The trial also checks the other direction, because the escape is the last gate.** Every dry-run
escape must come with a written reason that no admissible move avoided lethal projected damage: an
escape that fires while a safe move existed is a dodge that gave up, which is the failure mode the
2026-10-13 merge exists to remove ([IMPLEMENTATION-PLAN.md](IMPLEMENTATION-PLAN.md), Phase 3).

### The anti-regression test

With the dodge and the escape both disabled, the hook must change **nothing observable** — the same
packets, the same timing, the same behaviour. This is the test that protects the operator's game from
the tool, and it should be run after every change to the hook infrastructure, not just at the end.

### 5.1 The two-controller test (the one that matters most for safety)

The dodge and the escape are **one decision** in the design since the 2026-10-13 merge, but they are
still two possible actions over one player, and the conflict between them is **located, not
hypothetical**: `World.RequestEscape()`'s channelled branch cancels on movement
(`World.cs:13043-13047`), so a dodge that steers will cancel an in-progress nexus cast in the same
frame ([RISKS.md](RISKS.md) §3d).

**The test:** with the dodge live and the escape armed, force both to want to act in the same frame and
assert the documented precedence — the escape wins, the dodge yields, the cast is not cancelled by the
hook, and the session is not kicked.

Variants, because each exercises a different branch of `RequestEscape` that a single test would miss:

| variant | picks up |
|---|---|
| escape while knocked up | the normal movement branch is bypassed entirely during knock-up, so the dodge cannot steer and must not pretend to |
| escape while a `MovingTowards` is active | a scripted move can be cancelled by state the hook did not observe (`Player.StopMovingTowards`) |
| escape in a safe area | `RequestEscape` is a legitimate **no-op** there — the dodge must not mistake that for success |
| escape inside the world-entry grace window | the instant path is taken rather than the cast |
| **escape with the `Impermanence` totem** | the **channelled** path is taken and cancels on the first movement |

The totem variant is the one that matters and the one a naive test misses, because the ordinary
instant escape **is not** cancelled by movement — an earlier draft of this research got that wrong.
Only challenge runs take the channelled branch ([CLIENT-FINDINGS.md](CLIENT-FINDINGS.md) §5.3), so a
test suite that never equips the totem will pass while the real bug sits untouched.

### 5.2 The movement validation boundary

Because the server's movement check is a **distance-per-game-tick** bound rather than a
"programmatic vs human" test ([RISKS.md](RISKS.md) §2a), the test is a boundary search rather than a
pass/fail:

1. drive the player with increasingly large per-tick magnitudes until the server objects;
2. record the largest magnitude that is still accepted, and the `GmKicked` reason when it is not;
3. assert the design's budget `b = TilesPerSecond × frameSeconds` sits inside that bound **with
   margin**, at every `Slowed` tier and on the slowest and fastest tiles.

**The failure this catches is not "the dodge was detected" — it is "the dodge's budget was computed
with the wrong speed".** That is why the test sweeps `Slowed` tiers: a dodge that uses a nominal
speed produces a legal move at full speed and an illegal one exactly when the player is debuffed,
which is precisely when they need the dodge.

An immobility check belongs here too: with `Paralyzed` active, `TilesPerSecond` returns 0, and the
hook must emit **no move at all** and report "immobile" rather than a dodge the player cannot execute.

---

## 6. L4 — end-to-end on the wire

The relay is the only place several of these facts are visible at all.

| what to check | how | why only the relay can |
|---|---|---|
| the injected escape was **accepted** | `jq -c 'select(.pkt=="EscapeAck")' proxy/work/logs/events-*.jsonl` | the stock client **discards** `GmEscapeAck` (`docs/hook/AUTONEXUS.md` §5) |
| the server's **reason** if it refused | `GmForcedEscape` (id 184) carries a string16 | same |
| whether the server **kicked** us | `GmKicked` (id 185), reason decoded into `data.reason` and latched as `kickedReason` | the fastest explanation of a failed experiment there is |
| the escape **latency**, end to end | join the hook's `escape` event with the `EscapeAck` on `World.ClientTime` | spans both processes |
| the hook's own view of a decision | the new dashboard panel | there is no other window into the hook |

### The named-failure checks

Each of these is a specific, previously-observed failure with a specific log signature. Running them
is how a session is diagnosed rather than guessed at.

| symptom | check | likely cause |
|---|---|---|
| kicks shortly after the hook acts | `data.reason` on the `Kicked` event | **movement validation** — the decisive Phase 3 risk ([RISKS.md](RISKS.md) §2a) |
| the dodge moves and the character snaps back | the relay's `Move` records vs the server's next correction | a position write instead of the input path |
| the nexus cast is cancelled when the dodge acts | the client's own `EscapeCastState` pair in the log | the verified interaction bug ([RISKS.md](RISKS.md) §3d) |
| "no events from the hook" | `heartbeatSeq` staleness, then `ProcessHandle` liveness | hook dead vs game hung — the mapping cannot tell you which ([JAVA-BRIDGE.md](../bridge/JAVA-BRIDGE.md) §5.2) |
| the hook works but nothing appears in the dashboard | `magic`/`version`/`epoch` in the section header | a layout change, or a stale section from a previous hook instance |

---

## 7. Pre-flight checklist, in order, per session

```
[ ] L0 fingerprint green (script above)
[ ] hook installs; startup self-checks all pass (HOOK-ARCHITECTURE.md §9)
[ ] all four targets found by IL hash      <- a miss means an inlined target; use the documented fallback
[ ] field offsets resolved and logged
[ ] dry run ON
[ ] bridge: hook state visible in the dashboard, heartbeat fresh
[ ] anti-regression: with everything disabled, the game behaves normally
[ ] two-controller precedence exercised: escape vs dodge in one frame (§5.1)
--- play ---
[ ] no `Kicked` with a movement reason
[ ] no escape dispatched on stale HP
[ ] the hook's frame cost p99 inside budget
[ ] decisions logged with reasons
--- after ---
[ ] L2 metrics recomputed over the session
[ ] every death accounted for in a named bucket
[ ] any new false negative named, or the model is not trusted
```

---

## 8. What this playbook deliberately does not claim

- **It does not prove dodge quality.** No offline test can. The reference engine's audit is explicit
  that its own tests pin internal invariants rather than gameplay quality, and that *"live gameplay
  remains unverified"* for its newest stages. The layer-2 measurement is the closest thing to a quality
  signal available, and it measures the *sensor*, not the dodge.
- **It does not establish server acceptance.** Only a live run does, and only for the behaviours
  actually exercised — which is why the movement question is answered from the proxy first
  ([RISKS.md](RISKS.md) §2a).
- **It cannot distinguish "the dodge is bad" from "the content is undodgeable."** The ~74 % claim-free
  damage is undodgeable by construction; the accounting in §5 is what keeps those cases from being
  mistaken for failures.
- **It has no regression suite for the game itself.** If the hook destabilises the game, the game's own
  `StallProbe`/`UiThreadWatchdog` logs are the detector, not this document.

```

`docs/proxy/AUTONEXUS-GUIDE.md`:

```md
# Auto-nexus — usage guide

The operator's manual for the auto-nexus rule: how to turn it on safely, what dry run does and does not
do, how to pick a threshold, what to watch on the dashboard, and how to read the logs when something
went wrong. It assumes the relay is already carrying a session - see the
[README](../../proxy/README.md) for that.

The design, the gates and a control-by-control explanation live in
[AUTONEXUS.md](AUTONEXUS.md). Read this one if you just want to use the thing.

---

## 1. The short version

The rule is off by default and starts in dry run when switched on. Arm it for one run from the command
line, then tune it live from the dashboard:

```powershell
# 1. dry run: the rule decides and logs, and writes nothing to the server
java -jar drelay.jar -Ddrelay.nexus.enabled=true -Ddrelay.nexus.dryRun=true -Ddrelay.nexus.percent=35

# 2. play. read http://127.0.0.1:8765/ and proxy/work/logs/nexus-*.jsonl
#    then decide whether the threshold is where you want it

# 3. when you are satisfied, arm it for real - either restart without dryRun:
java -jar drelay.jar -Ddrelay.nexus.enabled=true -Ddrelay.nexus.dryRun=false -Ddrelay.nexus.percent=35
#    ... or turn dry run off in the dashboard's auto-nexus panel while the session runs
```

From a source tree, `.\proxy\drelay.ps1 -JarArg -Ddrelay.nexus.enabled=true` passes the same
properties through. The launcher does not have `-Nexus` flags of its own any more: every setting is a
`-Ddrelay.nexus.*` property, an environment variable, a route-table key or a dashboard control, which
is one mechanism instead of two.

Nothing is armed by default. `enabled` defaults to false, and even with it on, `dryRun` defaults to
true - the two gates are independent, and the second is the one that keeps the feature honest.

## 2. What dry run is, and what it is not

**Dry run is the whole rule minus the write.** The trigger, the gates, the threshold comparison, the
counters and the log lines all behave exactly as they do live. The single difference is that
`AutoNexus.fire()` is never called, so **no bytes reach the server** - and that one difference has two
knock-on effects, both listed below: the per-world budget is never consumed, and the "delay" clock never
starts.

| | dry run | live |
|---|---|---|
| reads `GmHealthUpdate`, computes the percentage | yes | yes |
| applies every gate (world, health, safe area, budget, threshold, ...) | yes | yes |
| increments `decisions`, `declines`, `dry runs` | yes | yes (`nexused` instead) |
| writes a `nexus` event per decision | yes, `DRY RUN would nexus: ...` | yes, `NEXUS: ...` |
| writes `GmEscape` to the server | **no** | yes |
| consumes the per-world budget | **no** | yes |
| starts the "delay" clock | **no** | yes |
| can be acked or refused by the server | **no ack exists** | yes |

Three consequences that catch people out:

- **The "delay ms" control does nothing in dry run**, because the clock it measures only starts on a
  real injection. That is not a bug; see [AUTONEXUS.md §8](AUTONEXUS.md#8-the-delay-option-and-why-it-looks-like-it-does-nothing).
- **`max/world` is never consumed in dry run**, so a dry run can report far more would-be nexuses per
  world than a live run would ever fire. That is deliberate: the point of dry run is to see how often
  the threshold is crossed, not to simulate the budget.
- **A dry run proves nothing about the server's verdict.** The only way to learn whether an injected
  escape is accepted is to send one and read `EscapeAck`, which the stock client discards. That is what
  step 3 above is for, and it is why the first live run should be a short one.

**A dry run cannot hurt the character.** It writes nothing at all on the client→server path - the
relay's only other writes are the client's own packets, forwarded unchanged.

## 3. Turning it on, three ways

Settings can come from any of the three surfaces, and the later ones win:

1. **`relay-routes.json`** - the checked-in defaults:

   ```jsonc
   "autoNexus": {
     "enabled": true, "dryRun": true, "thresholdPercent": 35,
     "useEffectiveHp": false, "skipInSafeArea": true,
     "minIntervalMillis": 1200, "maxPerWorld": 3, "rearmPercent": 0
   }
   ```

2. **System properties or environment variables** - one run, no file edit, and they override the file:

   | property | environment | meaning |
   |---|---|---|
   | `-Ddrelay.nexus.enabled` | `DRELAY_NEXUS_ENABLED` | master switch |
   | `-Ddrelay.nexus.dryRun` | `DRELAY_NEXUS_DRY_RUN` | decide only |
   | `-Ddrelay.nexus.percent` | `DRELAY_NEXUS_PERCENT` | threshold % |
   | `-Ddrelay.nexus.effective` | `DRELAY_NEXUS_EFFECTIVE` | count shield+barrier |
   | `-Ddrelay.nexus.delayMs` | `DRELAY_NEXUS_DELAY_MS` | minimum gap between injected escapes |
   | `-Ddrelay.nexus.maxPerWorld` | `DRELAY_NEXUS_MAX_PER_WORLD` | budget per world |
   | `-Ddrelay.nexus.skipSafeArea` | `DRELAY_NEXUS_SKIP_SAFE_AREA` | decline in town |
   | `-Ddrelay.nexus.rearm` | `DRELAY_NEXUS_REARM` | re-arm level % |
   | `-Ddrelay.nexus.castChannel` | `DRELAY_NEXUS_CAST_CHANNEL` | channelled escape (not on the dashboard) |

3. **The dashboard, live, mid-session** - the **auto nexus** panel. Press **apply**; the change takes
   effect on the next health reading, and it is written back into the route table the relay was started
   with so it survives a restart. Every change is recorded as a `note` event carrying the request,
   what was applied, and the whole resulting config, so the log always says which settings produced a
   run. The panel says whether the write succeeded; if it could not (a read-only install), the setting
   is still live for this run and the reason is printed under the controls.

Keys are forgiving: `threshold_percent`, `thresholdPercent` and `threshold-percent` are the same key,
and an unrecognised one is reported back as `unknown:<key>` rather than silently ignored.

## 4. Reading the dashboard

`http://127.0.0.1:8765/` (`-Ddrelay.web.port=0` disables it, `-1` takes any free port; if the configured
port is busy the next four are tried). The URL is printed at startup.

The header, left to right, tells you whether anything can happen at all:

| pill | what it means | if it is not what you expect |
|---|---|---|
| `connecting…` / `live` / `disconnected` | the page's link to the relay's API | the relay is not running, or the page was opened before it started |
| `no session` / `<route>#<n> · <phase>` | the **newest** session and its phase (`NEW`, `CONNECTED`, `HELLO`, `IN_WORLD`, `CLOSED`) | you are still in the lobby, or the newest session is not the one you are playing |
| `injection disarmed` / `injection armed` | the world gate: has the client's `Hello` **and** a `MapInfo` been seen | this is the usual reason nothing fires. `IN_WORLD` and `injection armed` go together |
| `auto-nexus off` / `auto-nexus dry run` / `AUTO-NEXUS LIVE` | the master switch and dry run | note that LIVE only means `enabled && !dryRun`; a threshold of 0 can never fire while it still says LIVE |
| `strip off` / `strip 11` / `strip 7,11` | the status-effect strip and the ordinals it is armed with (11 Confused, 7 Slowed, 6 Paralyzed) | it is on by default with Confused armed; `strip off` means server→client payloads are forwarded verbatim. See [INJECTION.md](INJECTION.md) §5 |

Then:

- **character hp** - the newest reading: raw percent, effective percent, how stale it is, and the
  shield/barrier/sample/world/safe-area/cast values behind it. The bar turns red at or below the
  threshold. If it never shows a number, no `HealthUpdate` has arrived in this world yet.
- **auto nexus** - the controls (§5) plus the counters. `decisions` is every reading the rule
  evaluated, `nexused` is escapes written, `dry runs` is would-haves, `declines` is everything else.
  In a healthy live run below the threshold you should see `nexused` increase by one and `declines`
  by a handful around it. The `last ack` line is the server's verdict.
- **status effect strip** - the effects to remove (Confused on by default, Paralyzed and Slowed off),
  the locator's evidence requirement, and the counters: `packets rewritten`, `entries removed`, and
  the last strip's object and byte sizes. Both this panel and the auto-nexus one save to the route
  table when you press **apply**; the line under the counters says where, or why not.
- **sessions** - every session, its phase, whether injection is armed, and its own health.
- **filters** / **packets** - the live stream. The default filter, *character hp*, keeps the health
  readings, the whole escape conversation, world entry, and every action the relay took. If you change
  nothing else, leave it: without the relay's own `nexus`/`inject` events the view shows the symptom and
  hides the cause.

## 5. Choosing a threshold

The threshold is the only setting that needs a real decision, and the dry run is how you make it.

1. **Set the threshold low and dry-run a session you would call normal.** 35% is a reasonable start.
2. **Look at what a dry run reports.** What matters is not the count of would-be nexuses but *where in
   the HP curve* they land, and whether they were single readings or the start of a slide.
3. **Read the shape of the ramp, not just the crossings.** In the recorded session the rule saw the
   character fall from ~97% to 33% over about twenty seconds, with the threshold crossed on the way
   down and never again. That is a good threshold: it fires on a real slide with hundreds of
   milliseconds of margin, not on a spike.
4. **If it fires constantly at 35%, the threshold is doing its job** - the character is genuinely
   living below it. Either the character needs better gear for the content, or you want a lower number
   and accept that the rule will only catch the last part of a slide.
5. **If it never fires, check `declines` before moving the threshold.** The dashboard's `last ack` and
   the nexus log both name the reason (see §7). "the server says this is a safe area" and "injection is
   not armed" are not threshold problems.

A useful cross-check while tuning: the HP panel shows both the raw percentage and the effective one.
Leave **hp+shield+barrier** off until you have seen the two diverge; turn it on when your gear gives you
a shield worth counting, and expect the rule to fire later (a shielded character's raw HP is lower than
its real pool).

## 6. Choosing the other settings

| setting | guidance |
|---|---|
| **delay ms** | leave it at 1200 unless you have a reason. It is a duplicate suppressor covering the gap between an escape and the world change; it cannot fire before the threshold is crossed, and it does nothing at all in dry run. [AUTONEXUS.md §8](AUTONEXUS.md#8-the-delay-option-and-why-it-looks-like-it-does-nothing) has the evidence. |
| **max/world** | 3 is generous. A world where the rule fires three times is a world where something already went wrong; the budget exists so a stuck-below-threshold character cannot be nexused on every reading. |
| **re-arm %** | leave at 0 unless you have seen repeated firing in one world. Setting it (say 70) makes the rule require a recovery before it will fire again, which is a preference rather than a safety property - and it can leave the rule disarmed when you want it. |
| **skip safe area** | leave it on. An escape in town achieves nothing. |
| **hp+shield+barrier** | see §5. On if your build carries a shield or barrier worth counting. |
| **cast channel** | not on the dashboard. Leave it off unless the server refuses the instant escape; it stalls both directions of the session for the whole wait, which freezes the client visibly. |

## 7. Troubleshooting: symptom → cause → fix

Every one of these is a line in the nexus log or a `declines` tick on the dashboard. Nothing in this
feature fails silently, which is the point.

| symptom | the log says | what it means, and what to do |
|---|---|---|
| the pill says disarmed and nothing happens | `injection is not armed (no world yet, or a fresh handshake)` | you are in the handshake or the lobby. Nothing to fix; wait for world entry. |
| the HP panel is empty, decisions all decline | `no HealthUpdate seen in this world` | the world just changed and the server has not sent a reading yet, or this is not a game session at all (the queue route is never evaluated). |
| declines say safe area | `the server says this is a safe area` | you are in town. `skip safe area` is on by default; leaving it on is correct. |
| declines say budget | `world budget spent (n/max)` | the rule has already fired `max` times in this world. A new `MapInfo` resets it. If this happens often, raise `max/world` deliberately or look at why the character keeps coming back below the threshold. |
| declines say interval | `only N ms since the last injection` | the duplicate suppressor working as intended, between an escape and the world change. Not a problem. |
| declines say re-arm | `waiting to re-arm (needs X%, at Y%)` | `re-arm %` is set and HP has not recovered. Lower it, or set it to 0. |
| everything says the threshold was not crossed | `N% is not below the M% threshold` | expected while healthy. Compare `N` with `M` before changing `M`. |
| it fires but nothing happens in game | `NEXUS: ...` with no `EscapeAck` after it | the escape went out and the server never answered. Check the acks below. |
| the server refused it | `injected escape #n REFUSED after X ms` | the instant form was not accepted. This is the case the channelled escape exists for; expect a visible freeze. |
| the ack is attributed to the client | `an escape was accepted (no injection pending in this session: the client sent it)` | you pressed the nexus key yourself. Not an injection; nothing was fired by the relay. |
| the pill says dry run and you expected live | nothing - dry run does not announce itself per event | `dry run` is still checked. Uncheck it and press **apply**. |
| nothing fires *and* `decisions` is 0 | - | `enabled` is off. The master switch returns before counting anything. |
| it fires but the client stutters for two seconds | `injected EscapeCastState` in the log | the channelled escape is on. Turn `useCastChannel` off in the config. |

## 8. Reading the logs afterwards

Two files, both under `proxy/work/logs/`, named by run:

- **`events-<run>.jsonl`** - everything, one JSON object per line: every packet with its raw payload
  and its decoded fields, plus every decision the relay made.
- **`nexus-<run>.jsonl`** - the subset worth reading first: the health readings, the whole escape
  conversation, world entry, and every `nexus`/`inject` event. Read it top to bottom and you have the
  story of the session in a minute.

```powershell
# the whole escape story, in order
Get-Content proxy/work/logs\nexus-*.jsonl | Select-String -Pattern '"pkt":"Escape'

# every decision the rule reached, with the numbers behind it
Get-Content proxy/work/logs\nexus-*.jsonl | Select-String -Pattern '"kind":"nexus"'

# did the server accept the escapes the relay sent?
Get-Content proxy/work/logs\nexus-*.jsonl | Select-String -Pattern '"pkt":"EscapeAck"'

# what the client sent on its own, that the relay did not
Get-Content proxy/work/logs\events-*.jsonl | Select-String -Pattern 'clientOwnEscape":true'
```

Three things to check, in this order:

1. **Was there an `EscapeAck` for every injected escape**, and did it carry `answersInjectionSeq`
   matching the injection's `seq`? That is the only proof the server accepted the relay's escape.
2. **What was `decisionLatencyMs`?** It should be 0-1 ms. If it is large, the relay thread was blocked
   by something else and the escape left late.
3. **How long was the window between the injection and the next world entry?** If it is much longer
   than the health cadence, the delay is doing real work in it; if the world changes immediately, there
   was nothing for it to suppress.

## 9. Turning it off

- **Right now, mid-session**: uncheck `enabled` in the dashboard and press **apply**.
- **For a run**: leave the `-Ddrelay.nexus.enabled` property off. The rule is off by default, so doing
  nothing is also a valid answer.
- **To make an accidental live run impossible**, set `"enabled": false` in the `autoNexus` block of your
  route table and do not pass the property. Dry run is not a substitute for off if what you want is for
  the relay never to write anything of its own.

## 10. Checking it without playing

None of these need the game, elevation, or a server:

```powershell
java -cp "proxy/target/classes;proxy/target/test-classes" networking.InjectionTests      # the gates, the budget, the interval, dry run, re-arming
python proxy/tools/tests\test_auto_nexus.py                        # the whole chain against a fake game server
python proxy/tools/tests\test_dashboard.py                         # the page parses, the endpoints have the right shape
```

`test_auto_nexus.py` drives a real relay against a fake server and asserts on the bytes that arrive:
nothing before the handshake, nothing before `MapInfo`, nothing while healthy, exactly one escape when
the threshold is crossed, and nothing more from a repeat reading. It is the closest thing to a
rehearsal of a live run.

```

`docs/proxy/AUTONEXUS.md`:

```md
# Auto-nexus — what it does, and how it is implemented

A report on the rule in `proxy/src/main/java/networking/AutoNexus.java`: the signal it uses, every gate it
applies, where it sits in the relay's threads, and what each control on the dashboard's **auto nexus**
panel actually changes. The companion document is [AUTONEXUS-GUIDE.md](AUTONEXUS-GUIDE.md), which is
the operator's manual (how to turn it on, how to tune it, how to read the logs).

Everything below is written against the code as it stands, and the measurements quoted are taken from
the runs recorded in `proxy/work/logs/`.

---

## 1. What it is, in one paragraph

The server sends `GmHealthUpdate` (game id 70, `0x46`) roughly ten times a second with the character's
`maxHealth`, `health`, `shield` and `barrier`. Auto-nexus reads that packet, converts it to a
percentage, and if the percentage is below a threshold it writes `GmEscape` (id 66, `0x42`) into the
client→server stream. The decision is taken on the same virtual thread that read the health packet and
the escape is written **before that packet is forwarded on to the client**, so the escape leaves the
relay within a millisecond of the reading arriving. It is off by default, and even when it is switched
on it starts in **dry run**, which decides and logs but writes nothing.

## 2. What it is not: there is no prediction

This is the single most important thing to understand about the feature, and it is a property of the
game rather than a shortcut in this implementation.

The technique people usually mean by "auto-nexus" (as in RotMG proxies) is **predictive**: it
intercepts the incoming hit, computes the damage it would do, applies it to a local estimate of HP,
and escapes *before* the damage lands. That needs a hook on the damage path. In RotMG that hook is the
client's damage acknowledgement, which a proxy can suppress. Darza's client does not send one - the
closest packets, `ProjectilesAck` and `AllyHit`/`ProjHit`, are positional or sparse, not a damage
report - so a proxy has nothing to intercept, and inventing a local damage model would be guessing.

So the only truthful signal is the server's own `HealthUpdate`, at ~10 Hz. Two consequences follow
directly, and both are worth stating plainly:

- **A burst that removes the rest of the bar between two health packets cannot be escaped.** There is
  no reading to react to, and no proxy logic changes that. Observed in the recorded runs: the cadence
  is a median of **52-61 ms** between readings (p10 ≈ 40-47 ms, p90 ≈ 101 ms), and a single hit that
  takes a character from 100% to 0% inside one of those gaps is invisible until it is over.
- **What the rule optimises is latency after a reading, not knowledge of the future.** The measured
  decision latency is **0-1 ms** (`decisionLatencyMs` in the log). The remaining time is the network:
  in the same run the server's verdict came back **245-305 ms** after each instant escape.

Note also that the rule only ever sees the **game** service. `Session.transition` returns immediately
for queue sessions, so nothing on port 6412 is ever evaluated.

## 3. The signal, the bytes, and where the write happens

| step | where | what |
|---|---|---|
| read | `Relay.pump` (downstream thread) | one length-prefixed message is read from the server socket |
| decode | `Session.onPacket` → `transition` | id 70 → `onHealthUpdate` stores the reading and emits the packet event |
| decide | `Session.onHealthUpdate` → `AutoNexus.onHealth` → `decide` | pure function, no I/O; produces a `Decision` with the reason string |
| act | `AutoNexus.fire` | takes the **upstream** writer's monitor and calls `Session.inject` |
| forward | `Relay.pump` | the health packet is then written to the client, under the **downstream** writer's monitor |

The injected message is five payload bytes framed with a four-byte big-endian length:

```
00 00 00 02 42 00        BE length 2, LE type id 0x0042 = GmEscape
```

Three properties of that write are load-bearing:

- **`Session.inject` refuses to write unless the caller already holds the stream's monitor**
  (`Thread.holdsLock`) and returns `-1` if it does not. Both pumps serialize their own writes on their
  `GameWriter`, so holding the upstream writer's monitor is what guarantees an injected frame lands
  whole and between two forwarded messages rather than inside one.
- **The event is logged before the bytes are written.** The intuitive order is the reverse, and it was
  the reverse until a stress test caught the consequence: a process that stops in the window between
  writing and logging leaves a packet on the wire that the log does not mention. For a safety feature
  that is the dangerous direction - an audit asking "did auto-nexus ever fire unexpectedly" would
  undercount. The log is therefore a **superset** of the wire, and a write that then fails is reported
  as a second `error` event naming the same injection sequence number.
- **Framing follows the session.** `Session.frameBigEndian()` carries the byte order the relay detected
  for that session, so an injected frame is byte-compatible with every forwarded one beside it. A
  session that resolved little-endian would otherwise be fed a big-endian length and desync instantly.

## 4. The gates, in the order the rule applies them

`decide` is a pure function over `(Session, Reading)` plus the rule's per-session scratch. Each gate
has its own message, and the message is what appears in the log and on the dashboard:

| # | condition to decline | message |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | `enabled` is false | *(returns before deciding; not even counted as a decision)* |
| 1 | no world yet, or a fresh handshake | `injection is not armed (no world yet, or a fresh handshake)` |
| 2 | no `HealthUpdate` yet **in this world** | `no HealthUpdate seen in this world` |
| 3 | `maxHealth <= 0` | `the server has not reported a maximum HP` |
| 4 | `health <= 0` | `HP is zero (dead or spirit form)` |
| 5 | `skipInSafeArea` and the server says safe | `the server says this is a safe area` |
| 6 | per-world budget spent | `world budget spent (n/max)` |
| 7 | too soon after the last injection | `only N ms since the last injection` |
| 8 | `rearmPercent > 0` and not yet re-armed | `waiting to re-arm (needs X%, at Y%)` |
| 9 | `thresholdPercent <= 0` | `threshold is 0, so the rule is off` |
| 10 | health not measurable | `health is not measurable yet` |
| 11 | percentage not below the threshold | `N% is not below the M% threshold` |
| — | **all of the above pass** | fires: `N% HP is below the M% threshold` |

Details that matter when reading a log:

- **Gates 6 and 7 come before 8-11**, so a spent budget or a short interval is reported even when the
  reading is not below the threshold at all. The first reason that matches wins; the order above is
  the order in the code.
- **Gate 1 is the whole state machine.** `injectionReady` is set by the client's `Hello` (id 55)
  followed by the server's `MapInfo` (id 5), and is *deliberately re-armed to false* on every new
  `Hello` - a realm transition reuses the same TCP connection with a fresh handshake, so anything
  injected during it could land in the middle of the server reading login fields.
- **`MapInfo` clears the world state**: the health reading, the safe-area flag, the cast flag, **and**
  the rule's per-world scratch (budget and interval clock). See §5.
- **Gate 5 defaults to on and is the reason `Nexus`/town is safe.** Across the recorded runs it declined
  four times while the character was below the threshold in a safe area - once during a dry run and
  three times in the live tail of the same session.
- **Percentage maths** (`Reading.percent`): with `useEffectiveHp` off, `health / maxHealth`; with it on,
  `(health + shield + barrier) / maxHealth`, with negative shield/barrier clamped to 0. `maxHealth <= 0`
