java -cp "proxy/target/classes;proxy/target/test-classes" networking.InjectionTests     # injected bytes, the state gate, the rule, the write lock
java -cp "proxy/target/classes;proxy/target/test-classes" networking.ClientPacketsTests # the client's clock field in Move/Shoot/ActivateObject
java -cp "proxy/target/classes;proxy/target/test-classes" networking.UpdateScanTests      # the GmUpdate walk, the strip, the player locator
java -cp "proxy/target/classes;proxy/target/test-classes" networking.SettingsTests        # settings parsing, the route-table write, the filter round trip
python proxy/tools/tests\test_relay.py                     # byte-exact forwarding
python proxy/tools/tests\test_relay_little_endian.py       # both length orders end to end
python proxy/tools/tests\test_reconnect_log.py             # a retarget is decoded and learned, and a kick reason reaches the log
python proxy/tools/tests\test_auto_nexus.py                # the whole auto-nexus chain against a fake server
python proxy/tools/tests\test_status_strip.py              # a server->client rewrite: on by default, narrow, re-framed
python proxy/tools/tests\test_dashboard.py                 # the page parses; every endpoint it reads has the right shape, and settings persist
python proxy/tools/tests\test_relay_stress.py              # both directions under concurrent load: no torn frames,
                                                     # monotonic event log, ring cursor skips nothing
python proxy/tools/verify_packet_ids.py                    # ids vs the client enums (needs DRELAY_DECOMP)
```

The Java checks live in `proxy/src/test/java` and are standalone main classes rather than a JUnit suite, so
they are run with `java -cp` (as above) instead of through Surefire — which is also why the jar does
not contain them. `proxy/tools/tests\test_relay_live.py` needs the real server to be up and the launcher
needs elevation; neither is part of the offline set.

### A layout discrepancy worth recording

`ClientPacketsTests` decodes a real captured `Move` and pins the offset of the client's clock, and in
doing so it turned up something that does not add up: the captured `Move` body is

```
0000E942 0000F142 B9F301 00
└─ X ──┘ └─ Y ──┘ └time┘ └ one byte ┘
```

whereas the decompiled `GmMove` declares `Position`, `Time`, then `HistoryCount` (a byte) followed by a
`HistoryCount`-long array of points. That trailing array has no room in the payload. The capture is
build 5.8.2 and the decompiled source is that same build, so either the field list is richer than the
source suggests or its order differs - and `Move` is one of the client's most frequent packets, so its
declared size and the captured one disagreeing is a real gap rather than a rounding error.

It does not affect anything shipped: the relay reads `Time` and stops, and `Time` is before the
unexplained field in both readings. It is recorded because the same assumption - that the decompiled
field list is complete - is the one that produced three wrong layouts elsewhere in this project
(see §1.1). Anyone extending `ClientPackets` to read further into a `Move` should decode a real
packet to its exact last byte first.

```

`docs/proxy/PROTOCOL.md`:

```md
# drelay — protocol and interception notes

Everything here was established from the **shipped client build 5.8.2** (decompiled with
ILSpy) and from live traffic checks on 2026-10-01. Where the original README disagrees with
this document, this document is correct.

## 1. Client shape

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Runtime | .NET 9 (`DarzasDominion.runtimeconfig.json`, `Microsoft.NETCore.App 9.0.x`) |
| Framework | MonoGame + SharpDX/SkiaSharp, no IL2CPP, no packing |
| Main assembly | `DarzasDominion.dll`, 50 MB, obfuscated (`hehe_*` identifiers, encrypted string literals) |
| Web API | `https://playdarzas.com/api/v1` |
| Log file | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\RippleStudio\Darza\logs\darza.log` |
| Settings | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\RippleStudio\Darza\settings.dat` (+ `.bak`) |
| Crash reports | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\RippleStudio\Darza\crashes\` |

The shipped DLL embeds its own dependencies' sources — including the full **Telepathy**
networking library and the `isrg_root_x1/x2.pem` trust anchors — so `ilspycmd -p` output is
effectively partial source, not just decompiled IL.

## 2. Service ports

From `DarzaCore.Networking.Ports`:

```csharp
public const int Game = 6410;
public const int Game_Slave = 6411;
public const int Queue = 6412;
public const int WebServer = 6406;
```

## 3. How the client learns each destination

This is the crux of why the old approach could only ever proxy Queue.

```
GET https://playdarzas.com/api/v1/checkversion   ->  {"ip":"playdarzas.com",
                                                      "url":"https://playdarzas.com",
                                                      "queueIp":"queue.playdarzas.com"}
GET https://playdarzas.com/api/v1/serverlist     ->  {"servers":[{"host":"18.145.161.25",
                                                                    "serverName":"Zenith",
                                                                    "region":"USW","time":0}]}
```

* **Queue** is addressed by the *hostname* `queue.playdarzas.com` (from `queueIp`), stored in
  `Queue.Ip` (`DarzasDominion.Darza.Networking.Queue`). A name can be shadowed.
* **Game** is addressed by the **bare IP** in `servers[].host` (`ServerInfo.Host`,
  `DarzaGameNet.Structures.ServerInfo`), consumed at `MainMenuScene` → `Client.CurrentHost` →
  `Client.Connect(host, callback)`. A hosts entry cannot express an IP.
* **Every port is an obfuscated constant.** `Client.Connect(host, callback)` passes
  `_E311_EE2E_F8F8_E14F_E1D6.hehe_F244_F670_F803_F5DD_EB9E(842)` as the port, and `Queue.Port` passes
  id 843. `DarzaCore.Networking.Ports` (`Game`/`Game_Slave`/`Queue`) is therefore dead code in this
  build: nothing references it, and no port literal appears in decompiled code at all, which is why
  searching for `6411` finds only its declaration. Two ids are pinned by observation: the queue
  dialled **6412** and the game dialled **6410**.
* **`Game_Slave` (6411) is never dialled by this client.** `Ports.Game_Slave` and the literal `6411`
  each occur exactly once in the whole decompiled assembly - the declaration itself. It is a
  *server-side* port; the only way the client could reach it is the next bullet.
* **`GmReconnect` is the third way a destination is learned, and the only dynamic one.** The server
  sends `GmReconnect` (game id 36) carrying `Host` (string32), `Port` (varint), `ToBeyond` (bool) and
  an optional `CharacterId` (int64); its handler calls
  `Client.Connect(gmReconnect.Host, gmReconnect.Port, …)`. The client dials whatever the server
  names, so no route table can pin that address in advance - which is exactly what `Game_Slave` is:
  not a host the client chooses, but a port the *server* would name. `networking.Relay` decodes this
  packet and logs the target (§6).

That single asymmetry is the whole "Game and Game_Slave could not be redirected" mystery - and 6411
turns out never to have been a destination at all.

### Confirmed dead ends

* **Editing the stored address.** `Prefs.preferred_server_host` in `settings.dat` *can* be
  changed (see §6), but the client cross-checks it against the live `/serverlist` response and
  clears it when absent (`MainMenuScene` ~line 1079). Verified live: with
  `preferred_server_host = 127.0.0.1` the client still dialled `18.145.161.25:6410`.
* **hosts + custom CA.** The API client installs a
  `ServerCertificateCustomValidationCallback` (`DarzasDominion.Darza.Networking.Api`) that
  builds an `X509Chain` with

  ```csharp
  chain.ChainPolicy.TrustMode = X509ChainTrustMode.CustomRootTrust;
  chain.ChainPolicy.CustomTrustStore.AddRange(<isrg_root_x1/x2 read from embedded PEM>);
  ```

  so only certificates chaining to the Let's Encrypt ISRG roots are accepted. It also rejects
  anything except a pure name mismatch before that check, which rules out self-signed certs.
  Without a real ISRG-chained certificate there is no way to terminate this TLS.
* **Frida / DLL injection.** Hooking `connect`/`WSASocketW`/`ConnectEx` in-process makes the
  client die within seconds with

  ```
  System.InvalidOperationException: Handle is not initialized.
     at System.Threading.Overlapped.GetOverlappedFromNative(NativeOverlapped*)
     at System.Threading.IOCompletionCallbackHelper.PerformSingleIOCompletionCallback(...)
  ```

  (reproduced 3x; crash reports under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\RippleStudio\Darza\crashes`). The crashes
  tracked *which* hook was installed rather than Frida's mere presence, so the channel was
  narrowed to `ConnectEx` only — and that is where it stops being viable at all.

### Why ConnectEx-only redirection was abandoned

Probed with a small .NET 8 `Socket.ConnectAsync` client, i.e. the same runtime path the game uses,
instrumenting the Winsock and `mswsock` exports from the process. The scripts that did it are not
kept in the repository (the approach is closed off, so they would only rot), but the measurements
are:

| Finding | Evidence |
|---|---|
| `mswsock.dll` does **not** export `ConnectEx` | 63 exports enumerated; none match |
| `WSAIoctl(SIO_GET_EXTENSION_FUNCTION_POINTER)` from our own thread fails | `rc = -1`, `WSAGetLastError = 0` |
| The runtime fetches **only the IPv6** extension GUID | logged GUID `b907a225…` = `{25a207b9-…}` (v6); v4 GUID `d5a34b2f…` never requested |
| Yet the IPv4 connect succeeds | probe reaches `18.145.161.25:6410` and reads the 14-byte opening frame |
| `ws2_32!connect` and `WSAConnect` are **never** called | both hooked at their exports, zero hits |
| All 62 hookable `mswsock` exports were instrumented | only provider-internal `Tcpip4/6_WSHOpenSocket2` and `Tcpip4_WSHGetSockaddrType` fired; no connect entry point |

So the connect entry point is not reachable by name, by GUID lookup, or by hooking the socket
exports, while `ConnectEx` (the one set that could be replaced without the older crash) is
never the function performing the connect. In-process redirection is therefore closed off, and
the address claim is the only remaining hook that needs no binary modification.

Two useful side results from the same probe: `ConnectEx`'s address is `mswsock+0x24a0`, and the
real server's opening frame is stable — a 10-byte payload `5C 00 …` prefixed by `0000000A`, which
appears on every live connect and is a reliable "the session reached a server" marker.

## 4. Wire format — per-service byte order and type width

```
[4 bytes] payload length   (order differs by service, see below)
[N bytes] payload; the payload starts with the packet type, whose width ALSO differs by service
```

| Service | Length prefix | Type field | Written by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Game / Game_Slave | 4 bytes **big-endian** | **2 bytes, little-endian ushort** | `GmPacket.GetData()` writes `TypeId`; Telepathy frames it |
| Queue | 4 bytes **little-endian** | **1 byte** | `QPacket.GetData()` writes `Id` (a byte) and its own length |

The game's two-byte type is the subtle one. Reading `payload[0]` alone is correct for every game id
below 256 — which is all of them except `JumpScare` (320) — so the mistake stays invisible until a
payload is decoded by hand. It was caught on 2026-10-02, when a live `GmReconnect` beginning
`24 00 0E 00 00 00 …` was read as a host of length 3584: with a one-byte type the string length
starts one byte early. `GmPing` is the clean proof — it is a single `DateTime`, and its live payload
is 10 bytes, exactly 2 + 8. `Relay.typeId`/`Relay.bodyOffset` now read the type per service.

The byte order is **not** uniform, and this was settled from live traffic after a static reading
of the decompiled client gave the wrong answer:

| Service | Order | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Game / Game_Slave | big-endian | live server sends `00 00 00 0A` before its 10-byte opening Ping (`proxy/tools/tests/test_relay_live.py`) |
| Queue | little-endian | live queue session sent `08 00 00 00` (little-endian 8); read big-endian that is 0x08000000 = 134217728 |

The relay originally assumed big-endian everywhere, reasoning from
`Telepathy.ThreadFunctions.ReadMessageBlocking` using `Utils.BytesToIntBigEndian`. That holds for
Telepathy (the game link) but not for the queue link, which the first live queue capture proved by
failing with `implausible payload length 134217728`. `Relay.SessionState` now detects the order
from the first header of a session and reuses it for both directions; `networking.FrameTests`
pins both observed headers.

Details worth keeping:

* The length counts the type field plus the body, and the two services express that differently:
  the queue writes its own prefix and excludes those 4 bytes
  (`BitConverter.GetBytes(array.Length - 4)`), while Telepathy writes the game's and covers
  everything after it.
* `HelloId` (the low byte of the type in the client's opening packet) gates verification
  (`if (Verified || b == HelloId)`); the rest of the handshake is not yet decoded.
* A fresh game-server connection's first server→client packet is a **10-byte payload** whose
  header reads `0000000A` (length 10) and whose type is `0x005C`:

  ```
  0000000A 5C 00 D5 32 F1 92 E7 1F DF 08
           ^^^^^ type 0x005C = 92 (GmPing), then 8 bytes of DateTime
  ```

  `GmPacketType[92]` is `Ping`, and the 9 bytes after the id match a single 64-bit timestamp
  (`GmPing` writes one `DateTime`), so this is the game server's opening ping. Observed on every
  live connect, which makes it a reliable "the session really reached a server" marker.
  (An earlier note here described it as 14 bytes; 14 was the recv() return including the 4-byte
  header. The payload is 10.)
* The original Java proxy wrote **little-endian** lengths while reading with a
  `> 1_000_000 → reverseBytes` heuristic. It happened to read correctly, but re-encoding to LE
  would desync every response. `networking.Relay` uses big-endian on both sides.

## 5. Interception designs (no binary modification)

### Current: claim the server address on the loopback interface

```
   game process
        |
        | dials 18.145.161.25:6410 (a bare IP from /serverlist; nothing is rewritten)
        v
   [that address is claimed on the loopback pseudo-interface]      proxy/tools/Set-AddressClaim.ps1
        |                                                         => the dial is delivered locally
        v
   [networking.Relay listens on 0.0.0.0:6410/6411/6412]   and dials the real server from upstreamHost
        |
        v
      real Game / Game_Slave / Queue
```

Run it with `.\proxy\drelay.ps1`: it claims each route's address, starts the relay with
`-Ddrelay.upstreamHost=<lan-address>`, follows the relay log, and releases the claims on exit.
Verified 2026-10-01 - the relay's startup dial to `18.145.161.25:6410` left the host through the LAN
address and the real server answered, with no local listener running yet.

Queue is the one service the client addresses by *name*. With the claim it needs no hosts entry,
provided the claimed address is the one DNS returns for `queue.playdarzas.com` (`44.242.119.50`,
measured with `nslookup queue.playdarzas.com 1.1.1.1` - nslookup ignores the hosts file, the Windows
resolver does not). The old `<lan-ip> queue.playdarzas.com` line does still put Queue in the relay's
path while the relay is running, but it must not be left in place: the launcher reports it and leaves
the file alone, and while the relay is stopped that name resolves to a local address nothing is
listening on, so the client's queue connection is refused and it drops back to the start menu instead
of reaching the real queue server. That stale entry was exactly the symptom observed on 2026-10-01.

### Superseded: the WinDivert packet redirect

An earlier version of drelay carried a packet-level redirector (a .NET program using WinDivert) that
rewrote the client's outbound `:6410/:6411/:6412` packets to a local address. Its code is no longer
in the repository, because the address claim replaced it, but the reasons it failed are worth keeping:
they are why the claim is the design it is.

* The redirect is machine-wide on the destination ports, so it also catches the relay's own upstream
  dials, and the relay then dials itself forever. A source-port *range* guard does not separate them,
  because the OS hands the client and the relay ephemeral ports from the same range; the fix was to
  pin the relay's dials to one knowable source port (`upstreamBindPort`) and exclude exactly that
  port from the filter. Windows permits one connection per local port, so this also serialized
  upstream dials and failed a second concurrent session - the queue and game overlapping.
* Rewriting a packet to a local address and re-injecting it did **not** deliver it to a local
  listener (`seen=21 redirected=21` and zero relay sessions; the client timed out).
* Dropping the first SYN and letting the retransmit through made the client connect **directly** to
  the real server: an untouched retransmit still goes to the public address, so the relay became a
  no-op.
* A packet marked with the loopback flag while its peer is a public address is dropped by Windows;
  forcing that flag made the client's own dial time out with the relay logging nothing at all.

The decisive measurement is that the relay must be listening on **the same address the client
dials**, which is what claiming that address achieves.

### A hosts-file trap worth knowing

The hosts line that makes the client's queue connection catchable is
`<lan-ip> queue.playdarzas.com`. That same line makes the **relay** resolve
`queue.playdarzas.com` to its own listen address, so a route table naming that host makes the
relay dial itself - and a reachability check reports "OK", because something is listening: the
relay. Route hosts must therefore be concrete addresses. The relay detects this case explicitly and
says `destination ... resolves to THIS MACHINE`.

### Verification status

| Layer | Verified? | How |
|---|---|---|
| Framing + byte-exact forwarding | yes | `proxy/tools/tests/test_relay.py` — 3 packets round-tripped, incl. all 256 byte values |
| Per-service byte order | yes | `networking.FrameTests` (both live headers) + `proxy/tools/tests/test_relay_little_endian.py` (both orders end to end) |
| Relay against the **real server** | yes | `proxy/tools/tests/test_relay_live.py` — relay carried the genuine `len=10 id=0x5C Ping` handshake both ways |
| Packet primitives and codecs | yes | `networking.PrimitiveTests` |
| Packet-id tables | yes | `proxy/tools/verify_packet_ids.py`, name-by-name against the client enums (needs a decompiled client; see the script) |
| Live Queue / Game / Game_Slave capture | **yes** for Queue + Game, Slave idle | the launcher, 2026-10-01: `[Queue#1]` Hello/Join, then a playable `[Game#2]` session (~400 named packets); no `[Game_Slave#N]` at all |
| Realm transition (`GmReconnect` retarget) | yes | 2026-10-02, and `proxy/tools/tests/test_reconnect_log.py` offline |

### Every non-elevated redirect route is closed

Measured on this machine, so nobody has to rediscover them:

| Mechanism | Result |
|---|---|
| `hosts` edit | denied (needs admin) |
| `netsh interface portproxy` | "The requested operation requires elevation" |
| `route add` | "requires elevation" |
| `New-NetIPAddress` (loopback alias) | access denied |
| raw socket (ARP/DNS spoofing) | `WinError 10013`, forbidden by access permissions |
| WinDivert without elevation | `Win32Exception: Access is denied` |
| in-process hooking | crashes the client (§3) |

Every one of those routes is closed without elevation, so interception needs exactly one elevated
step: the **address claim** (`proxy/tools/Set-AddressClaim.ps1`), which loads no driver and rewrites no
packets.

### Packet-level redirect: three mechanisms, all measured against the real client

The client dials a **bare IP** from `/api/v1/serverlist`, so a hosts entry cannot shadow it, and
rewriting that packet is the obvious approach. It does not work, and the reasons are worth
recording so nobody repeats them.

| Mechanism | Result |
|---|---|
| rewrite destination + re-inject | `[stats] seen=21 redirected=21` and **zero** relay sessions; the client timed out. Rewritten packets are not delivered locally |
| drop the first SYN, forward the retransmit untouched | the client **connected directly to the real server** (its own log shows `[Client] Connected` while the relay logged no game session); an untouched retransmit still goes to the public address, so the relay becomes a no-op |
| rely on local routing | measured: a socket bound to the LAN address dialling the public address on the same port **times out**, and no local listener sees it - Windows sends it out to the real server |

The decisive property: the relay must be listening on **the same address the client dials**.
Nothing short of claiming that address puts the relay in the path.

### The viable mechanism: claim the server address

Assign the game server's address to a local interface so the kernel routes the client's
connection into the local stack, then bind the relay to that address. No packet rewriting, no
injection, no hosts trickery.

`proxy/tools/Test-AddressClaim.ps1` probes **both halves** in one elevated run: a listener on the claimed
address plus an *unbound* client (the game client's shape) must meet, and the same listener plus a
client *bound to the LAN address* (the relay's upstream shape) must not meet. It claims on the
loopback pseudo-interface by default, which touches no hardware configuration, no DHCP setting and
no route.

Measured 2026-10-01, elevated, claiming on `Loopback Pseudo-Interface 1` with LAN address
`192.168.0.39`: probe 1 **accepted** the client's dial to `18.145.161.25:6410` (arriving from
`18.145.161.25:55187`), and probe 2's source-bound dial to `203.0.113.7:6410` left the host without
reaching the local listener. The mechanism is confirmed: the relay binds the claimed address
directly and needs no packet rewriting.

#### Two documented Windows behaviours that made the first revision fail and damage the NIC

Measured here on 2026-10-01, on `Ethernet 2`:

* `New-NetIPAddress` **switches DHCP off** on a DHCP-enabled interface
  ([docs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/nettcpip/new-netipaddress): "If you
  run this cmdlet to add an IP address to an interface on which DHCP is already enabled, then DHCP
  is automatically disabled"). The lease goes with it, so a cleanup that removes only the claimed
  address leaves the NIC static with no address at all: APIPA `169.254.x.x`, no default route, no
  DNS, adapter still "Up". Repair with `proxy/tools/Restore-DhcpAddressing.ps1`, or by hand:
  `netsh interface ipv4 set address name="<nic>" source=dhcp` then `ipconfig /renew "<nic>"`.
* The same page: "the new IP address is not usable until DAD successfully finishes". Binding
  straight after the add races duplicate address detection, and `Start()` fails with
  `WSAEADDRNOTAVAIL (10049) "The requested address is not valid in its context"` - exactly what the
  first run reported. Wait for `AddressState -eq 'Preferred'`.

#### The claim must live on the loopback interface

The boundary Windows enforces is the **loopback** one, not "any other interface". Measured:

| listener (a local address) | client source | result |
|---|---|---|
| `100.90.214.22` (Tailscale) | bound to `192.168.0.40` (Wi-Fi) | **not** delivered locally |
| `100.90.214.22` (Tailscale) | unbound | delivered locally |
| `192.168.0.40` (Wi-Fi) | bound to `192.168.0.40` | delivered locally |
| `192.168.0.39` (Ethernet) | bound to `192.168.0.40` (Wi-Fi), same subnet | **delivered locally** |
| `127.0.0.1` (loopback) | bound to `192.168.0.39` (Ethernet) | not delivered (`WSAEADDRNOTAVAIL`) |
| claimed `203.0.113.7/32` on loopback | bound to `192.168.0.39` (Ethernet) | not delivered - the dial left the host |

The fourth row is the trap, and it caught this project while the pieces were being wired together: a
claim on a **physical** NIC is not safe, because a dial from another NIC - even one on the same
subnet - can still be delivered locally. `networking.Relay` demonstrated it directly: with the
destination assigned to the Ethernet NIC and its upstream source bound to the Wi-Fi NIC it accepted
its own dials, hundreds of sessions per second, which is the loop signature described below.
Therefore `validateUpstream` refuses to start when a claimed destination sits on a physical
interface, `proxy/tools/Set-AddressClaim.ps1` only ever claims on loopback, and the loopback boundary
holds in both directions: the game client (which binds no source) lands in the local stack, while
the relay's source-bound upstream dial leaves the host.

The relay does not merely trust that measurement - `preflightClaimed` proves the escape at startup.
It binds a probe listener on the claimed address first and then dials through `upstreamHost`; if the
dial arrives at that probe, the relay exits (code 3) rather than starting a proxy that would accept
its own dials forever. The check runs **before** any listener starts, so a captured dial cannot be
mistaken for the real server answering.

Configuration consequences:

* `upstreamHost` - the LAN address - is **required** as soon as a route destination is claimed
  (`-Ddrelay.upstreamHost=...` overrides the file), because an unbound dial to a claimed address is
  delivered locally. The relay refuses to start without it, and also if it names a loopback address.
  The launcher works this out and writes it into the run's route table, so it only has to be set by
  hand when the relay is started directly.
* `upstreamBindPort` is unused by the claim path and should stay 0. It existed only to give the
  retired packet filter a source port to exclude, and a pinned port has a real cost: Windows allows
  one connection per local port, so it serializes upstream dials and fails a second concurrent
  session (a queue and a game session overlapping, for instance).
* A server address that is *not* claimed silently bypasses the proxy - the client reaches the real
  server directly - which is why the launcher claims before starting the relay and reports what the
  claim script verified. A realm address is claimed at runtime instead: when a `GmReconnect` names a
  host and port, the relay claims that address and learns the destination before forwarding the
  packet, so the client's follow-up dial cannot escape.
* `proxy/tools/Set-AddressClaim.ps1 -Status` reports what is claimed right now, and every runtime claim is
  recorded in `proxy/work/learned-claims.txt` so one that was killed can still be released.

### Why the packet redirect was abandoned

The redirector is gone from this repository; the address claim is the interception path. Its
diagnostics were what identified the failures recorded above, and the same questions apply to any
future attempt at a packet-level redirect:

| Observation | Meaning |
|---|---|
| the redirect counters rise, the relay shows no session | the rewrite happens but the packet never reaches a listener (a re-injection problem) |
| the counters stay at zero | the filter is not matching; check the port list and `DstPort` |
| a `notTcp` counter rises while `redirected` stays 0 | non-TCP/IPv4 traffic is matching; the client may be dialling over IPv6 |
| the relay logs `destination UNREACHABLE` | the route table address is stale |

## 6. Packet layer

`proxy/src/main/java/networking/packets/` implements the client's serialization model.

> **Writing packets, not just reading them.** The relay also injects now (auto-nexus), which adds two
> orderings this document does not cover: the frame order (a length that *includes* the 2-byte type id)
> and the session-state order (nothing may be written before the client's `Hello` and the server's
> `MapInfo`). Both are in [INJECTION.md](INJECTION.md) §1, along with the event log and the dashboard.

**Primitives** (`GameReader` / `GameWriter`, mirroring `DarzaCore.Tools.ByteReader/ByteWriter`):

| Client call | Wire format | Java |
|---|---|---|
| `Write(int/uint/short/ushort/long/float/double)` | little-endian (.NET `BinaryWriter`) | `writeInt32`, `writeUInt16`, `writeFloatLE`, ... |
| `WriteString8/16/32` | 1/2/4-byte length prefix + UTF-8 bytes | `writeString8/16/32` |
| `Write(bool)` | one byte, 1 or 0 | `writeBool` |
| `Write(GamePoint)` | two little-endian floats | `writePoint` |
| `Write(IntPoint)` | two varints | `writeIntPoint` |
| `WriteVarint(int)` | 6 value bits + sign bit (bit 6) + continuation bit (bit 7), then 7-bit groups starting at bit 6: the groups are **6, 6, 7, 7, …** | `writeVarint` |

The varint grouping is the one place a static reading of the client gave a wrong answer, because the
bit masks live in the encrypted constant pool. It was settled by measurement: `83 0B` is **707**, not
the 1411 that a 6, 7, 7 grouping produces, and the fixed-width `StatsType.Hp` int16 in the matching
`GmUpdate` is what proves it. See [INJECTION.md](INJECTION.md) §2.
`PrimitiveTests` pins the captured bytes.

The little-endian detail is easy to get wrong: the **framing header is big-endian** (4-byte
length) while **every payload field is little-endian**. The legacy proxy wrote little-endian
lengths; `Relay` writes big-endian.

**Ids.** `GmPacketType` (321 entries) and `QPacketType` (5 entries) are generated from the client
enums and verified name-by-name against the decompiled source by
`proxy/tools/verify_packet_ids.py`. Neither enum declares explicit values, so the id is the ordinal.

**Two id spaces.** Queue and Game do *not* share ids — queue `1` is `Hello` while game `1` is
`Update`, queue `4` is `Error` while game `4` is `RegisterResp`. Both services use identical
framing, so `PacketRegistry` keeps the registries separate and the relay picks one per route
(`Route.isQueue()`).

**Verified codecs:** on the game side `HealthUpdate` (70), `Escape` (66), `Reconnect` (36),
`EscapeAck` (158), `ForcedEscape` (184), `Kicked` (185), `EscapeCastState` (290) and `SafeAreaState`
(291); on the queue side `Hello` (1), `Position` (2), `Join` (3) and `Error` (4). Everything without a
codec is forwarded byte-for-byte, which is deliberate: re-encoding through a mis-modelled packet
silently corrupts a session.

`Kicked` is decoded for the log rather than for a rule: it carries the server's own string16 reason
for ending the session, which the relay records as `data.reason` on the packet event and as
`kickedReason` on the session-close event. It is the fastest explanation of a failed server→client
rewrite ([INJECTION.md](INJECTION.md) §5.5).

`networking.PrimitiveTests` is the gate:

```powershell
java -cp proxy/target/classes;proxy/target/test-classes networking.PrimitiveTests
```

It checks varint boundaries and round-trips (including exact byte layouts such as
`varint(250) = BA 03`), little-endian layout of ints/floats, string length prefixes under UTF-8,
`HealthUpdate`'s byte layout, all four queue packets, and the separation of the two id spaces.

### The queue → game handshake (captured 2026-10-01)

The first live capture through the claim (client build 5.8.2) shows the whole admission flow. Queue
is little-endian, game is big-endian, and **Queue hands the client the token that admits it to the
game**:

```
[Queue#1] /44.242.119.50:61652 -> 44.242.119.50:6412
[Queue#1 C->S] first header raw=08000000 -> LITTLE length 8
[Queue#1 C->S] len=8  id=0x01 Hello   01065A656E697468
                       01 Hello, 06 = string8 length, "Zenith"          <- servers[].serverName
[Queue#1 S->C] first header raw=22000000 -> LITTLE length 34
[Queue#1 S->C] len=34 id=0x03 Join    032057767A68517A746B796F6845454E527A50335564536871493942645A316B4F4D
                       03 Join, 20 = 32 bytes, "WvzhQztkyohEENRzP3UdShqI9BdZ1kOM"
[Queue#1 C->S] closed

[Game#2 C->S] first header raw=00000079 -> BIG length 121
[Game#2 C->S] len=121 id=0x37 Hello  3700 28 <24 bytes> 05 "5.8.2" 00 02 7F9739…9E01
                                     20 "WvzhQztkyohEENRzP3UdShqI9BdZ1kOM"      <- the same token
                                     14 "mMYVSvPiVzDT2YcEuqfm" 00 00 …
[Game#2 S->C] len=604 id=0x33 DailyGold    <- admission accepted
[Game#2 S->C] len=163 id=0x05 MapInfo      "The Tavern" / "TheTavernRemade_Halloween.bmap"
[Game#2 S->C] len=8   id=0x46 HealthUpdate
```

So the client asks Queue for the server **by name**, Queue answers `Join` with a 32-character token,
and the client presents that same token inside its game `Hello`, together with the version string
`5.8.2` and a 20-character account token. The session then streams `Update`/`Move`/`Projectiles`/
`Ping` and is fully playable through the relay.

`Game_Slave` (6411) was **never dialled** in this session, which is consistent with §3: the client
reaches it on the same host and that port is closed. That also shows why the two id spaces must stay
separate in `PacketRegistry`: `0x01` is Queue's `Hello` above, and `0x01` is the game's `Update` in
the live stream.

### The one packet that moves a session: `GmReconnect` (36)

Server to client, payload `24 00` onward. Fields in order: `Host` (string32), `Port` (varint),
`ToBeyond` (bool), `CharacterId` (int64, read only when bytes remain, otherwise `-1`). The client's
handler calls `Client.Connect(gmReconnect.Host, gmReconnect.Port, callback)` and *retries* that same
call on failure, so this packet decides where the rest of the session lives.

It is the whole of `Game_Slave`: 6411 is a port the **server** names, not one the client chooses, and
the address rotates per transition. Live capture on entering a realm, 2026-10-02:

```
[Game#2 S->C] len=31 id=0x24 Reconnect (codec)  24000E00000031382E3134352E3231352E3231338B64007F97390000000000
[Game#2 S->C]   RETARGET -> 18.145.215.213:6411  characterId=3774335  toBeyond=false

   24 00              type 36 (two little-endian bytes, see §4)
   0E 00 00 00        host length 14
   "18.145.215.213"   host
   8B 64              varint 6411
   00                 toBeyond
   7F 97 39 00 00 00 00 00    characterId = 3774335
```

The client's own log agrees: `[Client] Reconnecting to 18.145.215.213:6411...` then
`[Client] Reconnect connected, sending hello.` — that time straight to the real server, because the
address was not claimed. The next transition in the same session named `3.71.176.153:6411`, which is
the point: no static route can cover a destination the server invents per transition.

Because this is the one place a claimed-address relay loses a session, the relay acts on the packet
instead of only logging it. **Before** forwarding it (`networking.Relay.onRetarget`):

1. it claims the named address on the loopback pseudo-interface with
   `netsh interface ipv4 add address <loopback index> <ip> 255.255.255.255 store=active` — the same
   session-only store as `Set-AddressClaim.ps1 -SessionOnly` — refusing any address a real interface
   owns;
2. it records `host:port` in `Config.learned` for that port, which `handleSession` consults before
   the route table.

The write happens after both, so the client cannot dial the new address before the claim exists: the
transition pauses for the claim instead of escaping. Both steps are best effort — an unelevated relay
cannot claim, says so, and forwards anyway. Runtime claims are released by a shutdown hook and listed
in `proxy/work/learned-claims.txt`, so `Set-AddressClaim.ps1 -Release` (and `drelay.ps1 -Stop`) can clean
up after a relay that was killed.

Decoding never alters forwarding: the payload is still written on byte for byte, so a mis-read can
cost a log line but never a byte of the session.

## 7. settings.dat format

A flat key/value blob obfuscated with a **+1 byte shift on printable bytes** (`https` is stored
as `httpu`). `proxy/tools/decode_settings.py` reads it and can rewrite it:

```powershell
python proxy/tools/decode_settings.py                                   # dump keys/values
python proxy/tools/decode_settings.py --write out.dat --replace OLD NEW  # re-encode with an edit
```

Keys seen: `last_web_server_ip`, `preferred_server_host`, `preferred_server_name`,
`access_token`, `auto_activate`, `camera_offset`, plus UI/audio settings. Note that
`preferred_server_host` is validated against the server list at startup (§3), so editing it is
useful for inspection but cannot retarget the client.

## 8. Tooling used

| Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `ilspycmd` | decompile the shipped assembly for analysis; primary source of truth |
| `networking.Relay` (`proxy/src/main/java`) | the relay: per-route listeners, byte-exact forwarding |
| `networking.Launcher` | the packaged entry point: elevation, updates, claims, child relay |
| `proxy/tools/Set-AddressClaim.ps1` | claims and releases the server addresses on loopback |
| Java 25+ (`javac`, Maven or `build.ps1`) | the relay build; no third-party runtime dependencies |
| `proxy/tools/tests/test_relay.py`, `proxy/tools/tests/test_relay_little_endian.py`, `proxy/tools/tests/test_relay_stress.py` | framing, byte order and load, without the game |
| `proxy/tools/tests/test_relay_live.py` | the relay in front of the real server |
| `proxy/tools/decode_settings.py` | `settings.dat` codec |

Earlier versions of this project also used a WinDivert packet redirector, a Frida-based in-process
hook, and ConnectEx interception. All three are recorded above as failures, their code is not part of
the repository, and `tools/` no longer ships any of it: the address claim replaced them.

## 9. Still unknown

1. The queue handshake and match payloads — **captured 2026-10-01** through the claim, without any
   hosts entry: `[Queue#1]` `Hello`/`Join` and a full `[Game#2]` session; see §6.
2. **When** `GmReconnect` fires — **resolved 2026-10-02**: it fires when the client changes server.
   The first observed cases are entering a realm on `Game_Slave` (port 6411) and returning to the
   lobby (port 6410). The relay now claims and learns the named destination before forwarding the
   packet, so the session stays in the proxy. There is nothing to pre-claim, because the address
   only exists once the server names it.
3. Game_Slave — **resolved: it is not a client destination at all.** §3: `Ports.Game_Slave` and the
   literal `6411` occur exactly once each in the decompiled client (the declaration), the ports the
   client actually dials come from the obfuscated constant table (6412 queue, 6410 game, both
   observed live), and one full login → queue → character → game session produced no dial to 6411 at
   all — the route's listener saw nothing. The README-era `44.222.253.93` was a hard-coded line in
   the legacy proxy, never an observation. `6411` is a *server-side* port: the client would
   only dial it if the server sent a `GmReconnect` naming it. `relay-routes.json` keeps the route,
   marked `optional`, so such a dial is captured rather than bypassing the proxy, while its closed
   port is reported as a note instead of a warning.

```

`hook/README.md`:

```md
# autododge research — an in-process hook for Darza's Dominion

This directory is the research and implementation plan for replacing `drelay`'s **reactive**
auto-nexus with a hook that runs **inside the game process**: it dodges incoming damage before it
lands, and falls back to the client's own nexus only when no move can avoid it.

It is research plus a plan, **and Phases 0, 1 and 2 are built and closed**: the fingerprint gate and
the target table that pin the hook's four detour points by IL hash; the injection and hook skeleton
that matches all four against the live game; and the read-only sensor that predicts collisions and
compares them against the game's own decision ([`PHASE2-SCOPE.md`](../docs/hook/PHASE2-SCOPE.md), closed by
operator decision on 2026-10-13). No game file has been modified; the hook attaches at runtime.

Branch: `autododge-research`. The proxy stays Java; the hook is C++.

---

## Where the work stands

| phase | state |
|---|---|
| **0** — ground truth, and a build gate | **built.** The gate passes 15 checks against the installed build and refuses a mutated one at the *method* level; **six** targets are pinned by IL hash, cross-checked against the disassembly, and recorded in [`known-build.json`](known-build.json) (four Phase 0/2 targets, Phase 3's movement integrator, and the auto-aim target `AimbotSystem.FindTarget`, added by the auto-aim module below). The procedure is [`docs/hook/HOOK-BUILD-MATRIX.md`](../docs/hook/HOOK-BUILD-MATRIX.md). One item is open: the controlled `GmHit`-drop trial, which needs a live session and does not gate the hook |
| **1** — get in, and stay in | **built, confirmed live, and closed on 2026-10-12.** Three artefacts build clean — `Drelay.Hook.dll` (native), `Drelay.Bootstrap.dll` (the startup hook) and `Drelay.Launcher.exe` — and every offline check passes: ABI, the PE/MVID reader (including a deliberately tampered image) and a **127-check end-to-end injection test that passes 127/127** (90 when Phase 1 closed; Phase 2 added the managed replacement under forced full compacting collections, the sensor's read of the live set, the collision comparison and the predicate-semantics checks those last two need). Against the real game the whole chain works: injection before `Main`, the handshake, runtime validation, the JIT/EE GUID, the loaded-vs-file MVID check, the collection delay and its window, and the `compileMethod` detour seeing the compilation stream. **All four targets are matched by IL hash against the live game** — `frameTick` (IL 1286, token `0x06001FC5`, agreeing with Phase 0), `spawn` (2014), `collision` (989) and `escape` (335) — and `frameTick` is patched, with the hook reading live state from the real game: `arm state: ARMED`, the pointer chain and reflection agreeing on `Player.Position`, a plausible coordinate in `frames.csv`, and in the **hour-long acceptance run of 2026-10-12** 198 586 successful reads out of 209 897 frame calls at 53.8 Hz with no fault recorded and the read correctly paused at the window's close. Exit 2a (a denied log target costs evidence, never the game) passed all four of its assertions in the same round. The full accounting is [`PHASE1-VERIFICATION.md`](../docs/hook/PHASE1-VERIFICATION.md) §11; [`PHASE1-HANDOFF.md`](../docs/hook/PHASE1-HANDOFF.md) is the long record of how it got there — its earlier sections describe fixed faults and are historical, and the long-form record is [`PHASE1-SCOPE.md`](../docs/hook/PHASE1-SCOPE.md) §6 |
| **2** — observe, and find out whether the model is true | **closed by operator decision on 2026-10-13**, with two recorded waivers rather than every number clean: the sampler's p99 cost is deferred to the solver that has to share the frame (now Phase 3), and the false-negative count is an over-count from asking the collision predicate on every entry instead of every `true` ([`PHASE2-SCOPE.md`](../docs/hook/PHASE2-SCOPE.md) §4.15, §7). Its mechanism question was answered by measurement. Read-only. The goal is one question — does our prediction of a collision agree with the game's? — and four numbers: the warning distribution, the false-negative and false-positive rates, the per-frame cost p50/p99, and the fraction of real bullets that are straight. **How the sensor runs on the game's thread was resolved by measurement, and it cost the first two candidates.** A native detour that calls into managed code is flaky — about one run in four died inside the GC's mark phase even with every method pre-compiled and nothing allocating — because the runtime cannot unwind a managed stack that a native frame interrupts without a transition marker. What works is a **managed replacement**: MinHook's `jmp` lands directly in a managed method with the target's signature, so the game's own `call` is a managed-to-managed call, and it continues into the original through a **managed** function pointer to MinHook's trampoline. Seven runs survived 650 forced full blocking compacting collections, including with allocation, and run 8 of the injection suite re-runs that configuration on every invocation. Scope, the run tables and both verdicts: [`PHASE2-SCOPE.md`](../docs/hook/PHASE2-SCOPE.md) §4.3–§4.4. **And the first session that reached a zone found the sensor reading the wrong container:** fifteen minutes of real play, 54 600 frames with a world on all but one of them, a zone full of bullets in the game's own log — and `live=0` throughout, because the client keeps its projectiles in `World.GameObjectLayer.Children` and not in `World.Objects`, which is what CLIENT-MAP.md §5.2 had claimed and what the hook read. The synthetic host had modelled the same wrong shape, which is why every offline check passed. Both are corrected and §10.6 is closed by the measurement. **The next session read the real client's bullets** — 19 349 frames with a world, 12–28 live projectiles per frame on a layer of 210–265 nodes, a straight fraction of **0.695** over 585 000 sampled trajectories, and a read cost of `p50 <= 50 µs, p99 <= 100 µs` — and it also showed that the collision counter had been counting the game's per-frame *predicate questions* rather than its decisions: 418 328 entries against 48 resolved hits, which inflated the false-negative rate by however long each bullet spent near the player. The counter now gates on the game's own `true`, the fixture models the predicate and would catch a regression, and **one more live session produces the four numbers as the plan defines them**. The operator has waived the cost criteria for this close. [`PHASE2-SCOPE.md`](../docs/hook/PHASE2-SCOPE.md) §4.14–§4.15 |
| **3** — dodge, with the escape as its floor | **entered 2026-10-14; Spike 3.1 ANSWERED YES on 2026-10-14.** The movement question has a mechanism: a **fifth pinned target**, `World`'s movement integrator, with a **managed replacement** on its entry — the same route Phase 2 proved — so the hook writes `GameScene.GameInput.MoveAngle` / `.Moving` / `.MoveSpeed` and the *client* produces the position, the speed law, the collision and the history the outbound `GmMove` is built from. It is opt-in (`Drelay.Launcher.exe --move-steer sweep` or `hold:90:600`), bounded by frame counts, guarded by the game's own dead/safe/spirit gates, and it releases the input when the plan ends. **The live sweep of `20261014-040859-p22748` moved the player in eight commanded directions: the value read back from `MoveAngle` equalled the value written on every logged frame (worst `0.0000000 rad`), the heading followed the command to within 2°, and the per-frame displacement agrees with the resolved speed law and with the offline budget.** The one witness still outstanding is the wire's — run the sweep with `-RelayLog` to see `GmKicked` absent rather than assume it. The run reports through [`tools/steering_report.py`](tools/steering_report.py), which reads the pilot's own frame log, the install log and the **relay's wire log** — because the client's position cannot witness whether the server accepted the movement. Four invariants (T5, T6, T10, T7) plus a "must move" assertion, over five synthetic scenarios with known correct answers: green, and they found **seven defects on the day the solver was written** — including a `stand` candidate whose lookup field was never written, so the specification's preferred answer ("the best dodge is usually no dodge") was dead code, and a "nothing is safe" fallback that emitted moves admission had already refused. **T7 — predicted versus actual collision, the only test that can tell us whether the trajectory model is right — is wired and has never been run**: it needs a recorded session. What exists, what it cost, and the one command outstanding: [`SPIKE3.2-OFFLINE-SOLVER.md`](../docs/hook/SPIKE3.2-OFFLINE-SOLVER.md). **T7 has since been run against six recorded sessions** -- 0 % false negatives on the first, and a residual of 4-15 misses per session on the rest (that document, sections 4.3-4.7). **And the operator's own reading of the dodge -- *"it considers a projectile's entire path dangerous"* -- produced the plan model on 2026-10-15:** a candidate is no longer a point scored against a bullet's whole polyline, it is a direction the character walks in, tested against where the bullet's body will be at the same instant, plus an imaginary goal point projected along the measured course. `NoAdmissible` on the third recording falls from 1148 frames to 6 and the decision gets *cheaper*, with T5/T6/T10 holding and T7 unchanged to the collision. The trade the change leaves open -- `keeps its course` against `overrides intent` -- is the operator's to settle live: [`SPIKE3.2-OFFLINE-SOLVER.md`](../docs/hook/SPIKE3.2-OFFLINE-SOLVER.md) section 11. **The first live session after it then found something older and larger: 51.8 % of that session's threat records were the player's own projectiles**, because the sensor filtered by type and never asked the client's `HitsPlayer` question -- the same flag `DODGE-ALGORITHM.md` section 3.1 had named as "the threat filter" since the beginning. They were 959 of its 971 "already touching" verdicts and 255 of its 1140 moves, and they made the dodge take the wheel around the operator's own muzzle every time they fired. The sampler now declines them before sampling, and both the trace and the report carry the count: [`SPIKE3.2-OFFLINE-SOLVER.md`](../docs/hook/SPIKE3.2-OFFLINE-SOLVER.md) section 12 |
| **4** — the bridge | not started. Phase 3 does not depend on it |

### Building and checking Phase 1

```powershell
.\\hook\build.ps1                 # all three artefacts -> hook\out\
.\\hook\tools\Test-HookAbi.ps1    # offline ABI check, no game needed
.\\hook\tools\Test-PeReader.ps1   # PE/MVID reader, incl. a tampered image
.\\hook\tools\Test-Injection.ps1  # end-to-end, against a synthetic host (127 checks)
.\\hook\tools\Test-HookOffline.ps1  # everything that needs NO game: the ABI self-test, the two generated tables,
                                    # both report fixtures, and the launcher's configuration
                                    # invariants (C1-C8: the four sources, their per-field
                                    # precedence, the discovery walk and the environment the child
                                    # is given). The metadata reader's self-test joins them only
                                    # when the game is installed -- it reads the game's own PE --
                                    # and is named as not run when it is not.
```

If a native build fails with `LNK1104: cannot open file ...Drelay.Hook.dll`, a leftover game
process is holding it — kill any `DarzasDominion` or `Drelay.Launcher` first. It is not the
documented retry-once quirk.

### Running auto-aim

The hook's target selection: full 360 degrees, two modes, invulnerable enemies never
chosen. [`AUTOAIM.md`](../docs/hook/AUTOAIM.md) is the manual; the short version is one switch.

```powershell
.\\hook\out\Drelay.Launcher.exe --game "E:\SteamLibrary\steamapps\common\Darza's Dominion" --autoaim closest
.\\hook\out\Drelay.Launcher.exe --game "E:\SteamLibrary\steamapps\common\Darza's Dominion" --autoaim highesthp
```

`closest` is the nearest damageable enemy in the equipped weapon's range; `highesthp` is
the one with the most current health. Both replace the game's own
`AimbotSystem.FindTarget` — the shipped desktop aimbot is the same mechanism behind a
cone of `player.AimAssist * pi / 20`, which is zero without the gear affix, so this is
the difference between "nothing" and "everything in range". Everything downstream of the
choice — the projectile leading, the shot geometry, the highlight on the target — is the
client's own code, unchanged.

It sets the game's own aimbot setting on (`Prefs.enable_aimbot`), and the game persists
it; that is named in the log when it happens and in [`AUTOAIM.md`](../docs/hook/AUTOAIM.md) §4. It also
implies `--frame-replacement`, for the ordering reason in [`AUTOAIM.md`](../docs/hook/AUTOAIM.md) §1 —
the flag has to be armed from the game's own thread before the target is ever called.
The target is compiled only once a world exists, so the run's own log is in
`<run dir>\bootstrap.log` — look for `auto-aim: the replacement answered its first call`.

### Starting it with no arguments (the configuration file)

`Drelay.Launcher.exe` with **no arguments at all** is a supported way to start it, and it is what a
double-click does. It reads one file:

```text
%LOCALAPPDATA%\drelay\hook\drelay.config.json
```

and, if that file does not say where the game is, it looks for it: the Steam registry
(`HKCU\Software\Valve\Steam` → `SteamPath`, then `steamapps\libraryfolders.vdf` and every library in
it), then the `recordedFrom` path in [`known-build.json`](known-build.json), then the launcher's own
directory (which covers "unpacked into the game folder"). First hit wins.

**Discovery produces a candidate; the gate decides.** A directory is only accepted when the assembly
beside the apphost is the pinned build, so the `OpenGL\` apphost — which carries a *different*
assembly — is refused and named, rather than silently skipped for the next candidate.

Precedence is **per field**: command line > config file > discovery > compiled defaults. A config
that sets `GamePath` and two other fields keeps all three when you pass `--autoaim highesthp`, and a
flag the config does not mention keeps the launcher's default. There is deliberately no
environment-variable layer: the launcher deletes every `DRELAY_HOOK_*` name from the child's
environment, so a setting read from that namespace could never reach the hook.

**A first no-argument run writes that file if it is missing, and then runs with it** — so a
double-click is: the file appears, and the session aims at the closest damageable enemy and dodges,
which is what the written file says. `%LOCALAPPDATA%\drelay\hook` then holds what to change:

```jsonc
{
  // Required unless the game is discovered (§ above) or --game is given.
  "GamePath": "E:\\SteamLibrary\\steamapps\\common\\Darza's Dominion",

  "AutoAim": "closest",          // "closest" | "highesthp" | null (off)
  "Dodge": {
    "Enabled": true,             // run the solver every frame and log decisions
    "Act": true,                 // ...and let the decision steer the player.
                                 // false still solves and logs; it just never moves you
    "DecisionDisc": null,        // --dodge-disc; null means the solver's own default
    "WindowSeconds": null        // --dodge-window
  },

  "CollectDelayMs": 0,
  "DiscoveryWindowMs": 10000,
  "LiveSeconds": 5,
  "PauseAfterRun": false
}
```

The file is written by a first run and never overwritten, so editing it is how a session is
described from then on; setting `"AutoAim"` to `null` and `"Dodge"."Act"` to `false` leaves the hook
attached, reading the frame and running the solver's dry run, and moving nothing.

Every key is optional, `null` means "not set", unknown keys are ignored, and a *value* that is wrong
(a misspelled `AutoAim`, a number where a boolean belongs) refuses at startup naming the field — a
typo that silently resolved to "off" would cost a session spent watching the game not aim. The
test-harness switches (`--test-target`, `--frame-helper`, `--frame-replacement`, `--off`,
`--full-trace`, `--trace`, `--move-steer`, `--escape-test`, `--assembly`, `--exe`) are **not** in the
schema and not in the template; a config that offers `FrameHelper` would be offering a switch that
allocates 64 KB per frame on purpose.

`"Dodge": {"Act": true}` and `--move-steer` both say *this is what steers the player*: typed together
on the command line they are refused, but `--move-steer` beside the file's `Act` wins for that run,
with a `note :` line saying so, so `Run-Phase3Session.ps1 -Experiment Sweep|Hold` still works. The
solver keeps running and logging; add `"Enabled": false` to the file for a calibration run that does
not pay for it.

If discovery fails, a no-argument run prints the reason, points at the file to fill in, and waits for
a keypress — **only** from a double-click. A run whose standard input is redirected never blocks, and
a refusal the user cannot fix by editing a file (a missing DLL, an OpenGL install) is printed and
exits without pausing. The design, the decisions behind it and the ones it rejected are in
[`HANDOFF-LAUNCH-CONFIG.md`](../docs/hook/HANDOFF-LAUNCH-CONFIG.md).

### Running a Phase 3 session

One command, and it needs a person at the keyboard — the character has to be in a world, and the
client's menus cannot be driven from outside. **The character will walk on its own** during the
steering experiments, so run it somewhere it does not matter.

```powershell
# the whole spike in one sitting: calibration sweep, then a held heading, then the nexus floor
.\\hook\tools\Run-Phase3Session.ps1 -Experiment All -Seconds 240 -RelayLog <relay.log>

# or one experiment at a time
.\\hook\tools\Run-Phase3Session.ps1 -Experiment Sweep  -Seconds 240
.\\hook\tools\Run-Phase3Session.ps1 -Experiment Hold   -Seconds 180
.\\hook\tools\Run-Phase3Session.ps1 -Experiment Escape -Seconds 120

# re-read a run that has already been played
.\\hook\tools\Run-Phase3Session.ps1 -AnalyseOnly <run-dir> -RelayLog <relay.log>
```

It writes the checks and the raw report to `hook\obj\cases\phase3-session\verdict.txt` and exits
non-zero if any check failed. **Let the run last as long as the phases need** — `sweep:240` is about
35 s of gameplay for its eight phases and `hold` 600 frames is about 10 s; a run closed early reports
"no phase summary" and proves nothing. The protocol, the escape test and what each outcome means are
in [`PHASE3-SCOPE.md`](../docs/hook/PHASE3-SCOPE.md) §5.

### Recording a trace, and running the offline solver (Spike 3.2)

The dodge's solver is a pure function of a plain-data snapshot, so it runs — and is tuned — with no
game at all. Its input is either a synthetic scenario or a recorded session.

```powershell
# 1. With no game: five scenarios, each with a known correct answer.
.\\hook\tools\SolverHarness\bin\Release\SolverHarness.exe --scenario dodge

# 2. Record a session.  The character walks under the experiment's control; -Trace only records.
.\\hook\tools\Run-Phase3Session.ps1 -Experiment Hold -Seconds 300 -Trace

# 3. Then, with the game closed, run the solver over what was played.  THIS is the only way to
#    check invariant T7 -- whether the model's predicted collisions are the ones that happened.
.\\hook\tools\SolverHarness\bin\Release\SolverHarness.exe `
    --trace <run-dir>\trace.jsonl --collisions <run-dir>\bootstrap.log
```

`--frame N` prints one frame in full — every candidate and the admission rule that refused it — and
it is the first thing to reach for when a scenario fails. `--config w=...,w=...` overrides the
weights, which is what "tune in the harness, never in a live run" means concretely.

**Check the file grew before trusting it:** `(Get-Item <run-dir>\trace.jsonl).Length` — a few hundred
bytes means the header and nothing else. `--trace` sets all three variables a recording needs (the
recorder, the managed frame replacement it is called from, and the Phase 2 sensor whose threat set is
its input), because a run missing any one of them writes a valid, empty file that is
indistinguishable from "no bullet came near". The harness now fails on an empty recording — assertion
**F** — rather than reporting every invariant vacuously held.

**The recording is expensive** — about 265 KB per 900 frames with two bullets alive — so it is off by
default. `-Trace` is the switch.
[`SPIKE3.2-OFFLINE-SOLVER.md`](../docs/hook/SPIKE3.2-OFFLINE-SOLVER.md) is the handoff: what exists, the eight
defects it took to make the solver move, and the one run still outstanding.

### Running the Phase 2 session

One command, and it needs a person at the keyboard: the sensor only has anything to read once a
character is in a zone, and the client's window renders black to every capture path tried, so its menus
cannot be driven from outside.

```powershell
.\\hook\tools\Run-Phase2Session.ps1 -Minutes 60
```

It launches the game with the sensor attached (`--frame-replacement`, `DRELAY_FRAME_SENSOR=1`), waits,
closes the game, and writes the four decision numbers and the criteria they are checked against into
`hook\obj\cases\phase2-session\verdict.txt`. `-AnalyseOnly <runDir>` re-reads a session that has
already been played. What the verdict means, and a menu-state run analysed as a worked example, are in
[`PHASE2-SCOPE.md`](../docs/hook/PHASE2-SCOPE.md) §4.13.

Running it against the game is one command; the launcher streams the hook's log live and
prints the evidence when the game exits. From an unpacked release zip in the game's folder, that
command is **just the program**, because the configuration file and auto-discovery supply the path:

```powershell
.\\hook\out\Drelay.Launcher.exe
```

or, when the game is somewhere the discovery walk does not look:

```powershell
.\\hook\out\Drelay.Launcher.exe --game "E:\SteamLibrary\steamapps\common\Darza's Dominion"
```

**One environment note.** Launching the game from the DSH agent harness fails to create its run
directory under `%LOCALAPPDATA%` — child processes from that harness are confined to the workspace —
so a harness-launched run needs `--runroot` pointing inside the repository:

```powershell
.\\hook\out\Drelay.Launcher.exe --game "E:\SteamLibrary\steamapps\common\Darza's Dominion" `
    --runroot "G:\coding\javamapp\drelay\hook\obj\live-runs"
```

From the operator's own shell the default is fine.

`--live-seconds S` (default 5) is how long the hook records after the *discovery window* closes, and
the evidence files are written when that window ends — so it *is* the run as far as the evidence is
concerned. **The frame read stays open when it closes**, because that read is the sensor the dodge
runs on; `--pause-after-run` (`DRELAY_KEEP_READING=0`) stops it, which is what every earlier release
did. The hook no longer waits for the discovery window to be useful: a target is patched about half a
second after the game first compiles it, so the dodge and auto-aim are live within a second or two of
launch. `--collect-delay` (default 0, was 30000) and `--discovery-ms` (default 10000, was 30000) still
exist, and they now bound the *reporting* — which targets this build produced while anyone was
watching — rather than the patch. The two acceptance runs that need an operator are scripts,
because both have assertions rather than just an outcome — run them from an elevated shell if the
game itself runs elevated, since a launcher at a lower integrity level cannot inject into it:

```powershell
.\\hook\tools\Run-Exit2a-LogDenial.ps1        # Exit 2a: a denied log target
.\\hook\tools\Run-Endurance.ps1 -Minutes 60   # Exit 1 / M3: the hour of play
```

**Read the `target-size` lines first.** They say, per target, whether a method of that IL
size was compiled *at all* during the run — which distinguishes "the monitored process never
ran that code" from "it ran and its IL differs from `known-build.json`". Those two have
different owners and the middle ground between them cost three rounds.

**Two findings from Phase 1 are worth reading before anything else**, because both correct something
this research previously asserted, and both are in [`PHASE1-SCOPE.md`](../docs/hook/PHASE1-SCOPE.md) §5:

- **the shared block's layout is not hand-computable.** The first attempt at `[FieldOffset]` values was
  wrong in three places at once — and the answer is not a better guess. The layout is now *generated*
  from the native header (`tools/gen_shared_layout.py`), and the generator's model is itself checked
  by a compiled probe (`native/SizeProbe.c`) that the build runs and diffs. The generator's model was
  wrong twice, and the probe is what said so both times;
- **the `getMethodDefFromMethod` slot is determined by probing candidates at runtime, not by a
  hardcoded constant.** An earlier reading held that the slot was `0x7A` and that `0x76` was
  `runWithErrorTrap` on .NET 9 — **the live run falsifies that**: against the real game slot `0x7A`
  returned token `0x00000000`, and slot **`0x76` returned the correct `0x06001FC5`**, matching the
  token Phase 0 pinned for `frameTick`. So `0x76` *is* the correct slot on this runtime, and it is the
  runtime probe — not a written-down constant — that makes relying on it safe.

The gate is the thing that makes the rest safe rather than brave: it is what turns "the hook
crashed the game after an update" into "the hook printed one line and did nothing"
([HOOK-ARCHITECTURE.md](../docs/hook/HOOK-ARCHITECTURE.md) §6).

---

## What "proactive" means here, precisely

The word does a lot of work in this project, so it is worth pinning down before anything else, because
the honest answer is narrower than it sounds.

**Reactive** is the current rule: it reads the server's `GmHealthUpdate`, which reports damage *after*
the server has applied it, and escapes. Its decision point is downstream of the damage.

**Proactive** here means exactly one thing: the decision point moves **upstream of the damage**, to the
instant the client itself resolves a hit — which is measurably one server round trip *before* the
server applies it. It does **not** mean the damage is prevented. The hook's two tools are, in order:
**move out of the way** (dodge), and **leave before it lands** (preventive escape). Both are actions
taken *before* the damage, which is what makes them proactive; neither makes damage impossible.

And the scope of the improvement is bounded by measurement, not by hope: **74 % of measured HP falls
have no client-side hit claim at all**, so for most damage there is no earlier decision point to move
to. The hook is proactive wherever the client is the first to know, and helpless wherever the server
is. [RISKS.md](../docs/hook/RISKS.md) §2b and §5 list those cases individually.

---

## The answer in one page

### The frustration was real, and the reason is now measured

The current auto-nexus reads the server's `GmHealthUpdate` and escapes when HP is low. That packet is
a **notification of damage already applied**, not a warning — so the rule can never act before the
damage, and no amount of proxy logic changes that. Measured over the recorded sessions:

| quantity | value |
|---|---|
| `GmHealthUpdate` reflecting a hit, after the client resolved that hit | **+55.5 ms median, +98.1 ms p90** |
| one-way client→server leg (inferred from RTT) | **31 ms** fast cluster / **113 ms** slow cluster |
| server tick period | **200 ms** |
| worst burst inside one 200 ms window (measured over a lookahead window) | **493 HP = 81.1 % of max, ending in death** |
| `Escape` → `EscapeAck` at the relay | **290 ms median** |

> **A correction to an earlier reading of this project.** It was previously stated that the client
> sends no damage acknowledgement, and therefore that suppression was not an option. That is **half
> wrong**: the client *does* declare projectile hits, in `GmHit`/`ProjHit` (id 102), whose `ObjectId`
> is the local player when `PlayerProj = 0` — verified on 161 of 580 captured packets. What remains
> true is that it is not a general escape hatch: **74 % of HP falls (571 of 775) have no such claim
> within 400 ms**, and there is no equivalent for AoE, beam, contact or tick damage. The earliest
> client-side knowledge is still the collision test, not the health packet, because the client's own
> per-hit path is purely presentational (`TIMING.md` §4.3).

### The hook buys time, not clairvoyance

The client decides a bullet is hitting the player in `Projectile.HitCharacter()`
(`Objects/Projectile.cs:1514`), computes the exact damage, uses it **only to draw a number**, and then
tells the server — which applies the damage *afterwards*. Nothing in the client ever writes
`Player.Health`; only `GmHealthUpdate` does. So at the instant of that collision decision, the damage
is still in the server's future.

That is the window. It is worth **≈55–98 ms** over the current rule, plus one frame, and the hook is on
the right side of it by construction rather than by tuning.

Note what the burst measurement says about the alternative. The server emits **one reading per hit,
back to back**, not one summary per tick — so a burst is visible but only as a stream of readings
inside one or two milliseconds, and the first reading of the stream is already damage being applied
(`Game_Slave#11`: 439 HP of 608 gone in eight readings spanning 2 ms, dead one reading later). A hook
cannot act earlier than the first reading either, **unless it predicts the hit**. That is the whole
argument for the collision-anchored design rather than a threshold at the reading.

### But it does not make the nexus unnecessary in general — and this is the honest part

**74 % of measured HP falls (571 of 775) have no client-side hit claim at all.** The client only
claims hits it resolves itself — and the only claim packets in the assembly are for projectiles,
sweeps and beams. **AoE and bomb damage produces no claim whatsoever** (`Entity.HitBy(AoeData)`
contains no `SendPacket`; it resolves on a timer server-side). So for AoE, bomb detonations,
damage-over-time ticks and point-blank spawns the server is the only witness, and no in-process design
sees them coming.

So "the auto-nexus would never need to be triggered" is **half right**. A hook makes the nexus
*better and rarer* — it escapes in cases the reactive rule cannot — and it enables a real dodge for the
projectiles the client does see. It does not make damage preventable in general, and anyone promising
that is not reading the measurements.

### Why this was worth doing anyway

Three measured facts make the hook decisively better than the current rule, independent of dodging:

1. the current rule **can act on stale HP** — the recorded case is an escape injected on a 1 % reading
   **151 ms after HP had already reached zero**;
2. the current rule **cannot distinguish "a hit landed" from "a hit is coming"**, so it must be tuned
   conservatively in the direction that costs runs;
3. a dodge is genuinely achievable here, and was **not** achievable through packets: the stream never
   re-broadcasts a projectile's position, so a packet-only dodge is dead reckoning with unbounded
   error. In-process, the true position is one field read away.

### Why it is tractable

Five facts, all verified against the shipped binaries:

| | |
|---|---|
| `DarzasDominion.dll` is **pure IL** — no ReadyToRun, no native code | every game method is JIT-compiled, so a JIT-level hook sees all of it |
| `System.Runtime.TieredCompilation` is **`false`** | each method is compiled **once**; a patch is permanent, and the whole tier-promotion hazard does not exist |
| the JIT's vtable is **four slots, `compileMethod` at 0, `getVersionIdentifier` at 2** | verified by disassembling the shipped `clrjit.dll` — note the community tools hardcode slot **4**, which was right for .NET Core 3.1 |
| the client **never applies damage to itself** | so the collision decision is genuinely ahead of the server's damage |
| no anti-cheat, no integrity check, no driver | a plain self-contained .NET 9 apphost |

And the two things that would normally be the hard part are avoidable:

- **No trajectory reimplementation.** `ProjDesc.GetPosition` handles straight, wavy, parametric,
  boomerang, orbiting, curving, accelerating and bouncing families. The hook **calls it** instead of
  reproducing it — which also makes prediction exactly consistent with collision by construction. The
  reference engine reached the same conclusion independently.
- **No damage reimplementation.** Every damage constant has been recovered from the decrypted constant
  pool, so it *could* be recomputed — but the hook **calls `Entity.GetDamageTaken`**, because eight
  mitigation steps read live state and being subtly wrong means escaping one hit too late.

## The plan, in five lines

| phase | question | risk | estimate |
|---|---|---|---|
| **0** | what are we targeting, and can we prove it has not changed? | very low | 1–2 days |
| **1** | can native code get into this process, early, and survive? | **high** | 3–5 days |
| **2** | can we observe the truth, and does our model match it? | medium | 1–2 weeks |
| **3** | **can we move the player out of the way — and escape only when we cannot?** | **highest** | 3–6 weeks |
| **4** | does the relay see the hook, and is that useful? | low | 3–5 days |

**The dodge and the escape are one phase, and the escape is its floor** (merged 2026-10-13). The
client's `World.RequestEscape()` is reached at exactly one point in the decision — when the projected
damage over the horizon is lethal **and no admissible move avoids it** — so the deliverable is a dodge
that never needs the nexus where dodging is possible, rather than a predictive nexus that still ends
the run. The relay bridge, formerly phase 5, is now phase 4 and is additive to both.

**Phase 3 carries the whole risk.** Its risk is not the algorithm; it is whether the server accepts
hook-steered movement, which is the one question in this design with no precedent in the reference
engine and no measurement in the captures. That question is answered by a spike that uses **no dodge
logic at all**, and it can be probed **from the existing proxy, with no hook at all** — see
[RISKS.md](../docs/hook/RISKS.md) §2a.

**Phase 2 was the decision point, and it has been taken: the project proceeds to Phase 3.** Its four
numbers — how much warning prediction gives, the false-negative and false-positive rates, and the
per-frame cost — are what license the build. Had they been bad, the honest move would have been to
stop there and publish the measurement; with the escape folded in as a floor there is no longer a
consolation deliverable at that point, which is why the numbers were worth reading before Phase 3
starts.

---

## Four things worth knowing before starting

**1. The most valuable artefact is not the dodge.** It is the Phase 2 log that compares every predicted
collision against every collision the game actually made. A dodge's quality cannot be established by
unit tests — the reference engine's own audit says *"live gameplay remains unverified"* for much of its
newest code — but the *model's* correctness can be, and that log is the only thing that can tell us
whether the prediction is right. Build it before the solver.

**2. There is a verified interaction hazard waiting, scoped to challenge runs.**
`World.RequestEscape()`'s **channelled** branch cancels on movement:

```csharp
// World.cs:13043-13047
if (GameScene.GameInput.Moving) { CancelEscapeCast(); return; }
```

A dodge that steers **cancels an in-progress nexus cast in the same frame**. Precedence must be
designed before the dodge is enabled live, not patched after. **Scope it correctly, though:** that
branch is reached only with the `Impermanence` totem — ordinary escape is instant and is never
cancelled by movement. An earlier draft of this research stated that as a general hazard; it is not,
and the correction is recorded in [CLIENT-FINDINGS.md](../docs/hook/CLIENT-FINDINGS.md) §5.3. The practical
consequence is that a test suite which never equips the totem will pass while the real bug sits
untouched.

**3. Three things are deliberately out of scope, and one of them constrains the design.** AoE and bomb
damage is left to the player; point-blank spawns are treated as a positioning problem rather than a
reaction problem (and are mostly avoidable); and there is **no melee or contact damage** at all, which
removes a row rather than adding one.

The AoE decision is the one that costs something, because it makes **intent preservation a
requirement rather than a preference**: if the dodge fights the direction the player is steering, it
has taken away the tool they need for the channel it does not cover. The mechanism that keeps the
trade safe is a single rule — **an AoE volume may affect a candidate's score, but it must never remove
a candidate** ([DODGE-ALGORITHM.md](../docs/hook/DODGE-ALGORITHM.md) §5.7, [VERIFICATION.md](../docs/hook/VERIFICATION.md) §3
invariant I11).

**4. The reference repo was worth reading, but almost none of it should be copied.**
[Evergreen-Techworks/realm-engine-client](https://github.com/Evergreen-Techworks/realm-engine-client)
is a mature dodge engine for a different game, and what transfers is its **reasoning**, not its
numbers: a two-strike projectile retirement policy, fixed-step trajectory sampling, anchoring on the
live position every frame, freezing past the end of a trace rather than extrapolating, the
time-parametrised polyline as the sensor/solver interface, safety as a hard constraint with preference
as a score over the safe set, and degrade-the-candidate-set-never-the-tests under budget pressure.

What must **not** be copied: its time constants (calibrated to a 5 Hz server), its hit geometry (a
per-axis square, where our client's test is verified to be `DistanceSquared < r²` on circles), its
player half-extent (its player is a point; ours has a real radius the game adds for us), and its entire
IL2CPP offset layer. [DODGE-ALGORITHM.md](../docs/hook/DODGE-ALGORITHM.md) §12 has the full list, both directions.
