`hook/managed/Drelay.Bootstrap/EscapeTest.cs`:

```cs
// EscapeTest.cs -- Phase 3's floor, made enterable before it is needed.
//
// =====================================================================================
// WHY THIS EXISTS, AND WHY IT IS NOT PART OF THE DODGE
// =====================================================================================
//
// Phase 3's deliverable is a dodge, and the client's own `World.RequestEscape()` is its
// **floor**: the one thing reached when the projected damage over the horizon is lethal and
// no admissible move avoids it (`DODGE-ALGORITHM.md` section 7). A floor that has never
// been stood on is not a floor, and the 2026-10-13 live run is the receipt:
//
//     [ERROR]   escape       MISSING  never compiled in the discovery window.
//     [INFO ] target-size escape IL size 335: 6 same-size method(s) compiled,
//             none of them this target
//
// The reason is now known and is not a defect in the pinned identity: **nothing called it**.
// The operator never pressed the nexus key and no zone change called it either, so
// `RequestEscape` was simply never JITted -- and a target that is never compiled is a target
// the detour never sees, which the size table reports as the two-case middle ground it is
// (`docs/HOOK-BUILD-MATRIX.md`).
//
// So the question this file answers is narrower than the dodge's and comes before it:
// **can the hook make the client escape at all?** That is one call with no decision logic
// behind it -- no threat set, no solver, no snapshot -- and it is worth answering on its own
// because everything about the floor depends on it:
//
//   * the plan says the call is "indistinguishable from the player pressing the nexus key",
//     which is an argument from the source (it runs the client's own gates and sends the
//     client's own packet) and has never been *measured*;
//   * `MANAGED-ENTRY-HANDOFF.md` section 6 notes that the managed-entry question was left
//     open for exactly this call, and section 0.2 answers it for replacements -- this is the
//     first time that answer is used to reach a method the game itself has not called;
//   * the escalation's own gates are the client's, so an operator who has never seen
//     `GmEscape` leave the machine while the hook asked for it cannot tell a working floor
//     from a refused one.
//
// It does **not** replace Deliverable 3.4. Deliverable 3.4 is the decision -- project the
// undodgeable damage, call `Entity.GetDamageTaken`, and escape only when no admissible move
// avoids it. This is the actuator underneath that decision, tested alone, on purpose: if the
// call cannot be made, nothing about gate 6 matters.
//
// =====================================================================================
// WHAT IT DOES, EXACTLY, AND WHAT IT REFUSES TO DO
// =====================================================================================
//
// `--escape-test SECONDS` (launcher) -> `DRELAY_ESCAPE_TEST_SEC` -> this class. Once the
// world exists, it waits `SECONDS` and then calls `World.RequestEscape()` **once**. The
// delay is what keeps the test out of the way of the run it rides on: it is measured from
// the first frame with a live `World`, so it does not depend on how long the operator took
// to get into a zone.
//
// Five things are deliberate and each one is a way this could have been a bad tool:
//
//   1. **it fires once.** A repeating call would be a nexus key held down: in the ordinary
//      path that is a `GmEscape` every cooldown, and with the `Impermanence` totem it is a
//      cast that re-arms for ever. One call, then a latched flag, and the reason is logged.
//   2. **it does not require a world to be non-safe.** `RequestEscape` is a legitimate
//      no-op in a safe area -- the plan says so and `VERIFICATION.md` section 5.1 makes the
//      safe-area variant a case the two-controller test has to exercise. Firing there is
//      therefore *information*, not a mistake, and the log says which branch was taken.
//   3. **it never decides anything.** It reads no health, no threat, no damage. Its whole
//      input is "has the world existed for N seconds".
//   4. **it is off unless asked for.** No environment variable, no call, no behaviour: the
//      frame replacement publishes and calls through exactly as it does today.
//   5. **a failure is named, not swallowed.** The frame replacement's outer catch would
//      otherwise turn "the reflection call threw" into "the test never fired", which is the
//      same absent-evidence shape PHASE2-SCOPE.md section 4.12 and 4.15 both record.
//
// The call goes through reflection rather than a cached `MethodInfo` delegate, which is the
// one place this is not the cheapest thing available. It happens **once per run**, so the
// cost is irrelevant, and the reflection form means the hook fails at the call rather than
// at resolve if the method is not invocable -- the failure lands where the log line is.

using System;
using System.Globalization;
using System.Reflection;

namespace Drelay.Bootstrap
{
    public static class EscapeTest
    {
        private static bool _resolved;
        private static bool _enabled;
        private static string _statusLine = "not attempted";
        private static string _unresolvedReason = "not attempted";

        private static FieldInfo _worldSharedField;
        private static Func<object> _getWorld;
        private static MethodInfo _requestEscape;

        /// <summary>Seconds to wait after the world first exists. Zero means "the next frame".</summary>
        private static double _delaySeconds;

        private static bool _armed;
        private static bool _fired;
        private static bool _firedLogged;
        private static long _armedTicks;
        private static long _framesWaited;
        private static double _elapsedAtCallMs;
        private static int _failureLogged;

        public static bool Resolved => _resolved;
        public static bool Enabled => _enabled;
        public static bool Fired => _fired;
        public static string UnresolvedReason => _unresolvedReason;
        public static string Status() => _statusLine;

        /// <summary>
        /// Resolve the world handle and the method, and read the switch.
        ///
        /// Called from the same resolve callback the rest of the hook uses, so the failure
        /// path is uniform: return false with a reason, and the caller logs it and carries
        /// on. Nothing here is fatal to anything else.
        /// </summary>
        public static bool Resolve(Assembly game)
        {
            try
            {
                string raw = (Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("DRELAY_ESCAPE_TEST_SEC") ?? "").Trim();
                _enabled = raw.Length > 0;
                if (!_enabled)
                {
                    _statusLine = "the escape test is IDLE (DRELAY_ESCAPE_TEST_SEC unset); "
                                  + "RequestEscape is never called";
                    _resolved = true;
                    return true;
                }

                if (!double.TryParse(raw, NumberStyles.Float, CultureInfo.InvariantCulture,
                                     out _delaySeconds) || _delaySeconds < 0.0)
                {
                    _unresolvedReason = "DRELAY_ESCAPE_TEST_SEC is not a non-negative number of "
                                        + "seconds: '" + raw + "'";
                    _enabled = false;
                    _statusLine = "the escape test is NOT armed: " + _unresolvedReason;
                    _resolved = true;
                    return false;
                }

                Type worldType = game.GetType(ManagedArmingProbe.WorldTypeName);
                if (worldType == null)
                {
                    _unresolvedReason = "type " + ManagedArmingProbe.WorldTypeName + " not found";
                    _statusLine = "the escape test is NOT available: " + _unresolvedReason;
                    return false;
                }

                _worldSharedField = worldType.GetField("Shared",
                    BindingFlags.Public | BindingFlags.NonPublic | BindingFlags.Static);
                if (_worldSharedField == null)
                {
                    _unresolvedReason = "World.Shared not found";
                    _statusLine = "the escape test is NOT available: " + _unresolvedReason;
                    return false;
                }

                // THE ONE TARGET THE HOOK DOES NOT NEED THE GAME TO COMPILE.  `RequestEscape`
                // is a target in `known-build.json` because it is worth patching, but this
                // call does not depend on the patch at all: it needs a `MethodInfo`, and a
                // method the JIT has never looked at has one. That is the whole reason the
                // floor can be tested on a run where the target is reported MISSING.
                _requestEscape = worldType.GetMethod("RequestEscape",
                    BindingFlags.Public | BindingFlags.NonPublic | BindingFlags.Instance,
                    null, Type.EmptyTypes, null);
                if (_requestEscape == null)
                {
                    _unresolvedReason = "World.RequestEscape() was not found on this build";
                    _statusLine = "the escape test is NOT available: " + _unresolvedReason;
                    return false;
                }
                if (_requestEscape.ReturnType != typeof(void) || _requestEscape.IsStatic)
                {
                    _unresolvedReason = "World.RequestEscape is not a void instance method "
                                        + "(returns " + _requestEscape.ReturnType.Name
                                        + (_requestEscape.IsStatic ? ", static" : ", instance") + ")";
                    _statusLine = "the escape test is NOT available: " + _unresolvedReason;
                    return false;
                }

                _getWorld = FieldAccessor.Static(_worldSharedField);
                _resolved = true;
                _statusLine = string.Format(CultureInfo.InvariantCulture,
                    "the escape test is ARMED: World.RequestEscape() will be called ONCE, "
                    + "{0:0.###} s after the world first exists", _delaySeconds);
                return true;
            }
            catch (Exception ex)
            {
                _unresolvedReason = ex.GetType().Name + ": " + ex.Message;
                _statusLine = "the escape test is NOT available: " + _unresolvedReason;
                return false;
            }
        }

        /// <summary>Prints the plan once, at resolve time, like the pilot's does.</summary>
        public static void LogPlan()
        {
            HookEntry.AppendLog("INFO", Status());
            HookEntry.FlushLog();
        }

        /// <summary>
        /// One frame's worth. Called from the frame replacement, after the sensor, and
        /// **outside** the sensor's own switch: this is an actuator test, not a read, and
        /// gating it behind `DRELAY_FRAME_SENSOR` would mean the escape test could only be
        /// run by paying for the read path as well.
        /// </summary>
        public static void OnFrame()
        {
            if (!_resolved || !_enabled || _fired)
            {
                return;
            }

            try
            {
                object world = _getWorld();
                if (world == null)
                {
                    return;   // no world yet: the clock has not started
                }

                if (!_armed)
                {
                    _armed = true;
                    _armedTicks = Environment.TickCount64;
                    HookEntry.AppendLog("INFO", string.Format(CultureInfo.InvariantCulture,
                        "escape test armed: the world exists; calling World.RequestEscape() once "
                        + "in {0:0.###} s", _delaySeconds));
                    HookEntry.FlushLog();
                }

                _framesWaited++;
                double elapsedMs = Environment.TickCount64 - _armedTicks;
                if (elapsedMs < _delaySeconds * 1000.0)
                {
                    return;
                }

                _elapsedAtCallMs = elapsedMs;
                Invoke(world);
            }
            catch (Exception ex)
            {
                if (System.Threading.Interlocked.Exchange(ref _failureLogged, 1) == 0)
                {
                    HookEntry.AppendLog("ERROR", "the escape test threw; the game is unaffected "
                                                 + "and the frame update continues untouched: "
                                                 + ex.GetType().Name + ": " + ex.Message);
                    HookEntry.FlushLog();
                }
            }
        }

        /// <summary>
        /// `World.RequestEscape()`, once, with the outcome written down either way.
        ///
        /// THE LOG LINE BEFORE THE CALL IS THE IMPORTANT ONE. If the call itself is what kills
        /// the process -- which is the shape a wrong managed-entry assumption takes -- then a
        /// log written only afterwards leaves no evidence that the call was reached, and the
        /// run reads as "the test never armed". Two lines, then the verdict line: a reader can
        /// tell "reached it", "it returned" and "it threw" apart without a debugger.
        /// </summary>
        private static void Invoke(object world)
        {
            _fired = true;   // latched BEFORE the call, so a throw cannot re-arm it

            if (!_firedLogged)
            {
                _firedLogged = true;
                HookEntry.AppendLog("INFO", string.Format(CultureInfo.InvariantCulture,
                    "escape test: calling World.RequestEscape() now (world for {0:0} ms, "
                    + "{1} frame(s)) -- this line precedes the call so that a fault inside it "
                    + "still leaves the attempt on record",
                    _elapsedAtCallMs, _framesWaited));
                HookEntry.FlushLog();
            }

            try
            {
                _requestEscape.Invoke(world, null);
                HookEntry.AppendLog("INFO", string.Format(CultureInfo.InvariantCulture,
                    "escape test: World.RequestEscape() RETURNED after {0:0} ms. The client's own "
                    + "gates ran; whether it sent GmEscape, started an Impermanence cast or did "
                    + "nothing is a wire fact -- read the relay log for id 0x56 (GmEscape) or "
                    + "the escape-cast-state pair", _elapsedAtCallMs));
                HookEntry.FlushLog();
            }
            catch (TargetInvocationException tie)
            {
                // The game's own method threw. Reported with the inner exception, because the
                // wrapper is an artefact of calling through reflection and says nothing.
                HookEntry.AppendLog("ERROR", "escape test: World.RequestEscape() THREW "
                                             + (tie.InnerException != null
                                                ? tie.InnerException.GetType().Name + ": "
                                                  + tie.InnerException.Message
                                                : tie.Message)
                                             + " -- the call was made and the client refused it, "
                                             + "which is a different result from never reaching it");
                HookEntry.FlushLog();
            }
        }
    }
}

```

`hook/managed/Drelay.Bootstrap/FieldAccessor.cs`:

```cs
// FieldAccessor.cs -- read a field of a type the hook cannot name, without boxing it.
//
// THE PROBLEM THIS SOLVES IS MEASURED, NOT ASSUMED.  `FieldInfo.GetValue` returns `object`,
// so reading a `float` or a `GamePoint` through it BOXES: a twenty-bullet frame with six
// fields each allocates about a hundred and twenty small objects, and the collections they
// trigger land in the frame's tail.  The Phase 2 session analyser measured exactly that --
// the read path's p99 sat inside the 150 microsecond frame-tick slice while the sampler's
// sat in the 150-300 bucket -- and the named cause was this boxing (PHASE2-SCOPE.md
// sections 4.7 and 4.11).
//
// WHY A DELEGATE RATHER THAN AN OFFSET.  A measured offset plus an unsafe pointer read is
// the smaller thing on paper, and it is the wrong tool here for two reasons.  The field
// layouts are CoreCLR's to choose -- HOOK-ARCHITECTURE.md section 5.5 says so, and says
// offsets must be measured rather than derived -- so an offset is a number that has to be
// re-measured for every type, on every run, and a wrong one is a wild read rather than an
// exception.  A delegate emitted once from the `FieldInfo` the resolver already found has
// neither problem: the JIT computes the offset from the field token, exactly as it would
// for a hand-written `obj.field`, and the read is a plain `ldfld` with no allocation and
// no pointer arithmetic of ours.
//
// The delegate is built once, on the resolve callback, and the frame path calls it.

using System;
using System.Reflection;
using System.Reflection.Emit;

namespace Drelay.Bootstrap
{
    public static class FieldAccessor
    {
        /// <summary>`float Get(object)` for a `float` field, with no boxing.</summary>
        public static Func<object, float> Float(FieldInfo field)
        {
            DynamicMethod method = NewMethod(typeof(float), field.Name, typeof(object));
            ILGenerator il = method.GetILGenerator();
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ldarg_0);
            EmitReceiver(il, field.DeclaringType);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ldfld, field);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ret);
            return (Func<object, float>)method.CreateDelegate(typeof(Func<object, float>));
        }

        /// <summary>`int Get(object)` for an `int` field, with no boxing.</summary>
        public static Func<object, int> Int(FieldInfo field)
        {
            DynamicMethod method = NewMethod(typeof(int), field.Name, typeof(object));
            ILGenerator il = method.GetILGenerator();
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ldarg_0);
            EmitReceiver(il, field.DeclaringType);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ldfld, field);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ret);
            return (Func<object, int>)method.CreateDelegate(typeof(Func<object, int>));
        }

        /// <summary>`double Get(object)` for a `double` field, with no boxing.</summary>
        public static Func<object, double> Double(FieldInfo field)
        {
            DynamicMethod method = NewMethod(typeof(double), field.Name, typeof(object));
            ILGenerator il = method.GetILGenerator();
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ldarg_0);
            EmitReceiver(il, field.DeclaringType);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ldfld, field);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ret);
            return (Func<object, double>)method.CreateDelegate(typeof(Func<object, double>));
        }

        /// <summary>
        /// `bool Get(object)` for a `bool` field, with no boxing.
        ///
        /// THE `float` ONE ABOVE WAS NOT ENOUGH, AND ITS ABSENCE WAS FOUND THE EXPENSIVE
        /// WAY. `World.PlayerDead` and `Character.SpiritMode` are `bool`, and a caller
        /// that had only the numeric accessors reached for `FieldInfo.GetValue` instead --
        /// which boxes on every read, on the frame path, for the exact reason this file
        /// exists. The frame guard reads two of them per frame.
        /// </summary>
        public static Func<object, bool> Bool(FieldInfo field)
        {
            DynamicMethod method = NewMethod(typeof(bool), field.Name, typeof(object));
            ILGenerator il = method.GetILGenerator();
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ldarg_0);
            EmitReceiver(il, field.DeclaringType);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ldfld, field);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ret);
            return (Func<object, bool>)method.CreateDelegate(typeof(Func<object, bool>));
        }

        /// <summary>
        /// `float Get()` for a `static float` field -- `World.WorldRotation`, which is
        /// `public static` (`World.cs:4212`) and is the camera's own rotation.
        ///
        /// Deliberately takes no argument, unlike every other accessor here: the field is
        /// static, so the caller has no object to pass and inventing a dummy parameter
        /// would let a caller pass the wrong one and still compile. The call sites wrap it
        /// with the object-shaped lambda they need, which makes the static-ness visible at
        /// the call site rather than hidden in a signature.
        /// </summary>
        public static Func<float> StaticFloat(FieldInfo field)
        {
            DynamicMethod method = NewMethod(typeof(float), field.Name);
            ILGenerator il = method.GetILGenerator();
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ldsfld, field);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ret);
            return (Func<float>)method.CreateDelegate(typeof(Func<float>));
        }

        /// <summary>`void Set(object, bool)` for a `bool` field, with no boxing.</summary>
        public static Action<object, bool> BoolSetter(FieldInfo field)
        {
            DynamicMethod method = NewSetter(typeof(bool), field.Name, typeof(object));
            ILGenerator il = method.GetILGenerator();
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ldarg_0);
            EmitReceiver(il, field.DeclaringType);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ldarg_1);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Stfld, field);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ret);
            return (Action<object, bool>)method.CreateDelegate(typeof(Action<object, bool>));
        }

        /// <summary>
        /// `void Set(object, float)` for a `float` field, with no boxing.
        ///
        /// THE WRITE PATH IS WHERE THE PILOT LIVES. Phase 3's actuator is three of these
        /// per frame (the movement integrator's input), and `FieldInfo.SetValue` would box
        /// a `float` and build an `object[]` for each; on the game's own frame thread that
        /// is an allocation per frame per field, which is the cost PHASE2-SCOPE.md
        /// section 4.6 measured the hard way.
        ///
        /// This setter is also what makes the actuator possible for a *value type* field:
        /// `MoveAngle` is an inline `Angle` struct, and the receiver here is the boxed
        /// `Angle` itself, so `castclass` unboxes in place and `stfld` writes straight into
        /// it. No copy, no constructor call, no `GamePoint`.
        /// </summary>
        public static Action<object, float> FloatSetter(FieldInfo field)
        {
            DynamicMethod method = NewSetter(typeof(float), field.Name, typeof(object));
            ILGenerator il = method.GetILGenerator();
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ldarg_0);
            EmitReceiver(il, field.DeclaringType);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ldarg_1);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Stfld, field);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ret);
            return (Action<object, float>)method.CreateDelegate(typeof(Action<object, float>));
        }

        /// <summary>`object Get(object)` for a reference field.</summary>
        public static Func<object, object> Reference(FieldInfo field)
        {
            DynamicMethod method = NewMethod(typeof(object), field.Name, typeof(object));
            ILGenerator il = method.GetILGenerator();
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ldarg_0);
            EmitReceiver(il, field.DeclaringType);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ldfld, field);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ret);
            return (Func<object, object>)method.CreateDelegate(typeof(Func<object, object>));
        }

        /// <summary>`object Get()` for a static reference field -- `World.Shared`, `DarzaWindow.Time`.</summary>
        public static Func<object> Static(FieldInfo field)
        {
            DynamicMethod method = NewMethod(typeof(object), field.Name);
            ILGenerator il = method.GetILGenerator();
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ldsfld, field);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ret);
            return (Func<object>)method.CreateDelegate(typeof(Func<object>));
        }

        /// <summary>
        /// `float Get(object)` for a `float` inside an inline value-type field -- the shape
        /// that matters most here, because a position is a `Vector3` (or a `GamePoint`) and
        /// reading the struct to get at it is what boxes.
        /// </summary>
        public static Func<object, float> NestedFloat(FieldInfo outer, FieldInfo inner)
        {
            DynamicMethod method = NewMethod(typeof(float), outer.Name + "." + inner.Name,
                                             typeof(object));
            ILGenerator il = method.GetILGenerator();
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ldarg_0);
            EmitReceiver(il, outer.DeclaringType);
            // ldflda gives the address of the inline struct inside the object, and the
            // second ldfld reads straight out of it -- no struct copy and no box.
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ldflda, outer);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ldfld, inner);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ret);
            return (Func<object, float>)method.CreateDelegate(typeof(Func<object, float>));
        }

        /// <summary>
        /// `void Set(object, float)` for a `float` inside an inline value-type field -- the write
        /// counterpart of <see cref="NestedFloat"/>, and Phase 3's actuator's actual instruction.
        ///
        /// WHY THIS HAD TO EXIST, AND WHAT ITS ABSENCE COST. `FloatSetter(field)` compiles
        /// `castclass field.DeclaringType; stfld field` -- so its receiver is an instance of the
        /// field's *declaring* type. `GameInput.MoveAngle` is an `Angle` **struct**, so
        /// `FloatSetter(Angle.Radians)` writes into a boxed `Angle` and nothing else: it cannot
        /// reach the `MoveAngle` inside a `GameInput`. The first live steering run is the receipt.
        /// The pilot wrote the angle "successfully", every frame, into its own private box, while
        /// the input the client reads kept the client's own value -- and the log shows both halves
        /// side by side:
        ///
        ///     steer frame 31 phase 1 cmd 0.0deg wrote 0.0000rad read-back 4.7124rad ...
        ///
        /// 4.7124 rad is 270 degrees: the player walked due south at 0.133 units a frame for both
        /// phases, whatever the commanded angle, and the sweep could not tell the two writes apart
        /// because the *read-back* used the nested accessor and the *write* did not.
        /// `ldflda` gives the address of the inline struct inside the receiver and `stfld` writes
        /// through it, which is the only way to set a field of a value-type field.
        /// </summary>
        public static Action<object, float> NestedFloatSetter(FieldInfo outer, FieldInfo inner)
        {
            DynamicMethod method = NewSetter(typeof(float), outer.Name + "." + inner.Name, typeof(object));
            ILGenerator il = method.GetILGenerator();
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ldarg_0);
            EmitReceiver(il, outer.DeclaringType);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ldflda, outer);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ldarg_1);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Stfld, inner);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ret);
            return (Action<object, float>)method.CreateDelegate(typeof(Action<object, float>));
        }

        /// <summary>
        /// `byte Get(byte[,] array, int x, int y)` for the client's collision grid, emitted
        /// because the reflective route allocates once per cell.
        ///
        /// WHY THIS EXISTS AT ALL, AND WHY IT IS NOT `Array.GetValue`. `World`'s walkability map
        /// is a genuine two-dimensional `byte[,]` (`CLIENT-FINDINGS.md` section 5.4), and the
        /// obvious way to read one is `((byte[,])array)[x, y]` -- which a hook that cannot name
        /// the array cannot write, so the reflective equivalent is `Array.GetValue(x, y)`.
        /// `GetValue` returns `object`, and it therefore **boxes every cell it reads**: a grid
        /// window is 2 401 cells, the recorder re-reads it whenever the player changes tile, and
        /// this project has already paid once for exactly that mistake in the sensor's path
        /// (PHASE2-SCOPE.md sections 4.7 and 4.11).
        ///
        /// MULTIDIMENSIONAL ARRAYS ARE A DIFFERENT IL THAN ONE-DIMENSIONAL ONES, and that is why
        /// this is not `ldelem.u1`. The runtime lays out a `byte[x, y]` with a `Get(int, int)`
        /// method on the array's own type, so the emitted body is literally `call instance uint8
        /// uint8[0..., 0...]::Get(int32, int32)` -- the same call the game's own `CollisionMap`
        /// makes (see the IL dump, `World::'hehe...'`), which means the hook and the client cannot
        /// disagree about which cell a coordinate names.
        ///
        /// The bounds check is explicit and throws `IndexOutOfRangeException`, exactly as the
        /// CLR's own accessor would. Callers that expect an out-of-map coordinate to be
        /// answerable must check the bounds first -- `World`'s own query does, and so does the
        /// recorder.
        /// </summary>
        public static Func<object, int, int, byte> ByteArray2D(Type arrayType)
        {
            if (arrayType == null || !arrayType.IsArray || arrayType.GetArrayRank() != 2
                || arrayType.GetElementType() != typeof(byte))
            {
                throw new ArgumentException("ByteArray2D needs a byte[,]; got "
                                            + (arrayType == null ? "null" : arrayType.ToString()));
            }

            System.Reflection.MethodInfo get = arrayType.GetMethod("Get",
                new[] { typeof(int), typeof(int) });
            if (get == null)
            {
                throw new MissingMethodException(arrayType.ToString(), "Get(int,int)");
            }
            System.Reflection.MethodInfo getLength = typeof(Array).GetMethod("GetLength",
                new[] { typeof(int) });

            DynamicMethod method = new DynamicMethod(
                "DrelayGrid2D",
                typeof(byte),
                new[] { typeof(object), typeof(int), typeof(int) },
                typeof(FieldAccessor).Module,
                skipVisibility: true);

            ILGenerator il = method.GetILGenerator();
            Label inBounds = il.DefineLabel();

            // x >= 0 && x < GetLength(0) && y >= 0 && y < GetLength(1)
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ldarg_1);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ldc_I4_0);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Blt, inBounds);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ldarg_1);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ldarg_0);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Castclass, arrayType);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ldc_I4_0);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Callvirt, getLength);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Bge, inBounds);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ldarg_2);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ldc_I4_0);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Blt, inBounds);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ldarg_2);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ldarg_0);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Castclass, arrayType);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ldc_I4_1);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Callvirt, getLength);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Bge, inBounds);

            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ldarg_0);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Castclass, arrayType);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ldarg_1);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ldarg_2);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Callvirt, get);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ret);

            // Out of bounds: the same answer the game's own query gives for a coordinate outside
            // the map, which is "not a wall". Returning 0 rather than throwing is deliberate:
            // this is called from the frame path of a live game, and the caller cannot see the
            // map's dimensions to check them itself.
            il.MarkLabel(inBounds);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ldc_I4_0);
            il.Emit(OpCodes.Ret);

            return (Func<object, int, int, byte>)method.CreateDelegate(typeof(Func<object, int, int, byte>));
        }

        /// <summary>
        /// Put the receiver on the stack in the form the field instruction needs.
        ///
        /// `castclass` IS INVALID IL WHEN THE DECLARING TYPE IS A VALUE TYPE, AND THIS IS NOT A
        /// TECHNICALITY -- IT IS THE DEFECT THAT STOPPED THE GAME STARTING ON EVERY RUN.
        ///
        /// Every accessor here used to emit `castclass field.DeclaringType` and then the field
        /// instruction. That is correct for the reference types the sensor reads (`GameObject`,
        /// `Projectile`, `Node`, `Player`, `GameInput`, ...) and *wrong* for a struct: the IL
        /// specification has no `castclass` to a value type, the C# compiler never emits one
        /// (it emits `unbox.any`), and RyuJIT's handling of it is not a rejected cast but
        /// undefined behaviour. Measured, in a standalone reproduction of this exact IL on this
        /// runtime, one process per case:
        ///
        ///     castclass Angle; ldarg.1; stfld Radians   -> Fatal error. Internal CLR error. (0x80131506)
        ///     castclass Angle; ldfld Radians            -> a garbage float, no exception
        ///     unbox Angle;     ldarg.1; stfld Radians   -> 0.25, correct
        ///     unbox Angle;     ldfld Radians            -> 0.25, correct
        ///
        /// Phase 3's actuator is the first code in this project to touch a *value-typed* receiver
        /// -- `GameInput.MoveAngle` is `DarzaCore.Geometry.Angle`, a `sealed` value type -- so it
        /// was the first to hit it, and it hit it as an access violation at
        /// `System.Private.CoreLib!CastHelpers.ChkCastClassSpecial`, which no `catch` can hold:
        ///
        ///     Fatal error. System.AccessViolationException: ...
        ///        at System.Runtime.CompilerServices.CastHelpers.ChkCastClassSpecial(Void*, System.Object)
        ///        at DynamicClass.DrelayField_MoveAngle.Radians(System.Object)
        ///        at Drelay.Bootstrap.SteeringPilot.Warm()
        ///
        /// `unbox` is the instruction that means "the receiver is a boxed value of this type, give
        /// me the interior pointer", which is exactly what a `stfld` into a box, an `ldfld` out of
        /// one, and the `ldflda` a nested read starts with all need. The type check is the same
        /// one `castclass` performs and it fails the same way -- a catchable
        /// `InvalidCastException` -- which the reproduction confirms: `NestedFloat`'s class-typed
        /// cast on a boxed struct throws, as it always did, while the value-type case above no
        /// longer faults.
        ///
        /// A reference type keeps `castclass`, so nothing that works today changes behaviour.
        /// </summary>
        private static void EmitReceiver(ILGenerator il, Type declaringType)
        {
            il.Emit(declaringType.IsValueType ? OpCodes.Unbox : OpCodes.Castclass, declaringType);
        }

        private static DynamicMethod NewMethod(Type returnType, string what, params Type[] parameters)
        {
            // skipVisibility, because the fields this reads are private on the game's own
            // types -- `Projectile._angleSin` and `_startTime` are both private, and a
            // getter emitted without it would throw at invoke time rather than at build.
            return new DynamicMethod("DrelayField_" + what,
                                     returnType, parameters,
                                     typeof(FieldAccessor).Module,
                                     skipVisibility: true);
        }

        /// <summary>
        /// The setter counterpart. `void`-returning and with a `void` first parameter slot,
        /// so the two helpers cannot be confused by a caller that reached for the wrong
        /// one: a getter has no second parameter and this one has no return.
        /// </summary>
        private static DynamicMethod NewSetter(Type valueType, string what, Type ownerType)
        {
            return new DynamicMethod("DrelaySet_" + what,
                                     typeof(void), new[] { ownerType, valueType },
                                     typeof(FieldAccessor).Module,
                                     skipVisibility: true);
        }
    }
}
```

`hook/managed/Drelay.Bootstrap/FieldLookup.cs`:

```cs
// FieldLookup.cs -- find a field by any of several names, up the type hierarchy.
//
// WHY NAMES NEED A LIST.
//
// The hook cannot reference the game at compile time, so every field it reads is found by
// name -- and a name is a guess until it is checked against the shipped build.  Two things
// make one name not enough:
//
//   * the synthetic host and the real client spell things differently (`AgeMs` versus
//     `_startTime`, `Sin` versus `_angleSin`), and the same hook has to work against both,
//     because the host is how the sensor is tested;
//   * `Type.GetField` walks base classes for PUBLIC instance fields but not for private
//     ones, and the fields a projectile carries are spread across three types --
//     `Projectile`, `GameObject` and `Nodes.Node`.  `GameId` and `Radius` are declared on
//     `GameObject`, `Position` on `Node`, `_startTime` and `_angleSin` privately on
//     `Projectile`, and a lookup that only asks `Projectile` finds two of the six.
//
// That second point cost this project a wrong finding: a search restricted to the
// `Projectile` class concluded there was "no `GameId` field anywhere in the assembly",
// which was written into PHASE2-SCOPE.md section 4.9 before a search of the base classes
// found `GameObject.GameId` four thousand lines earlier.  A hierarchy walk is not
// defensive; it is the difference between an answer and a guess.
//
// WHICH NAME WAS FOUND IS RETURNED, NOT JUST THE FIELD.  The evidence has to say what the
// hook resolved, because "the field is missing" and "the field has a different name than
// the one this build looks for" are different problems with different owners, and only the
// name tells them apart.

using System;
using System.Reflection;

namespace Drelay.Bootstrap
{
    public static class FieldLookup
    {
        private const BindingFlags Any = BindingFlags.Public | BindingFlags.NonPublic
                                       | BindingFlags.Instance | BindingFlags.Static;

        /// <summary>
        /// The first of <paramref name="candidates"/> that exists on <paramref name="type"/>
        /// or any base type below <see cref="object"/>.
        /// </summary>
        public static FieldInfo Find(Type type, out string foundName, params string[] candidates)
        {
            foundName = null;
            if (type == null || candidates == null)
            {
                return null;
            }

            for (Type current = type; current != null && current != typeof(object); current = current.BaseType)
            {
                for (int i = 0; i < candidates.Length; i++)
                {
                    // DeclaredOnly, because the walk already visits every level: without it
                    // the same inherited field would be reported as declared by the derived
                    // type, and the log would name the wrong owner.
                    FieldInfo field = current.GetField(candidates[i], Any | BindingFlags.DeclaredOnly);
                    if (field != null)
                    {
                        foundName = current.Name + "." + candidates[i];
                        return field;
                    }
                }
            }
            return null;
        }

        /// <summary>Convenience for a single name, keeping the call sites readable.</summary>
        public static FieldInfo Find(Type type, out string foundName, string name)
        {
            return Find(type, out foundName, new[] { name });
        }

        /// <summary>Where the type sits in its own hierarchy, for the evidence.</summary>
        public static string Hierarchy(Type type)
        {
            string text = "";
            for (Type current = type; current != null && current != typeof(object); current = current.BaseType)
            {
                text = text.Length == 0 ? current.Name : text + " : " + current.Name;
            }
            return text.Length == 0 ? "(none)" : text;
        }
    }
}
```

```cs
        public const int Off_managedAimReplacement = 178824;
        public const int Off_managedAimTrampoline = 178832;
        public const int Off_reserved = 178840;
    }
}

```

`hook/managed/Drelay.Bootstrap/PathPlanner.cs`:

```cs
// PathPlanner.cs -- Spike 3.2, HANDOFF-DIRECTED-DODGE.md section 4: an opinion about the future.
//
// =====================================================================================
// WHY THIS FILE EXISTS
// =====================================================================================
//
// Measured in HANDOFF-DIRECTED-DODGE.md section 3, on `tools/dodge_direction_report.py`: the dodge
// OUTRUNS on 40-50 % of its own moves, and on three of the five recordings outrunning is the single
// most common thing it does. The design reason is stated there in one sentence and it is worth
// repeating where the consequence lives:
//
//     "Every candidate is one step, scored in isolation ... Nothing in the candidate set can
//      express 'this step is bad because of the step after it'."
//
// The score has one term about direction (`GoalProgress`, which rewards moving along the player's
// own line) and the safety terms are all about this frame. So on a frame where the player is walking
// away from the shooter, "away from the shooter" and "along my own line" are the same direction, and
// the biggest step wins. There is no way for a single step to know that the step after it is worse.
//
// THIS FILE IS THE MISSING OPINION, AND IT IS DELIBERATELY NOT A CANDIDATE. The actuator takes one
// heading and one magnitude per frame; the path never reaches the input. What it produces is a
// WAYPOINT -- a point the character would like to be walking toward once this step is over -- and the
// solver scores each already-admissible candidate by its alignment with that waypoint. The admission
// rules are untouched, so `HANDOFF-DIRECTED-DODGE.md` section 5.3's doctrine holds unchanged: a
// preference term can only rank options that already passed the safety boundary.
//
// =====================================================================================
// THE FOUR DECISIONS INSIDE THIS FILE, AND THE ALTERNATIVE EACH ONE REJECTED
// =====================================================================================
//
//   1. THE SEARCH RUNS ON THE CLIENT'S OWN GRID, one world unit per cell, through
//      `CollisionWindow` -- which is the same `byte[,]` rule 2 already tests against, windowed and
//      read by the same truncating `(int)world - Origin` conversion the game itself uses. There is
//      no second collision model here and there must never be one: a pathfinder that disagrees with
//      the client about where a wall is would steer the player into it, and the disagreement would
//      only be visible as a death.
//
//   2. COST IS DISTANCE PLUS DANGER, AND THE DANGER IS IN SPACETIME. This is the part that makes it
//      a DODGE path rather than a nav route, and it is the same one-clock model `PlanWalk` uses: the
//      player is at cell `c` at time `t`, where `t` is how long the path took to get there at the
//      player's own speed, and the question asked of every projectile is where ITS BODY IS AT THAT
//      INSTANT. A cell is not "dangerous"; a cell is dangerous for a player who arrives at time `t`.
//      That is what lets a path thread a volley instead of treating the bullet's whole remaining
//      trajectory as a static wall.
//
//   3. THE TARGET IS A CELL ON THE GOAL RAY, NOT A DESTINATION. The goal is the player's held
//      direction (section 13), and a ray has no cell to search to. The target is the cell the
//      character would reach by walking along that ray for `PathTargetSeconds`, and a target that is
//      behind a wall or inside a projectile is a legitimate and important case: the search then
//      routes around the obstacle toward it, which is the behaviour this whole file exists to make
//      possible. When the target is not reachable at all, the answer is `NoPath` and the solver falls
//      back to the goal term it had before -- a pathfinder that can produce no answer must not be
//      able to produce no move.
//
//   4. THE WAYPOINT IS THE FIRST NODE MORE THAN ONE STEP AWAY, HELD BY ITS OWN HYSTERESIS. A path
//      recomputed every frame changes its mind every frame, and a dodge that follows it changes its
//      mind with it; section 10.4 and section 13.2 are both recorded lessons about smoothing an
//      angle. The hold is dropped the moment the waypoint is no longer on the path -- the same
//      discipline `Hysteresis` applies to a heading, and for the same reason.
//
// =====================================================================================
// WHAT THIS FILE MAY TOUCH, WHICH IS NOT A STYLE RULE
// =====================================================================================
//
// `DodgeSnapshot.cs` may name no game type, and neither may this. Everything here is a float, an int,
// a bool or an array of them, and the file is compiled into `Drelay.Bootstrap` AND into
// `tools/SolverHarness` through the same `Compile Include` mechanism as the solver's other two
// sources -- so a change that reaches for a game type breaks the offline build immediately, which is
// exactly when you want to find out.
//
// AND IT ALLOCATES NOTHING ON THE FRAME PATH. Every buffer below is a field sized once, at
// construction, for the largest grid the class is willing to search; a `List<Node>` per frame is the
// one thing this project has measured repeatedly and refused.

using System;
using System.Globalization;

namespace Drelay.Bootstrap
{
    /// <summary>Why the planner produced no waypoint. A closed set, so a log can be counted.</summary>
    public enum PathReason
    {
        /// <summary>A waypoint was produced.</summary>
        Found = 0,

        /// <summary>The pathfinder is switched off in this configuration.</summary>
        Disabled = 1,

        /// <summary>The frame carries no collision grid -- the honest degradation. See `CollisionWindow.Present`.</summary>
        NoGrid = 2,

        /// <summary>The grid is larger than the planner's fixed buffers. Refused, never truncated silently.</summary>
        GridTooLarge = 3,

        /// <summary>No goal direction was measured this frame, so there is no ray to aim at.</summary>
        NoGoal = 4,

        /// <summary>The target cell itself is a wall or lies outside the grid window.</summary>
        NoTarget = 5,

        /// <summary>The search expanded its node cap without reaching the target.</summary>
        NodeCap = 6,

        /// <summary>The search completed and the target is genuinely unreachable behind walls.</summary>
        Unreachable = 7,

        /// <summary>The player's own cell is a wall -- pinned against scenery, which is a real state and not an error.</summary>
        StartBlocked = 8,
    }

    /// <summary>
    /// The planner's own numbers, for the harness's report and for the `--decisions` columns.
    ///
    /// THE REASON A PATHFINDER NEEDS THIS IS NOT TIDINESS. `HANDOFF-DIRECTED-DODGE.md` section 6:
    /// "A pathfinder that is silently absent prints as 'the outrun ratio did not move', which is the
    /// same output as a pathfinder that ran and did nothing." Every field here is a column in the
    /// decision dump, so "the path was never found" and "the path was found and had no effect" are
    /// two different lines in one file.
    /// </summary>
    public sealed class PathStats
    {
        /// <summary>Searches run since the last <see cref="PathPlanner.ResetCounters"/>.</summary>
        public long Searches;

        /// <summary>Searches that hit the node cap. See <see cref="PathReason.NodeCap"/>.</summary>
        public long NodeCapHits;

        /// <summary>Frames on which no waypoint was produced, for any reason.</summary>
        public long NoPath;

        /// <summary>Frames on which the waypoint came from the previous frame's hold rather than a fresh path.</summary>
        public long Held;

        /// <summary>
        /// CORNER CUTS THE SEARCH PRODUCED: path steps whose two cells are both walkable but whose
        /// diagonal crosses a solid pair. Must be 0 on every frame of every scenario and recording.
        ///
        /// WHY THIS IS A COUNTER AND NOT A TEST. The diagonal rule -- a diagonal step is allowed only
        /// when both orthogonal neighbours are walkable -- is the one part of this file that can put a
        /// path THROUGH a wall, and the consequence would be a dodge that steers confidently into
        /// scenery. The scenario suite has walls (`corridor`: 165 solid cells) and its paths are 24.7
        /// units against `dodge`'s 12, which is *consistent* with going round -- but a longer path is
        /// inference, and this project's own rule is that a number which cannot be read off a file is
        /// not evidence. The check is cheap enough to run on every search rather than in a unit test
        /// nothing calls: one walk of a path that is at most a few dozen nodes, once per frame.
        /// </summary>
        public long WallCrossings;

        /// <summary>Searches since the last <see cref="PathPlanner.ResetCounters"/> in which a path was found.</summary>
        public long PathsFound;

        /// <summary>Sum of `Nodes` over every path found, for the mean.</summary>
        public long NodesTotal;

        /// <summary>Sum of `Length` over every path found, for the mean.</summary>
        public double LengthTotal;

        /// <summary>Total microseconds spent inside <see cref="PathPlanner.Plan"/>.</summary>
        public double MicrosecondsTotal;

        /// <summary>Why the most recent failure happened. Counted separately because one reason is not the others.</summary>
        public long NoGridFrames;
        public long DisabledFrames;
        public long UnreachableFrames;
        public long NoGoalFrames;
    }

    /// <summary>
    /// A bounded A* over the client's collision grid, with a spacetime danger cost, producing one
    /// waypoint per frame. See this file's header for the design and for what each decision rejected.
    /// </summary>
    public sealed class PathPlanner
    {
        /// <summary>
        /// The largest window the fixed buffers will search, per axis.
        ///
        /// IT IS A BUFFER SIZE AND NOT A MAP SIZE. The snapshot's window is what it is
        /// (`CollisionWindow`), and a window larger than this is REFUSED with
        /// <see cref="PathReason.GridTooLarge"/> rather than searched partially: a search that
        /// silently ignored the far half of its own grid would be a path that steers confidently into
        /// a region it never looked at.
        /// </summary>
        public const int MaxGridWidth = 192;
        public const int MaxGridHeight = 192;

        /// <summary>8-connected neighbourhood, orthogonals first so the cheaper step is tried first.</summary>
        private static readonly int[] DirX = { 1, -1, 0, 0, 1, 1, -1, -1 };
        private static readonly int[] DirY = { 0, 0, 1, -1, 1, -1, 1, -1 };

        private DodgeConfig _config;

        // --- The grid, as this frame sees it, cached per frame ---------------------------------
        private CollisionWindow _grid;
        private int _gridW;
        private int _gridH;
        private int _cells;
        private float _playerX;
        private float _playerY;
        private float _speedPerSecond;
        private bool _targetSet;
        private int _targetIndex;

        // --- The per-threat danger envelope, resolved once per frame ---------------------------
        //
        // ONE TIGHT RADIUS PER THREAT, WHICH IS THE WHOLE COST OPTIMISATION HERE. The honest question
        // is "how close does this threat's body come to this cell, at the time the player would be
        // there", and answering it by walking 21 samples of all 48 threats for every expanded node
        // would be a hundred thousand distance tests a frame. Two facts make that unnecessary: a
        // bullet's body is within `collisionRadius` of its own path, and its path is sampled at 30 ms
        // -- so a sample whose position is further than `radius + pad + half a sample step` from a
        // cell cannot make that cell dangerous, at any time. `_threatNear` is that bound, per threat,
        // computed once; the per-node test is then a subtraction and a compare.
        private Trajectory[] _threats = new Trajectory[0];
        private int _threatCount;
        private float[] _threatNear = new float[0];
        private float[] _threatRadius = new float[0];
        private float[] _threatStepMs = new float[0];
        private int[] _threatSamples = new int[0];

        // --- The search buffers, sized once -----------------------------------------------------
        private float[] _gScore = new float[0];
        private float[] _costScore = new float[0];
        private int[] _cameFrom = new int[0];
        private bool[] _closed = new bool[0];
        private bool[] _inOpen = new bool[0];
        private int[] _heap = new int[0];
        private float[] _heapKey = new float[0];
        private int _heapCount;

        // --- The result --------------------------------------------------------------------------
        private int[] _pathIndex = new int[0];
        private int _pathCount;

        private float _waypointX;
        private float _waypointY;
        private float _waypointHeading;
        private bool _waypointValid;

        private float _heldX;
        private float _heldY;
        private bool _holdValid;
        private float _heldTakenMs;

        private PathReason _reason = PathReason.Disabled;
        private int _nodes;
        private float _length;
        private float _cost;
        private bool _fresh;
        private bool _fieldReady;
        private readonly PathStats _stats = new PathStats();

        public PathPlanner(DodgeConfig config)
        {
            _config = config;
            EnsureCapacity(MaxGridWidth, MaxGridHeight);
        }

        /// <summary>
        /// Replaces the configuration. The hook re-reads it when the world changes, so the planner
        /// must search the new world's numbers on the frame the map does.
        /// </summary>
        public void Configure(DodgeConfig config)
        {
            _config = config;
        }

        /// <summary>
        /// True when the last <see cref="Plan"/> left a danger field that a reader may use.
        ///
        /// IT IS NOT "THE PATH EXISTS" AND THE DIFFERENCE MATTERS. A path can fail for reasons that
        /// have nothing to do with the danger field -- an unreachable target, a blocked start -- while
        /// the field is perfectly well built, and a caller asking "is there danger in front of me"
        /// must not be told no because the route to a goal behind a wall could not be found. It is
        /// true when the frame had a grid and at least one threat to put in the envelope.
        /// </summary>
        public bool FieldReady => _fieldReady;

        /// <summary>
        /// The half-width of the patch a projected-danger probe reads around a future position.
        ///
        /// IT IS THE COLLISION DISC AND NOT A TUNING FUDGE. The danger field is non-zero only within
        /// `player radius + bullet radius + pad` of a bullet's body, so a probe read at a single point
        /// asks "is a bullet exactly here", which is the wrong question and answered no everywhere. At
        /// this radius the nine reads of a 3x3 patch ask "is a bullet near here", which is the
        /// question that decides whether a step leads somewhere better.
        ///
        /// It is built from the last frame's envelope -- the pad and the player's own radius -- so it
        /// tracks the game's own geometry rather than a constant, and it falls back to the configured
        /// pad alone when no envelope exists.
        /// </summary>
        public float ProbeRadius
        {
            // The FIRST threat's tight radius stands for the frame's, which is honest here: the tight
            // radius is `player.Radius + threat.Radius + pad`, and the threat radius varies by a
            // couple of tenths across a session's bullets while the player's half is constant. Taking
            // one number per frame keeps the probe the same size for every candidate of that frame,
            // which is what makes the term comparable across the ring.
            get { return _threatCount > 0 ? _threatNear[0] : 0.5f; }
        }

        /// <summary>The planner's counters. Read by the harness; reset by <see cref="ResetCounters"/>.</summary>
        public PathStats Stats => _stats;

        /// <summary>True when the last <see cref="Plan"/> produced a usable waypoint.</summary>
        public bool WaypointValid => _waypointValid;

        /// <summary>The waypoint's world position, valid when <see cref="WaypointValid"/>.</summary>
        public float WaypointX => _waypointX;
        public float WaypointY => _waypointY;

        /// <summary>The world heading from the player toward the waypoint, radians.</summary>
        public float WaypointHeading => _waypointHeading;

        /// <summary>Path nodes the last search expanded.</summary>
        public int Nodes => _nodes;

        /// <summary>Path length in world units, as the search found it.</summary>
        public float Length => _length;

        /// <summary>Total edge cost including danger, in the same units as length when danger is zero.</summary>
        public float Cost => _cost;

        /// <summary>Why the last search produced no path, or <see cref="PathReason.Found"/>.</summary>
        public PathReason Reason => _reason;

        /// <summary>True when the last waypoint came from the hold rather than from this frame's path.</summary>
        public bool Held => _waypointValid && !_fresh;

        /// <summary>
        /// The danger field's own value at a point and time, for the harness's `--frame N` dump.
        ///
        /// IT IS PUBLIC BECAUSE THE FIELD NEEDS AN INSTRUMENT AND NOT BECAUSE IT NEEDS AN API. The
        /// first version of this planner produced a path whose cost equalled its length on 90 % of
        /// frames and did not change at a danger weight of 20 -- which is a field that returns zero,
        /// and one that is either broken or honestly empty. `pathcost`/`pathlen` cannot tell those
        /// apart; one probe can, and this is it. It reads the envelope built by the last `Plan`, so it
        /// is meaningful only immediately after one.
        /// </summary>
        public float DebugDangerAt(float x, float y, float seconds)
        {
            return DangerAt(x, y, seconds);
        }

        /// <summary>
        /// The danger field's value at a point and time, in `[0,1]`, for the SOLVER as well as the
        /// instrument.
        ///
        /// THE FIELD IS THE PLANNER'S MOST USEFUL EXPORT AND THE PATH IS ONLY ITS FIRST CUSTOMER.
        /// `SPIKE3.2-OFFLINE-SOLVER.md` section 15.5 measured why the first version was only a partial
        /// fix: the retreat is paid for by `resolve` and `clearance`, which are both right about one
        /// step, and a waypoint is a DIRECTION -- so a preference built on it cannot say "this step is
        /// bad because of the step after it", which is the sentence the whole task starts from.
        ///
        /// This answers that sentence directly for any point and any time, so
        /// `DodgeSolver.ProjectedDanger` can ask it about where a candidate LEADS. It is the same
        /// one-clock question `PlanWalk` asks, from the same samples and the same envelope, so a
        /// candidate scored this way is scored on the model's own geometry and not on a second one.
        ///
        /// It reads the envelope built by the last `Plan`, so it is meaningful only after one; with no
        /// threats, no grid or the planner disabled it returns 0 and costs a loop over an empty array.
        /// </summary>
        public float Danger(float x, float y, float seconds)
        {
            return DangerAt(x, y, seconds);
        }

        /// <summary>
        /// One threat's own numbers, as the danger field sees them, for the harness's frame dump.
        /// This is the same probe as <see cref="DebugDangerAt"/> one level down: it reports what the
        /// early-out compared, not what it concluded.
        /// </summary>
        public string DebugThreat(int i)
        {
            if (i < 0 || i >= _threatCount)
            {
                return "none";
            }
            Trajectory t = _threats[i];
            if (t == null || t.Count <= 0)
            {
                return "empty";
            }
            return "radius=" + _threatRadius[i].ToString("0.###", CultureInfo.InvariantCulture)
                 + " near=" + _threatNear[i].ToString("0.###", CultureInfo.InvariantCulture)
                 + " samples=" + _threatSamples[i]
                 + " stepMs=" + _threatStepMs[i].ToString("0.###", CultureInfo.InvariantCulture)
                 + " count=" + t.Count
                 + " first=(" + t.Xs[0].ToString("0.##", CultureInfo.InvariantCulture) + ","
                 + t.Ys[0].ToString("0.##", CultureInfo.InvariantCulture) + ")";
        }

        /// <summary>Threats in the last frame's danger envelope. See <see cref="DebugDangerAt"/>.</summary>
        public int DebugThreatCount => _threatCount;

        /// <summary>The tight radius used for threat <paramref name="i"/>. See <see cref="DebugDangerAt"/>.</summary>
        public float DebugThreatNear(int i)
        {
            return i >= 0 && i < _threatCount ? _threatNear[i] : 0.0f;
        }

        /// <summary>Drops the held waypoint and the counters. A zone change, or a disabled dodge.</summary>
        public void Reset()
        {
            _holdValid = false;
            _waypointValid = false;
            _reason = PathReason.Disabled;
            ResetCounters();
        }

        /// <summary>Zeroes the report counters without touching the held waypoint.</summary>
        public void ResetCounters()
        {
            _stats.Searches = 0;
            _stats.NodeCapHits = 0;
            _stats.NoPath = 0;
            _stats.Held = 0;
            _stats.WallCrossings = 0;
            _stats.PathsFound = 0;
            _stats.NodesTotal = 0;
            _stats.LengthTotal = 0.0;
            _stats.MicrosecondsTotal = 0.0;
            _stats.NoGridFrames = 0;
            _stats.DisabledFrames = 0;
            _stats.UnreachableFrames = 0;
            _stats.NoGoalFrames = 0;
        }

        private void EnsureCapacity(int width, int height)
        {
            int cells = width * height;
            if (_gScore.Length < cells)
            {
                _gScore = new float[cells];
                _costScore = new float[cells];
                _cameFrom = new int[cells];
                _closed = new bool[cells];
                _inOpen = new bool[cells];
            }
            int heapCap = cells + 8;
            if (_heap.Length < heapCap)
            {
                _heap = new int[heapCap];
                _heapKey = new float[heapCap];
            }
            if (_pathIndex.Length < cells)
            {
                _pathIndex = new int[cells];
            }
        }

        // ===================================================================================
        // The per-frame entry
        // ===================================================================================

        /// <summary>
        /// One frame: build the danger envelope, search from the player's cell to a cell on the goal
        /// ray, and reduce the path to a single waypoint.
        ///
        /// IT IS CALLED ONCE PER FRAME, NOT ONCE PER CANDIDATE. 77 candidates times an A* each is not
        /// a thing the frame budget survives; `HANDOFF-DIRECTED-DODGE.md` section 4.1 states the
        /// budget as "under 50 us, because the sampler and the sensor share the 300".
        /// </summary>
        /// <param name="snapshot">The frame. Its grid, threats and player are read; nothing is written.</param>
        /// <param name="goalRadians">The world heading of the forward goal, already resolved by the solver.</param>
        /// <param name="goalValid">Whether that heading is a measurement rather than a default.</param>
        /// <param name="stepRadius">
        /// One full step, `budget`. The waypoint is the first path node beyond it, so the steer cannot
        /// jitter between the current cell and the next.
        /// </param>
        /// <param name="budget">The player's own coverage this frame, world units.</param>
        /// <param name="playerRadius">The player's collision radius, already defaulted.</param>
        public void Plan(DodgeSnapshot snapshot, float goalRadians, bool goalValid,
                         float stepRadius, float budget, float playerRadius)
        {
            long startTicks = System.Diagnostics.Stopwatch.GetTimestamp();

            _nodes = 0;
            _fieldReady = false;
            _length = 0.0f;
            _cost = 0.0f;
            _fresh = false;
            _waypointValid = false;

            if (!_config.PathEnable)
            {
                Fail(PathReason.Disabled, snapshot);
                _stats.Searches++;
                _stats.DisabledFrames++;
                _stats.MicrosecondsTotal += Elapsed(startTicks);
                return;
            }

            if (!goalValid)
            {
                Fail(PathReason.NoGoal, snapshot);
                _stats.Searches++;
                _stats.NoGoalFrames++;
                _stats.MicrosecondsTotal += Elapsed(startTicks);
                return;
            }

            // --- The grid, and the frame's danger envelope. ---------------------------------
            if (!BeginFrame(snapshot, goalRadians, budget, playerRadius))
            {
                Fail(_reason, snapshot);
                _stats.Searches++;
                _stats.MicrosecondsTotal += Elapsed(startTicks);
                return;
            }

            _stats.Searches++;

            int startIndex = IndexOf(_playerX, _playerY);
            if (startIndex < 0 || !WalkableIndex(startIndex))
            {
                // THE PLAYER'S OWN CELL IS A WALL. This happens for real -- pinned against scenery is
                // the state three of Spike 3.1's eight phases ended in -- and the honest answer is not
                // to search from the nearest walkable cell, which would be a path that starts
                // somewhere the player is not. No path, and the goal term decides as before.
                Fail(PathReason.StartBlocked, snapshot);
                _stats.NoPath++;
                _stats.MicrosecondsTotal += Elapsed(startTicks);
                return;
            }

            if (!Search(startIndex, _targetIndex))
            {
                Fail(_reason, snapshot);
                _stats.NoPath++;
                if (_reason == PathReason.NodeCap)
                {
                    _stats.NodeCapHits++;
                }
                else if (_reason == PathReason.Unreachable)
                {
                    _stats.UnreachableFrames++;
                }
                _stats.MicrosecondsTotal += Elapsed(startTicks);
                return;
            }

            _stats.PathsFound++;
            _stats.NodesTotal += _nodes;
            _stats.LengthTotal += _length;

            // --- The waypoint, and its hysteresis. ------------------------------------------
            //
            // THE WAYPOINT IS A POINT ALONG THE PATH, AND WHERE ALONG IT IS THE WHOLE DESIGN
            // QUESTION. Two earlier answers were wrong in the same way, and both measurements are
            // worth keeping because the second one is a geometric fact rather than a bug:
            //
            //   "The first node beyond one step" (the handoff's section 4.3) measured nothing. A path
            //   node is one world unit wide and a step is `budget`, about 0.14 units, so the waypoint
            //   was the first cell centre and its direction was the grid's own rounding: it alternated
            //   sides of the goal on adjacent frames (`p26156` frame 26 `wp 60`, frame 27 `wp -60`,
            //   goal -135 on both).
            //
            //   "A fixed distance along the path" fixed the noise and changed nothing else, and the
            //   reason is the shape of the answer: **a path that detours only at its far end still
            //   points at the goal for its whole first half.** Every node up to the obstacle carries
            //   the goal direction, so a waypoint near the player is the goal term wearing a
            //   pathfinder's name -- which is exactly what the danger measurement showed: cost minus
            //   length 0 on 90 % of frames, and `|wp - goal|` 0.3 degrees at the median.
            //
            // So the waypoint is a point a FRACTION of the way along the path, where the route has
            // had the distance to commit to its detour: `PathWaypointFraction` of the path's length,
            // never less than `PathWaypointUnits`. The first node beyond that distance is the
            // waypoint, and a path shorter than that is its own far end.
            int waypointNode = -1;
            float waypointReach = _length * _config.PathWaypointFraction;
            if (waypointReach < _config.PathWaypointUnits)
            {
                waypointReach = _config.PathWaypointUnits;
            }
            if (waypointReach <= 0.0f)
            {
                waypointReach = stepRadius;
            }
            float waypointDist2 = waypointReach * waypointReach;
            for (int i = 0; i < _pathCount; i++)
            {
                float wx = WorldX(_pathIndex[i]);
                float wy = WorldY(_pathIndex[i]);
                float dx = wx - _playerX;
                float dy = wy - _playerY;
                if ((dx * dx) + (dy * dy) >= waypointDist2)
                {
                    waypointNode = i;
                    break;
                }
            }
            if (waypointNode < 0 && _pathCount > 0)
            {
                waypointNode = _pathCount - 1;   // a path shorter than the waypoint distance: its far end is the direction
            }
            if (waypointNode < 0)
            {
                Fail(PathReason.Unreachable, snapshot);
                _stats.NoPath++;
                _stats.MicrosecondsTotal += Elapsed(startTicks);
                return;
            }

            float newX = WorldX(_pathIndex[waypointNode]);
            float newY = WorldY(_pathIndex[waypointNode]);

            _fresh = true;
            if (_holdValid && OnPath(_heldX, _heldY) && WithinDwell(snapshot))
            {
                // THE HELD WAYPOINT IS STILL A NODE OF THIS FRAME'S PATH, so the world did not change
                // its mind about it and neither does the dodge. The hold is not "ignore the new path":
                // the new path has been computed and it still contains the old answer, which is the
                // strongest form of agreement available.
                _waypointX = _heldX;
                _waypointY = _heldY;
                _fresh = false;
                _stats.Held++;
            }
            else
            {
                _waypointX = newX;
                _waypointY = newY;
                _heldX = newX;
                _heldY = newY;
                _holdValid = true;
                _heldTakenMs = snapshot.ClockMs;
            }

            float hx = _waypointX - _playerX;
            float hy = _waypointY - _playerY;
            if ((hx * hx) + (hy * hy) < 1e-6f)
            {
                Fail(PathReason.Unreachable, snapshot);
                _stats.NoPath++;
                _stats.MicrosecondsTotal += Elapsed(startTicks);
                return;
            }
            _waypointHeading = (float)Math.Atan2(hy, hx);
            _waypointValid = true;
            _reason = PathReason.Found;
            _stats.MicrosecondsTotal += Elapsed(startTicks);
        }

        private bool WithinDwell(DodgeSnapshot snapshot)
        {
            float dwellMs = _config.PathHysteresisDwellSeconds * 1000.0f;
            return snapshot.ClockMs - _heldTakenMs < dwellMs;
        }

        /// <summary>True when the held waypoint is one of this frame's path nodes, within half a cell.</summary>
        private bool OnPath(float x, float y)
        {
            for (int i = 0; i < _pathCount; i++)
            {
                float dx = WorldX(_pathIndex[i]) - x;
                float dy = WorldY(_pathIndex[i]) - y;
                if ((dx * dx) + (dy * dy) <= 0.25f)
                {
                    return true;
                }
            }
            return false;
        }

        private void Fail(PathReason reason, DodgeSnapshot snapshot)
        {
            _reason = reason;
            _waypointValid = false;
            if (reason != PathReason.Found && reason != PathReason.Disabled && reason != PathReason.NoGoal
                && reason != PathReason.NoGrid && reason != PathReason.GridTooLarge)
            {
                // The hold is dropped on every failure that could have had a path. A hold that
                // survives a frame with no path is a direction from a world that no longer exists --
                // the same reasoning the adapter uses when it clears a pending command every frame.
                _holdValid = false;
            }
            if (reason == PathReason.NoGrid && snapshot != null && !snapshot.Grid.Present)
            {
                _stats.NoGridFrames++;
            }
        }

        // ===================================================================================
        // The frame's own quantities
        // ===================================================================================

        /// <summary>
        /// Resolves the grid, the player, the target cell and the per-threat danger envelope. False when
        /// the frame cannot be searched; <see cref="_reason"/> says which of the ways it cannot.
        /// </summary>
        private bool BeginFrame(DodgeSnapshot snapshot, float goalRadians, float budget, float playerRadius)
        {


            CollisionWindow grid = snapshot.Grid;
            if (!grid.Present || grid.Cells == null || grid.Width <= 0 || grid.Height <= 0)
            {
                _reason = PathReason.NoGrid;
                return false;
            }
            if (grid.Width > MaxGridWidth || grid.Height > MaxGridHeight)
            {
                _reason = PathReason.GridTooLarge;
                return false;
            }

            EnsureCapacity(grid.Width, grid.Height);
            _grid = grid;
            _gridW = grid.Width;
            _gridH = grid.Height;
            _cells = _gridW * _gridH;


            _playerX = snapshot.Player.X;
            _playerY = snapshot.Player.Y;
            _speedPerSecond = snapshot.Player.SpeedPerSecond;
            if (_speedPerSecond <= 0.0f)
            {
                _speedPerSecond = budget > 0.0f && snapshot.FrameSeconds > 0.0f
                    ? budget / snapshot.FrameSeconds
                    : 1.0f;
            }

            // --- The target: one cell on the goal ray, at a fixed travel time. ----------------
            float reach = _speedPerSecond * _config.PathTargetSeconds;
            float tx = _playerX + (reach * (float)Math.Cos(goalRadians));
            float ty = _playerY + (reach * (float)Math.Sin(goalRadians));

            // AND IT IS PULLED INSIDE THE WINDOW BEFORE IT IS INDEXED. A goal ray that leaves the
            // recorded window is the normal case, not an error: the window is ~128 units across and a
            // 1.5 s lookahead at 8.2 units/s is 12.3 units, but the player is not always at the
            // centre of play. Clamping keeps the search inside the region the client's grid actually
            // covers, which is the only region this planner is entitled to have an opinion about.
            if (!_grid.InWindow(tx, ty))
            {
                tx = Clamp(tx, _grid.OriginX + 1.0f, _grid.OriginX + _gridW - 2.0f);
                ty = Clamp(ty, _grid.OriginY + 1.0f, _grid.OriginY + _gridH - 2.0f);
            }

            _targetIndex = IndexOf(tx, ty);
            _targetSet = _targetIndex >= 0 && WalkableIndex(_targetIndex);
            if (!_targetSet)
            {
                _reason = PathReason.NoTarget;
                return false;
            }

            BuildDangerEnvelope(snapshot, playerRadius);
            // THE FIELD IS READY EVEN WHEN THE PATH IS NOT. See `FieldReady`: a frame with threats in
            // it has a danger field whether or not a route to the goal could be found, and the
            // projected-danger term is a question about the field.
            _fieldReady = _threatCount > 0;
            return true;
        }

        private static float Clamp(float v, float lo, float hi)
        {
            if (v < lo) { return lo; }
            if (v > hi) { return hi; }
            return v;
        }

        /// <summary>
        /// One tight radius per threat, and the per-threat numbers the danger test needs.
        ///
        /// THIS IS NOT AN OPTIMISATION OF THE ANSWER, IT IS THE ANSWER. See the comment on the fields:
        /// a bullet's body is within its collision radius of its own sampled path, so a cell further
        /// than that from every sample cannot be hit by it whenever the player arrives. Everything
        /// inside that bound is tested exactly, by interpolation, below.
        /// </summary>
        private void BuildDangerEnvelope(DodgeSnapshot snapshot, float playerRadius)
        {
            int n = snapshot.Threats.Count;
            if (_threats.Length < n)
            {
                _threats = new Trajectory[n < 8 ? 8 : n];
                _threatNear = new float[n < 8 ? 8 : n];
                _threatRadius = new float[n < 8 ? 8 : n];
                _threatStepMs = new float[n < 8 ? 8 : n];
                _threatSamples = new int[n < 8 ? 8 : n];
            }
            _threatCount = 0;
            for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
            {
                Trajectory t = snapshot.Threats[i];
                if (t == null || t.Count <= 0)
                {
                    continue;
                }
                float step = t.StepMs > 0.0f ? t.StepMs : 30.0f;
                // HALF A SAMPLE STEP IS THE OTHER HALF OF THE BOUND. The path between two knots is
                // covered by the segment test below, but a cell that is off the path by less than the
                // distance the bullet covers between knots can still be crossed between samples.
                float near = playerRadius + t.Radius + _config.PathDangerPadUnits + (0.5f * step * 0.001f * SpeedOf(t, step));
                _threats[_threatCount] = t;
                _threatNear[_threatCount] = near;
                _threatRadius[_threatCount] = playerRadius + t.Radius;
```
